Re: Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing, Docket No. FTC-2026-1057

I submit this as an individual consumer. I am not affiliated with any company that does personalized pricing, and no one is paying me to file this.

I am not defending the conduct in the Commission's examples. Charging more for a hotel room because data suggests someone is traveling to a funeral, or more for milk because a household has children, or more for a security camera because someone was recently robbed, is predatory. I would support the Commission going after all of it, hard.

My concern is that this Proposed Statement will not accomplish that, and may make things worse for consumers like me. I have six objections.

1. Disclosure legitimizes the practice instead of stopping it.

The remedy proposed is that companies disclose personalized pricing rather than stop it. Applied to the Commission's own examples, that produces an absurd result: a hotel posting "this price is higher because our data indicates you are traveling for a funeral" would apparently comply. Footnote 20 admits the Commission has not decided whether that conduct is unfair even when disclosed. The document describes conduct that outrages people, then offers a remedy that permits it with a notice attached. I do not want a disclosure. I want the practice prohibited where it is clearly exploitative.

2. The disclosure will not inform me, because none of them do.

I have never read a cookie banner or a privacy policy, and neither has anyone I know. The Commission proposes that companies disclose "the basis for that personalization and the types of data on which the personalization is based" at the moment a price is shown. In practice that is a dense paragraph I will click past like every other notice, and the company will have met its obligation. That is a compliance checkbox, not consumer protection.

3. What I actually want is an opt-out, and it is not in here.

The Commission says the purpose of disclosure is to let consumers "take steps to avoid the higher prices." But the Proposed Statement never requires companies to offer any way to do that. Telling me my price is personalized while giving me no way to turn it off leaves me exactly where I started. I would ask the Commission to require a simple, working opt-out to a standard non-personalized price. That one requirement would do more for consumers than every disclosure in this document combined.

4. The undefined scope threatens discounts I actually use.

Nowhere does the Commission define "personalized pricing." The operative phrase is prices that "vary based on their personal data." That covers my grocery loyalty card, emailed coupons, and app-only prices. Those save me money. If businesses cannot tell which practices are covered, the safe response is to stop personalizing altogether, and the first thing to disappear will be the discounts, not the surcharges. Please state explicitly that loyalty and membership pricing, coupons, promotional codes, and randomized price testing are outside the scope.

5. The Commission has not established what consumers actually expect.

The deception theory rests on the claim that consumers reasonably expect prices not to vary by person. I do not hold that expectation, having shopped at stores where the shelf tag openly displays a member price and a non-member price. The research cited measures whether people think personalized pricing is fair, which is a different question from whether they expected it. The Commission should test the premise by asking consumers before building enforcement on it.

6. The Commission admits it does not know the effects.

The Proposed Statement says the extent of personalized pricing "is not well understood" and its effects "are unclear," and cites research calling the welfare effects "ambiguous and thus a matter of empirical measurement." I take the Commission at its word, and that is my point. That describes something needing study, not a basis for announcing that conduct is likely unlawful.

What I am asking for:

- Prohibit outright the use of data indicating vulnerability, illness, bereavement, disability, or emergency to raise prices. Do not make it disclosable. Make it illegal.
- Require a functioning opt-out to a standard price, not just a notice.
- Define personalized pricing, and exclude loyalty pricing, coupons, and promotional discounts so consumers do not lose them.
- Conduct a 6(b) study and real consumer-perception research before enforcing.
- Resolve the question left open in footnote 20 before this takes effect.

I appreciate the Commission taking this issue up. I am asking it to write the narrow, strong rule instead of the broad, weak one.

Respectfully submitted,

Jesse Shettleroe

The excuse that this lets budget travelers “pay only for what they use” doesn’t hold up when basic things like a carry-on or a assigned seat have quietly become “extras.” Airlines aren’t offering optional luxuries — they’re carving mandatory costs out of the base fare and calling it choice. Meanwhile the psychological trick is well known in the industry: once someone’s 10 minutes into a booking flow, they rarely walk away over a $40 surprise fee, even if they would’ve picked a different airline had they seen the real price upfront.

This isn’t free-market pricing flexibility. It’s a deliberate strategy to win the click with a fake low number and extract the real price after the customer is already committed. Full transparency — one price, all fees included, before checkout — is the bare minimum standard other industries are held to. Airlines fighting that tooth and nail tells you exactly whose interest they’re protecting.

Subject: Complaint Regarding Airline Fee Practices and Declining Passenger Comfort/Value

To the U.S. Department of Transportation, Office of Aviation Consumer Protection:

I am writing to file a formal complaint regarding the current practices of U.S. airlines related to pricing transparency, escalating ancillary fees, and the corresponding decline in passenger comfort and service quality.

Fee Concerns:
Airlines routinely advertise low base fares that do not reflect the actual cost of travel. By the time mandatory or near-mandatory fees are added — for carry-on bags, seat selection, and other items that were once included in the ticket price — the final cost is often significantly higher than the advertised fare. This practice misleads consumers and makes genuine price comparison across airlines difficult or impossible at the point of search.

Value and Comfort Concerns:
At the same time these fees have increased, seat pitch and width have shrunk, legroom has decreased, and basic amenities once included in the fare (snacks, checked bags, seat assignments) have been stripped out and resold as add-ons. Passengers are effectively paying more for less — higher total costs paired with a materially reduced level of comfort and service compared to prior years.

Requested Action:
I urge the Department to:

1.Enforce and strengthen upfront, all-in fee disclosure requirements at the point of search, before a consumer begins the booking process
2.Investigate whether current fee structures constitute deceptive pricing practices
3.Consider minimum standards for seat pitch/width or other passenger comfort protections, given that shrinking space has coincided with rising total travel costs

As a paying consumer, I should be able to see the true, total cost of my ticket before I commit to a purchase, and I should not be expected to accept declining physical comfort as the tradeoff for fees that continue to rise.

Thank you for your attention to this matter

I am writing to file a formal complaint regarding the current practices of U.S. airlines related to pricing transparency, escalating ancillary fees, and the corresponding decline in passenger comfort and service quality.

Fee Concerns:
Airlines routinely advertise low base fares that do not reflect the actual cost of travel. By the time mandatory or near-mandatory fees are added — for carry-on bags, seat selection, and other items that were once included in the ticket price — the final cost is often significantly higher than the advertised fare. This practice misleads consumers and makes genuine price comparison across airlines difficult or impossible at the point of search.

Value and Comfort Concerns:
At the same time these fees have increased, seat pitch and width have shrunk, legroom has decreased, and basic amenities once included in the fare (snacks, checked bags, seat assignments) have been stripped out and resold as add-ons. Passengers are effectively paying more for less — higher total costs paired with a materially reduced level of comfort and service compared to prior years.

Requested Action:
I urge the Department to:

1.Enforce and strengthen upfront, all-in fee disclosure requirements at the point of search, before a consumer begins the booking process
2.Investigate whether current fee structures constitute deceptive pricing practices
3.Consider minimum standards for seat pitch/width or other passenger comfort protections, given that shrinking space has coincided with rising total travel costs

As a paying consumer, I should be able to see the true, total cost of my ticket before I commit to a purchase, and I should not be expected to accept declining physical comfort as the tradeoff for fees that continue to rise.

Thank you for your attention to this matter

comment:
The Commission's intent is misguided.

Price discrimination, although perhaps unpleasant to the ear of some, is a long-recognized economic tool observed in in any robust retail market. Price discrimination is a basic form of personalized pricing that allows sellers to offer discounts to customers who are otherwise less likely to purchase while still maintaining a price above the marginal cost of production. A coupon (whether targeted or made available all), a rebate, even a weekly sale are all forms of price discrimination, often discriminating in favor of the buyer willing to make the extra effort to utilize the discount.

The Commission errs when it seeks to restrict the actions of free actors in the market based on what the Commission decides consumers reasonably expect. The long-established norm the Commission must recognize is that sellers may use any legally obtained information to set prices in their best interest, and buyers may and should be encouraged to do the same. The Commission may encourage consumers to take economic classes, but they must not require sellers to teach them at every checkout opportunity. The example provided in section III, in which the Commission indicates a straightforward indication of personalized pricing would be insufficient because does not contain an unspecified amount of information, suggests the Commission intends to apply a standard to online purchases not currently applied to the price discrimination examples given above.

The Commission should not shape the future of commerce. Governments do consumers no favors by seeking to restrict prices or commerce in general. The Commission must not seek to prohibit personalized pricing of any sort without highly specific evidence of significant harm that outweighs a benefit to the overall market. The theoretical examples provided do not meet this standard and are generally not examples of consumers being vulnerable to personalized pricing but rather of consumers being vulnerable to a lack of competition. The Commission should encourage removal of barriers to entry in these markets rather than making it more costly and more risky for companies to operate in them.

comment:
I am submitting this comment to urge the FTC to scrutinize, regulate, and make illegal personalized pricing—the practice of charging consumers different prices for identical products based on data-driven predictions of their willingness to pay.

This practice undermines fair markets by replacing transparent pricing with hidden, data-driven discrimination between buyers. Consumers cannot verify whether they are receiving a fair price, eroding trust in commerce. Those with less time, technical literacy, or resources to detect and circumvent these practices bear a disproportionate burden. Moreover, because pricing algorithms often rely on data correlated with race, gender, age, or geography, personalized pricing risks reproducing discriminatory outcomes even absent explicit intent, potentially violating consumer protection and anti-discrimination principles.

I respectfully urge the agency to require transparency in algorithmic pricing practices and to investigate whether current personalized pricing practices violate existing consumer protection standards.

Respectfully submitted.

There is a significant difference in stated prices and negotiated prices.

In negotiated prices, both parties have the opportunity to come to a point of willing buyer and willing seller. Government should not interfere with this as government simply does not have sufficient information to be involved at all.

If someone states a price in a public setting, people should be assured that everyone will be required to pay that price, or informed otherwise. Changing the price based on conjured information about the prospective buyer is akin to a fraudulent misrepresentation by the seller designed to trick the buyer into believing the lie that everyone pays this price. If the seller wants to engage in this price manipulation the government should not stop it, rather the seller should be required to post their flexible price as a "buy it now" price and give the buyer the opportunity to offer a lower price, thereby creating an honest negotiation on price.

Algorithmic price discrimination exploits personal consumer data—such as browsing history, device type, geographic location, and perceived willingness to pay—to charge different consumers different rates for the exact same essential connectivity. This practice undermines market transparency, disproportionately penalizes low-income and vulnerable communities with higher costs, and turns routine consumer data collection into an extractive pricing weapon. Broadband and telecommunications services are fundamental utilities in the modern economy, not luxury commodities to be auctioned off based on behavioral tracking; the FCC must establish clear regulatory safeguards that require transparent, non-discriminatory pricing across the industry.

comment: I would like to share an experience I had on the Amazon website just this week.  I had planned to buy some food and other items on Amazon this past Tuesday (8/18/2026), late morning/early afternoon.  I had read that it was a good time to purchase items at that time due to spikes in prices on the site.   I want to highlight a particular item, Bob's Red Mill Old Country Style Museli.  My parents and I have bought this numerous times on Amazon before, and the price has fluctuated a bit (from 34-$39) since we started purchasing it as early as March of 2025. The ramp up in price definitely felt personalized. That day or maybe the next I installed a price app to alert me of price drops and it gives me a history of the price of the item going back a week. I know stores/businesses have to make money, but this sort of thing is excessive.  All of us do not have time to purchase items like it is a stock on the Dow Jones Industrial Avg.  It's not just amazon, but other stores too.  I have attached photos from my Amazon experience and I also attached one from Walmart of the same item (taken on 8/21/26). The photos from the amazon website show the app (which layers over the Amazon website page) i mentioned and you can see the jump in price on this particular item.  I hope you can do something about this.  The consumer / American citizen is getting squeezed in every direction.  Our government needs to help when they can.  This should be one of those times.  Thank you.

comment: The FTC should absolutely regulate personalized pricing schemes. At the very least, sellers who use this pricing technique should be required to disclose at the point of sale the distributions of sale prices offered and accepted so that consumers can have the information necessary to make rational economic decisions. Capitalism works best when information flow is maximized. The problem with “covert” pricing schemes like this is that the consumer doesn’t know when they’re being fleeced or rewarded. Yes, it’s extra trouble to provide this information, but if a seller has the resources to use this pricing technique, they have the resources to keep track of offers and acceptances, and make those available to prospective buyers. This way, you preserve a sellers freedom to charge as they want, but you also allow consumers to make more optimal choices.

comment:
I am submitting this comment as an ordinary consumer. I am not affiliated with any company, trade group, or organization.I believe personalized pricing based on data surveillance is wrong, and that allowing it to continue unchecked puts us on a very slippery slope. But the part that alarms me most is how few people know it is happening at all.
Before writing this, I asked my husband, my family, and my friends. Not one of them knew this was going on, or that it was even possible. Every one of them assumed that the price on a website is simply the price, the same number anyone else would see. That assumption is so basic that most people have never thought to question it.
What prompted me to look into this was a video I came across in which three people in the same city pulled up the same item on target.com — a can of Spam — and were each shown a different price. The same group repeated the test on Uber, scheduling the same pickup and drop-off for the same date and time, and got wildly different fares. They tried it again booking a hotel, with the same result. Nowhere on any of those sites was there a word telling them the price they were seeing had been shaped by their own data.
That omission is the whole problem. If a retailer told me plainly that my price was personalized, I would act differently. I would comparison shop, check another device, clear my browser, look at a competitor — I would not simply accept the first number I was given. Without that disclosure, I do not know there is anything to push back against. Silence is what makes the practice work, and silence is what makes it unfair.
This hands corporations an enormous advantage over the average consumer, who has no way to detect it and no idea to look for it. And I have to ask where it ends. If companies can use these methods unrestricted and under the radar, what stops the inputs from expanding? Race. Income. Occupation. Marital status. Number of children. Age. Gender. Spending habits. These are exactly the characteristics we have decided, as a country, that people should not be treated differently on. If consumers are protected from discrimination in the workplace, why should they not have comparable protection at the point of sale?
I want to note the scale of public reaction here, because I think it speaks to the deception issue directly. Beyond my own informal polling of the people around me, the video I referenced — posted on tiktok by the account @christheproducer21 — has drawn over 16,600 comments. The overwhelming response is shock and outrage, and, more tellingly, complete unawareness that this was ever happening. When a practice can operate for years without the public having any idea of it, that is strong evidence that it defies reasonable consumer expectations.
My position is that this should not be happening at all. If you and your neighbors live in the same city and shop at the same store, the price should be the same across the board.
If the Commission concludes it cannot prohibit the practice outright, then at an absolute minimum the disclosure requirement must be real:
1.It must appear where the price appears — on the product page, at the moment I see the number — not buried in a privacy policy or terms of service that no one reads.
2.It must state clearly that the price is personalized, identify the categories of personal data used, and explain how that data affected the price I am being shown.
3.It must be specific enough that an ordinary person can act on it, because a disclosure that does not let me change my behavior is not a disclosure at all.
Most people today are juggling more than enough already. They should not also have to worry that the store is quietly sizing them up. I urge the Commission to adopt the strongest possible reading of its Section 5 authority here and to enforce it aggressively.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

comment:
Static pricing is the only way for companies to reliably be able to compete with each other, this is the backbone of capitalism. We have also established that it is not legal to charge individuals different prices based on their background - is it fair to pay more because your income is higher? That’s absolutely one of the metrics this personalized pricing is going to detect, that smells like socialism to me.

Is it fair to pay more because your political background suggests you accept that price? Is it fair to pay more because your race suggests you would be willing to?

And how is this data being gathered? By tracking you, spying on you, gathering information you never consented to. And then it is used to take advantage of you.

Who is this benefitting? Family businesses can’t even dream of mimicking this model, nor would they want to. Consumers lose both their privacy and their right to a fair price that others pay. Imagine paying more because you have a higher income, and live in a nice suburb - that’s a very real outcome of this. Does that seem fair?

Any company that “needs” to use this pricing model to turn a profit does not deserve to remain in business - they’re a failure of a company.

comment:
After reading the proposal, I am fully in support of this policy. It’s about time we hold companies accountable for their deceptive practices.
As a low-income consumer, I have to be very careful and attentive when shopping, even my basic needs. Many times I have compared the price I received for a good or service with the price a family or friend received and been disgusted by the differences. This is to be expected in certain arenas, such as insurance, buying a car, or loans. But, groceries, household goods, and other “priced as marked” items and services should not differ. The money I earn should have the same value as any other person’s money. I should be able to reasonably estimate my expenses and plan for them.
I believe that requiring businesses to display personalized pricing and inform consumers what data was used to inform those prices is reasonable, but I fear that businesses will do the bare minimum required. I foresee a “specially priced” notification and a generic list of data that “may” have been used to determine that price. That is not transparency. It will allow me the agency to choose business that do not engage in surveillance pricing, but due to consolidation that has been allowed in the US, often there isn’t a competitor to support.
The surveillance pricing violation examples presented in this proposal are egregious. Why are companies even allowed to collect some of these variables? Since when does a hotel have a valid need to assess whether a customer has a funeral or other personally important event? Since when have rideshare companies been allowed to collect data about a person’s immediate medical condition? These sound like blatant violations of privacy that, if prosecutes appropriately, would reduce the risk of this data being used against the consumer. We have laws that regulate the kinds of data certain businesses can reasonably collect. Sounds like the first step is to investigate and prosecute companies for their data aggregation strategies. If the Uber app asked if it could access my Google fit data, I would immediately delete the app. Buying the info from a data broker should be illegal and the business should be held accountable for every individual user it violated.
I realize the examples were intended to highlight the most objectionable possible offenses. But they also highlight how lax the FTC has been in policing data privacy. I read the privacy policies and would never allow an app to estimate why I was traveling or whether I was having a medical emergency. No app has ever disclosed the variables they estimate based on the data we allow them to collect. That’s what we need to handle next I guess. Jesus.
In sum, I support the FTC’s policy to require companies to clearly personalized prices and provide transparency about the data used to determine those prices. Maybe when people see companies are estimating extremely private information about their lives, more will be done to protect our privacy.

comment:
There must be extreme limits on personalized pricing and it must be enforced for retail, recreation, hotels, airlines, etc.
No business has any reason ever to be all up in our personal business or charging more simply because there may be indicators of higher income.

That is how we get more inflation and higher costs of living because people would have to spend more money to get even less!
Our dollar is so weak and prices are growing at such an unsustainable rate causing shrinkflation - where companies raise prices and also make the product smaller or sell less of it per unit.

I cannot afford 35% of what I used to buy 5 years ago, I dread the word Walmart now due to how high their prices are.

Now imagine this - a gas station that detects Bob from Sales got a raise and immediately charges him 30 cents more for fuel because "he makes more money"
Absolutely not!
He would go patronize somewhere else after discovering such nonsense.

Personalized anything including pricing is an absolute non-starter, the people not need to be identified, tracked, marked, marketed, harassed, or hassled to complete a transaction or do business with a company:

Example:
I need product X, company A sells it for $5 and company B sells it for $4, I will seek out company B for the sale.
Company B can't bump that price up to $5 because it discovered I searched company A first.

Note the following:
- Collection of personal data should be strictly opt-in for things like loyalty rewards.
- Collections of personal data should be purgeable on-demand by the person involved.
- Data collected to complete a transaction - name, address, credit card information, phone number - should be banned from collation into marketing databases.

The only allowed change from the advertised and published price would be credits, loyalty rewards, coupons/discount codes sent via promotional means - email, mail, SMS, etc. various government sponsorships like faculty, 65+, military, etc. - Things we're already used to or enjoy to get a $5 discount on a pack of meat kind of thing.

Again, the price cannot change for any other reason, it cannot be personalized ever and the takeaway is no company can ever charge people more purely for the sake having a larger paycheck.

This practice should be banned. It's 100% wrong. The only dynamic pricing that's acceptable is load-bearing- like a state government charging more to use an express lane during rush hour. Those extra fees benefit everyone. This here is just adding margin for big companies. And it's manipulative.

If it's not, where does it end? Should Nabisco be able to charge more for a package of cookies if they deem a person to be too heavy based on BMI standards? They'll buy the data from that person's vehicle manufacturer, which gets their weight from the car seat and size from clothing purchase history.

The FTC should use this issue to make a bigger play - legislation in the form of a national privacy law. People should *own* the copyright to their own data and no business should be able to collect PID without expressed written permission.

The surveillance commercial businesses are able to do are mind blowing and most consumers are clueless about it.

comment: Dynamic pricing and personalized pricing are plain and simple discrimination, and should be banned. Beyond that, the collection of such personalized data by retailers and employers constitutes an unwanted invasion of privacy, particularly because many consumers have no idea how their data is being collected or by whom, and have little recourse to opt-out or request its removal. Such practices turn even non commercial personal activities such as internet browsing, and consequently the individuals behind them, into commodities that are sold to retailers in a transaction where the party sold has no leverage to negotiate the terms of their own sale. Therefore, even if it is beyond the scope of the FTC's current power, they should take steps to prohibit such discriminatory pricing practices to the extent possible until congress creates appropriate legislation fully banning it.

comment:
I support the FTC’s proposed policy statement and urge the Commission to enforce meaningful disclosure requirements for personalized pricing.

Consumers should not have to guess whether the price they see is the same price offered to everyone else—or whether it has been increased because an algorithm has inferred they are less likely to comparison-shop, more urgent, or more willing to pay. If a company uses a consumer’s profile, browsing behavior, purchase history, location, device, household characteristics, or data obtained from third parties to set a price, it should disclose that plainly before purchase.

Disclosure should include:

- That the price is personalized rather than broadly available.
- The principal data categories and factors used to set it.
- Whether the consumer is receiving a discount or paying more than a generally available reference price.
- The dollar amount—or, at minimum, the percentage—by which the personalized price differs from the standard price.

A vague statement such as “a specially selected price for you” is not transparency. It can conceal a penalty imposed because a business believes a consumer lacks alternatives or faces an urgent need. Consumers deserve enough information to decide whether to buy, comparison-shop, change their privacy settings, or take their business elsewhere.

Market forces cannot operate effectively when sellers have asymmetric access to personal data and can quietly charge different customers different prices for the same item at the same time. Transparent pricing supports real competition: consumers can compare offers, reward brands that price fairly, and avoid those that exploit personal data to extract more from them.

The FTC’s proposed approach appropriately recognizes that undisclosed personalized pricing can be deceptive or unfair under Section 5. I encourage the Commission to make clear that adequate disclosure must identify both the existence and meaningful basis of personalization, and should require a usable price comparison so consumers can understand the financial impact. Thank you!

comment:
I am writing as the son of a disabled American who relies on online grocery and delivery services because they have voluntarily stopped driving. I want the Commission to understand how surveillance pricing affects people like my father, and why disclosure alone will not be enough to protect him and other like him.

When a grocery chain or delivery service learns that my father does not drive, that information becomes a lever. They know he has fewer alternatives and less ability to shop around, walk out, or drive to a competitor for a better price. That is not a hypothetical risk. It is the direct, foreseeable consequence of combining personal data with pricing algorithms, and it falls hardest on people whose circumstances are already visible in their data: the elderly, the disabled, and anyone with a fixed income and limited mobility.

He has no meaningful way to see what profile these companies have built on him, correct it, or remove himself from it. He did not consent to have his mobility limitations used as pricing input, yet there is no default protection preventing it. The same is true of his finances. Because there is no default “no data sharing” standard for financial data, his bank balance and spending patterns are likely already available to data brokers and, by extension, to the very companies pricing his groceries.

I want to raise three specific concerns with the proposed policy statement:

1. Disclosure is not enough. Telling customers that a price was personalized does not restore their bargaining power. He still cannot drive, still cannot shop elsewhere, and still has no leverage. A company can fully “disclose” that it is charging him more because of his disability and still be acting unfairly. I ask the Commission to treat pricing based on disability status, age, or mobility limitations, whether used directly or through proxies like delivery frequency or address type, as inherently unfair under Section 5, not merely as something that becomes acceptable once disclosed.

2. Consumers need a real right to see and remove their data. Disclosure of pricing practices means little if customers cannot see the underlying data profile driving the price, correct it, or opt out of its use. I ask the Commission to pair any disclosure requirement with an enforceable right to access, correct, and delete the personal data used in pricing decisions, at no cost and through a genuinely accessible process.

3. Financial data needs default protection. Static savings and fixed incomes should not be treated as fair game for pricing algorithms simply because banks and financial services lack a default no sharing standard. I ask the Commission to consider whether the undisclosed use of financial account data for pricing purposes should be treated as a per se unfair practice, not something cured by fine print disclosure.

I recognize the Commission has stated it lacks authority to ban personalized pricing outright. To the Commissioners of the Federal Trade Commission:

I write to urge the Commission, in the strongest possible terms, to pursue rulemaking and enforcement action that would make personalized pricing — the practice of charging different consumers different prices for identical goods or services based on data collected about them individually — unlawful in the United States. This practice is not a neutral pricing innovation. It is a systematic exploitation of the information asymmetry between firms and consumers, and it should be treated as an unfair and deceptive practice under Section 5 of the FTC Act.

1. Personalized pricing inverts the basic premise of a competitive market

Markets are supposed to work because consumers can compare prices and firms compete for their business on a level playing field. Personalized pricing destroys that premise. When a firm knows a consumer's income bracket, browsing history, device type, location, purchase urgency, or even how long they hesitated before clicking "buy," it can calculate the maximum that specific individual will pay — and charge exactly that. This is not price discovery. It is the elimination of the consumer's ability to shop, compare, or negotiate in any meaningful sense, because the "market price" no longer exists as a stable, comparable reference point. Every consumer effectively faces a market of one, priced against them by an entity with vastly superior information.

2. It is built on nonconsensual surveillance

Personalized pricing depends on extensive behavioral profiling: tracking cookies, device fingerprinting, purchase history, geolocation, and inferred demographic and psychographic data, frequently obtained and combined without consumers' meaningful knowledge or consent. Consumers do not expect — and did not agree — to have their willingness to pay algorithmically estimated and monetized. The Commission has long treated covert data practices that harm consumers as a core area of concern; personalized pricing should be recognized as one of the clearest cases where covert data collection translates directly into concrete financial injury.

3. It disproportionately harms the consumers least able to detect or resist it

Evidence gathered by researchers and journalists has repeatedly shown that algorithmic pricing systems can charge more to consumers in lower-income ZIP codes, to consumers using older or lower-cost devices, to consumers with less time to shop around, and to consumers in areas with fewer retail alternatives. Far from personalization delivering better deals to price-sensitive shoppers, the incentive structure runs the other way: the algorithm's entire purpose is to find the highest price each individual will tolerate. This is regressive by design and falls hardest on people with the least market power.

4. Existing legal frameworks are inadequate to the scale of the practice

The Robinson-Patman Act addresses price discrimination between business purchasers, not consumer-facing algorithmic pricing. State-level unfair-practices statutes are inconsistent and rarely equipped to address opaque, real-time algorithmic pricing at scale. Only the FTC, exercising its Section 5 authority over unfair and deceptive acts and practices, has both the jurisdiction and the technical capacity to address this as a nationwide practice. The Commission's own 2024 study on surveillance pricing confirmed that firms are actively developing and deploying these tools; the time for a study-only posture has passed.

5. Recommended Commission action

I urge the Commission to:

Issue a rule under Section 5 categorically prohibiting the use of individually-targeted, non-transparent price variation based on personal data unrelated to the actual cost of providing the good or service.
Require disclosure at minimum, as an interim step, mandating that any price shown to a consumer that differs from a general list price due to personalized factors be conspicuously labeled as such, with an explanation of what data was used.
Ban the use of protected or proxy-protected characteristics (race, income proxies, disability status, age, ZIP code as a proxy for demographic composition) in any pricing algorithm, full stop.
Compel algorithmic transparency and audit rights, requiring firms deploying dynamic or personalized pricing systems to make them available for independent, ongoing regulatory audit.
Impose meaningful penalties, including disgorgement of profits attributable to personalized pricing, sufficient to remove the financial incentive for noncompliance.

Personalized pricing is not a minor pricing technique — it is a fundamental threat to the basic bargain of a fair marketplace: that price is public, comparable, and not secretly calibrated to extract the maximum a given individual can be made to pay. I urge the Commission to act decisively and treat this as the urgent consumer protection issue it is.

To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing to ask you to completely ban "surveillance pricing." Companies should not be allowed to use our personal data to charge different people different prices for the exact same item.

Simply forcing companies to "disclose" this practice is not enough. If you only require disclosure, it will just turn into endless, confusing legal fine print that we are forced to accept just to buy everyday goods.

We have already seen this fail with internet tracking cookies and the resulting “disclosure” pop-ups. Those warnings did absolutely nothing to stop companies from tracking us. They just became an annoying hurdle we have to click through out of fatigue. A disclosure rule for pricing will end up exactly the same way. It will give companies a loophole to legally discriminate against buyers under the guise of "informed consent."

Real consumer protection means stopping this unfair practice entirely, not just making us sign a form agreeing to it. Please protect regular people and ban algorithmic surveillance pricing.

comment:
I support the FTC’s proposed enforcement policy statement, but I do not think disclosure alone is enough to address surveillance pricing.

When I shop for a product, I expect to see the same price offered to another person shopping for that product at the same time. I find it deeply troubling that a business could use my browsing history, location, purchasing habits, financial circumstances, or other personal information to decide that I am willing, or desperate enough, to pay more.

The FTC’s own examples show the potential harm. A person should not be charged more for transportation to a medical facility, food delivery when they cannot leave home, or a hotel room when traveling for a funeral merely because a business has data revealing their urgent circumstances.

Simply telling consumers that a price has been personalized does not make the practice fair. Most people have no realistic way to know what information a business has collected, whether that information is accurate, or how to prevent it from being used. Consumers should not have to use a private browser, hide their location, or conceal their identity to receive a fair price.

I recognize that ordinary dynamic pricing based on objective market conditions may be legitimate and that individualized discounts may benefit some consumers. But those potential benefits do not justify charging someone more based on a hidden profile of that person’s finances, behavior, vulnerability, or willingness to pay.

The FTC states that it is not presently taking a position on whether some personalized-pricing practices may be unfair even when fully disclosed. I urge the FTC to examine that issue through rulemaking. Any rule should distinguish ordinary price changes based on supply and demand from prices tailored to an individual consumer. It should prohibit businesses from charging a person more based on sensitive personal information, an urgent need, a perceived vulnerability, or information purchased from data brokers.

Congress should also enact legislation that clearly prohibits abusive surveillance pricing and gives the FTC the authority and enforcement tools needed to protect consumers.

The proposed policy statement is a good first step, but it should not be the last. If surveillance pricing is allowed to become standard business practice, it will be much harder to control later. The FTC and Congress should act before that happens.

I strongly oppose personalized pricing based on consumer data and support the FTC’s efforts to investigate and restrict this practice.

Consumers reasonably expect that a listed price is determined by the product, service, and ordinary market conditions—not by a hidden calculation of how much a particular person might be willing or forced to pay. Using browsing history, location, purchase history, household composition, medical circumstances, financial information, or other personal data to charge different consumers different prices is fundamentally deceptive when it occurs without their knowledge.

Personalized pricing also undermines meaningful comparison shopping. A competitive market depends on consumers being able to compare the same offers. If each consumer sees a different price based on information collected about that person, there is no longer a reliable market price to compare. Consumers cannot make informed choices when they do not know whether the displayed price reflects the value of the product or an algorithm’s estimate of their vulnerability, urgency, or ability to pay.

I am particularly concerned about pricing based on sensitive circumstances. A person should never pay more because data suggest that the person is experiencing a medical emergency, traveling for a funeral, caring for children, recently experienced a crime, lacks transportation, or has few practical alternatives. Disclosing that such exploitation is occurring would not necessarily make it fair. Certain uses of personal data should be considered unfair even when disclosed because the consumer may have no reasonable way to avoid the harm.

Personalized pricing also creates serious privacy and discrimination concerns. Algorithms may use seemingly neutral information as a proxy for income, disability, race, age, family status, religion, health, or geographic location. Consumers may never know what information was used, whether it was accurate, or how to correct it. Businesses should not be permitted to avoid responsibility by outsourcing these decisions to data brokers, software vendors, or pricing algorithms.

As a small-business owner and healthcare professional, I recognize that not every price difference is improper. Prices may legitimately vary because of differences in products, services, costs, insurance contracts, publicly disclosed discounts, geographic markets, or changing supply and demand. Those ordinary and explainable differences are distinct from secretly charging an individual more because data suggest that the person will tolerate a higher price.

I urge the FTC to finalize and strengthen its proposed policy by:

1. Requiring clear, prominent disclosure whenever personal data influence a consumer’s price.
2. Requiring disclosure of the specific basis and categories of data used—not vague phrases such as “special price” or “personalized offer.”
3. Giving consumers access to a non-personalized price and a meaningful opportunity to opt out.
4. Holding businesses responsible for pricing decisions made by their vendors and automated systems.
5. Treating the use of health information, emergencies, personal hardship, or other vulnerabilities to increase prices as presumptively unfair.
6. Requiring a practical process for consumers to identify and correct inaccurate information.
7. Preserving the FTC’s ability to find that certain personalized-pricing practices are unfair even when technically disclosed.

A person’s private information should not become a tool for extracting the highest price that person can be pressured into paying. Americans deserve transparent prices, genuine competition, and confidence that personal data will not be used against them. I encourage the Commission to adopt the strongest protections available under its existing authority and to recommend additional congressional action if further authority is needed.

comment:
Hello, I am an honest, tax-paying, voting citizen who believes government exists to do for “we the people” that which we alone cannot do for ourselves. Personalized pricing is a clear example of the power corporations wield over consumers, who often can’t understand or resist it on their own. Using technology and the vast troves of personal information consumers unwittingly hand over, these corporations continue to squeeze individuals for every available penny. Companies like Walmart draw customers into subscription and loyalty programs with promises of fast shipping and lower prices, then use the data they collect to build billion-dollar advertising and analytics businesses built on that same customer information.

I’m glad the FTC recognizes the harms of surveillance pricing, but recognition isn’t enough—the practice itself must be stopped.

The Commission’s own report documents how consumers are charged more based on data showing they’re homebound, have young children, are traveling for a funeral, or have recently been crime victims. Research the Commission cites confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less consumers benefit overall, and that gains for some come paired with losses for others. The most vulnerable pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

Disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling consumers they’re being charged more based on a data broker’s estimate of their desperation doesn’t undo the harm—it just asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of exploitation in real time. The Commission itself notes that two-thirds of Americans understand little about what companies do with their data, meaning consumers cannot reasonably avoid prices they can’t see.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing outright, not merely require disclosure of it.

comment:
I appreciate that the Federal Trade Commission has acknowledged the harm "surveillance pricing" causes consumers, but acknowledgment alone isn't sufficient—this practice needs to end entirely.

The Commission's report contains numerous troubling illustrations of how harmful surveillance pricing can be: consumers charged more because data shows they're stuck at home, raising young kids, en route to a funeral, dealing with a medical crisis, or recently victimized by crime. Studies referenced by the Commission show that as these tactics grow more advanced, fewer consumers come out ahead, and that when some people benefit, others bear the cost. Those least able to afford it end up paying the most, based on their most private information.

I'm calling on the Commission to ban surveillance pricing altogether, since simply disclosing it doesn't make up for unfair pricing. Informing someone they're paying more because a data broker calculated their willingness to pay doesn't erase the damage—it just puts the burden on people who are ill, frightened, or in crisis to opt out of being taken advantage of as it's happening. The Commission has itself noted that roughly two-thirds of Americans have little to no understanding of how companies use their personal data, meaning consumers can't realistically dodge price increases they never see coming.

I'm asking the FTC to fully exercise its authority to prohibit surveillance pricing, not just mandate that companies disclose it. Thank you for your consideration.

comment:
I am gratified to see that the Federal Trade Commission recognizes the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but what good is recognition if it is not followed up by action? The practice itself must be stopped. This is absolutely necessary. The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is - especially for the most vulnerable and needy people. Research cited by the Commission itself confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

Therefore, I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. It is a heinous and immoral practice. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

The FTC MUST USE IT'S FULL AUTHORITY TO BAN SURVEILLANCE PRICING! Merely requiring companies to disclose their practice is a worthless action. Thank you.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

I think the FTC needs to stop "personalized" pricing altogether. It's basically giving companies carte blanche to engage in surveillance on their customers. Not only that, but personalized pricing is basically saying that companies can just discriminate against whoever they want for whatever reason they want! As a person of color, I think that's toeing a line that's basically nonexistent. Companies should not have the right to decide that one person can pay one price for a product, and another person, at the very same store, can pay a different price for the very same product.

The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data that they quite frankly shouldn't have. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. In the end, the most desperate and vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because a person shouldn't have to disclose--whether intentionally or otherwise--the intimate details of their life just for a "discount." It's downright exploitative. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

comment:
Subject: Opposition to FTC "Personalized Pricing" Rules and Surveillance Price Gouging

I am writing to express my strong opposition to any Federal Trade Commission rule that would facilitate "surveillance pricing"—or "personalized pricing"—allowing retailers to leverage big data to inflate prices based on a consumer's perceived ability to pay.

Disclosing these practices does not make price gouging acceptable. Permitting corporations to use personal data and surveillance metrics to maximize profit margins at consumers' expense is fundamentally unfair. If wealthier individuals should pay more, that goal should be achieved through progressive taxation for societal benefit, rather than handing corporations a green light to extract extra cash for their bottom lines.

I urge the FTC to protect consumers by banning surveillance pricing entirely.

comment:
I am a Massachusetts resident and an information security professional with more than 25 years of experience working with technology, data, privacy, and cybersecurity. That experience has given me a deep appreciation for both the value of data and the extraordinary amount that can now be inferred about an individual from information collected across websites, applications, devices, data brokers, and other sources.

I am glad to see the Federal Trade Commission recognize the harms that “surveillance pricing” poses to consumers, but recognition and disclosure are not enough. The practice itself should be prohibited.

What concerns me most about surveillance pricing is that it fundamentally changes the relationship between a consumer and a seller. A price has traditionally reflected factors such as the cost of providing a product, market conditions, inventory, and competition. Surveillance pricing introduces a very different factor: what a company believes it can extract from a particular individual.

The examples identified by the Commission demonstrate why this distinction matters. A consumer could potentially be charged more because data indicates that they are homebound, have young children, are traveling for a funeral, are experiencing a medical emergency, have recently been the victim of a crime, or simply appear to have fewer alternatives. These are not legitimate differences in the cost of providing a product or service. They are differences in a person’s circumstances and vulnerability.

From my work in information security, I also know that consumers cannot realistically understand the full extent of the data being collected about them or the conclusions being drawn from it. Individual pieces of information that seem innocuous can become extraordinarily revealing when combined. Location, browsing behavior, purchase history, device information, search activity, demographic information, and data purchased from brokers can collectively reveal circumstances that a consumer never knowingly disclosed to the company setting the price.

That is why disclosure is not an adequate solution.

A notice telling me that my personal information may influence the price I receive does not give me meaningful control over the process. I cannot evaluate whether the price displayed to me is higher than the price offered to another person. I cannot know which data contributed to that decision, whether those data are accurate, what inferences were made from them, or whether refusing collection would actually result in a different price. There is no meaningful market transparency when each consumer may effectively be presented with a market of one.

There is also a broader issue of fairness. Families already make purchasing decisions under constraints of income, time, geography, health, childcare, and other circumstances. Those constraints should not become signals that an automated system can use to determine that a particular consumer can be charged more precisely because they have less ability to walk away.

The increasing sophistication of artificial intelligence and large-scale data analytics makes this issue more urgent, not less. Companies will become progressively better at predicting what an individual needs, how urgently they need it, what alternatives are available to them, and the maximum price they are likely to tolerate. Once those capabilities become embedded throughout digital commerce, attempting to address the problem through disclosure requirements will be far more difficult than establishing clear boundaries now.

Consumers should not have to become privacy or cybersecurity experts simply to know whether they are receiving a fair price.

I therefore urge the FTC to use its full authority to prohibit surveillance pricing rather than merely requiring companies to disclose it. Companies may legitimately adjust prices based on products, costs, supply, demand, inventory, and market conditions. They should not be permitted to secretly adjust the price offered to an individual based on surveillance of that person’s behavior, characteristics, circumstances, vulnerabilities, or inferred willingness to pay.

Disclosure is not enough. Surveillance pricing itself is the problem, and it should be stopped.

I am glad to see the Federal Trade Commission recognize the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but recognition is not enough—the practice itself must be stopped and permanently forbidden!

The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

Let's call this what it is! Surveillance pricing is just another trick in the retailer's book to squeeze more money out of more people, for the retailer's own, singular benefit!!! It is just GREED with another label lapped on it!!! People are willing to accept variations in pricing due to logical conditions such as cost of transporting goods, distance from the source, or changes in value, for example, but otherwise we expect the price to be the same for EVERY shopper that goes in the door!!! We are NOT willing to accept prices that change according to what the retailer knows about us, which could be wrong!!! And why the hell does the retailer know so much about us to begin with? We are sick and tired of being taken advantage of by greedy merchants because of our personal information, which should remain just that, PERSONAL and PRIVATE!!!

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

Every day, American consumers struggle to be able to afford everyday necessities while billionaires continue to pocket more and more money. Surveillance pricing will make this even worse and will make it even harder for Americans to afford these necessities because companies will have the right to charge them more money for completely arbitrary reasons based on surveillance data. No one should have to pay more money than their neighbor for a product simply because a corporation decided they should. The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information. This is price gouging at its worst and there is absolutely zero reason for a company to engage in it besides unethical practices. And disclosure is not enough. Companies may disclose that they are participating in price gouging and consumers can theoretically choose other retailers, but for many Americans in rural communities or in food deserts, they simply do not have alternatives to turn to if their only accessible grocery store chooses to engage in surveillance pricing. I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

comment:
It is galling to sit next to someone in an airplane and find out they paid half the price you did. It is galling to go online to buy tickets and find that the prices have changed since you looked on that site a day or two before. If pricing varies, it should vary in the same way for everyone: for example: a train fare will be 10% less in off-peak hours. We should be able to read the rules of the game and know them.
When I go into a grocery store, I expect to pay the same price for a product as everyone else. The price should be indicated on the product itself or on the shelf. I should be able to read the price and check my receipt. I always check my receipt because so many errors are made in grocery stores.
Already, restaurants list food/beverage items without prices. I thought they were required by law to post prices. I ask the server and they don't know because they don't run the cash register.
Consumers are not piggy banks. We are people operating on a budget. Businesses are not there to fleece us, they are there to sell us goods and services at fair prices and under fair conditions. It should not matter what time I buy my groceries or how much I usually buy or what products I buy. When I buy a can of tuna, I should be paying the same as all the other people in the checkout line. At any hour at any time of day.
"Personalized" pricing is a euphemism for exploiting consumers.

comment:
I am glad to see that the Federal Trade Commission recognizes the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but recognition is not enough—the practice itself must be stopped.

The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. THIS INFORMATION IS PRIVATE and no-one has the right to even have this information, let alone use it for the greedy benefit of corporations. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information. This really is outrageous and I cannot believe that this is even happening in the USA. Whatever happened to freedom and liberty. As a retiree on a fixed income what I do in my life and how I spend my money is my business and mine alone.

Please do the right thing. I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. It would stop me from purchasing anything and indeed, I will continue to grow my own food, buy from the local farmer whom I trust and make whatever I need to live comfortably. I certainly don't trust any government/state officials or agencies to support the "common person" when they can make money out of us. Disgusting. Who on earth would want to live in America and bring children up in such a place.
The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

comment:
I am writing to urge the FTC to go beyond mere disclosure requirements and instead use its full authority to prohibit surveillance pricing outright. Disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing.

The Commission's proposed enforcement policy treats nondisclosure as the harm to address. But disclosure does not fix the underlying unfairness—a sick, stranded, or grieving person cannot 'opt out' of being exploited simply by being told they are being charged more.

With multiple states—including New Jersey, Maryland, and Connecticut—already passing legislation to ban or restrict surveillance pricing, federal action is urgently needed to prevent a patchwork regime. A strong FTC position now will provide clarity for businesses and consistent protection for consumers nationwide.

The examples in the Commission's report—charging higher prices to homebound consumers, families with young children, those traveling for funerals, or victims of crimes—are not hypothetical edge cases. They represent systematic exploitation of life's most difficult moments. My community/family/workplace includes many who would face these exact situations.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

comment:
The Federal Trade Commission is considering a new rule that could open the floodgates to new ways for stores to raise prices on you: Surveillance pricing.
They’re calling it “personalized pricing,” but let’s be clear: What stores like Walmart are considering is a way to raise prices on people who the data says can afford it. And that money will go straight to their bottom line. It’s a way to use big data to make things even more expensive than they already are.
The rule that the FTC is currently considering would give corporations a green light to price gouge so long as they disclose that they’re doing it. That’s not good enough. Even if you think the wealthy should pay more, why should corporations be the ones who benefit? If you want the wealthy to pay more, tax the rich, and use the money for something useful to our society!
I am glad to see the Federal Trade Commission recognize the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but recognition is not enough—the practice itself must be stopped.
The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.
I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.
I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

I am glad to see the Federal Trade Commission recognize the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but recognition is not enough—the practice itself must be stopped.

I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

My name is Narendra and I live in Austin,TX. I'm not a lawyer, and no one is paying me to write this. I pay a phone bill and an internet bill, and I've become convinced something is being done to me and my neighbors that most of us can't see and would never agree to if asked.
To be clear: I'm not talking about sales, coupons, or airfare costing more at Thanksgiving. That's dynamic pricing — it answers to the market, and everyone faces the same number. Surveillance pricing answers to me: my browsing history, my ZIP code, my device, my estimated income, whether my phone battery is low, whether I look like someone in a hurry. When the FTC studied this, it found intermediaries using everything from precise location to mouse movements to tailor prices, and that a handful of those firms served hundreds of clients.

Why this is the FCC's business. Carriers are the headwaters. Section 222 exists precisely because Congress understood we don't choose to generate this data — it's an unavoidable byproduct of using an essential service. That logic applies fully to pricing. If an inference drawn from my network data ends up in what I'm charged, the harm Section 222 was written to prevent has occurred. This isn't hypothetical: the Commission already fined all four major carriers for failing to protect subscriber location data. You've established that the pipes leak. I'm asking you to find out where the water goes.
It is regressive by design. These systems hunt for the customer who can't walk away — and because location is an input, the model knows exactly how many providers serve my address. The households with the fewest alternatives are where the algorithm can push hardest with the least risk. Rural counties. Neighborhoods that lost competitive buildout decades ago. Congress directed you to address discrimination in the terms and conditions of broadband, including on the basis of income level. Price is the term and condition.
Disclosure alone won't fix it. If my provider adds a line saying it may use my data to set prices, what have I gained? I still don't know what my price is based on, what anyone else pays, or whether I'm being overcharged — and I still can't leave. Disclosure works when it enables a choice. Where the practice is universal and the market concentrated, it just launders the practice, turning a violation into something I technically agreed to without changing a single price.
What I'm asking:
Open a Notice of Inquiry into the use of customer data to set prices and offers for communications services.
Ask carriers directly whether they use individualized data to set or vary pricing and retention offers, and what they sell to pricing intermediaries.
Confirm that using CPNI, or inferences drawn from it, to set individualized prices requires express opt-in consent — not a terms-of-service update.
Establish that a carrier cannot escape Section 222 by routing customer data through a vendor. The duty should follow the data.
Require that the price on a broadband label be uniform for everyone at a service address. A personalized label isn't a protection; it's theater.
I'll close with the part I have trouble explaining to my own family. When I say this bothers me, they say everybody has data on everybody, that ship has sailed. I feel that exhaustion too. But this is where surveillance stops being merely creepy and starts taking money out of the account. It's a decade of watching, turned around and pointed at the price tag.
What I want is simple. When I look at a price, I want it to be the price — the same one my neighbor sees, the same one a stranger sees. A fact about the product instead of a conclusion about me. We're losing that quietly, one A/B test at a time, without anyone ever voting on it. I'm asking you to notice it's being lost, and to decide on purpose whether we let it go.
Thank you for keeping open a process where someone with no lawyer and no lobbyist can be heard.

comment:
I am encouraged that the Federal Trade Commission is recognizing the harm surveillance pricing can cause, but simply recognizing the problem is not enough. Consumers should not have to wonder whether the price they are being shown has been quietly increased because a company believes they are desperate, vulnerable, or simply willing to pay more.

What concerns me most is how deeply personal information can be used against ordinary people. Someone who is homebound, caring for young children, traveling because of a death in the family, facing a medical emergency, or recovering from a crime should not be seen as an opportunity to charge more. Those are moments when people deserve fairness, not exploitation.

This also strikes me as fundamentally different from ordinary discounts or competitive pricing. Consumers often have no idea what information has been collected about them, how it has been interpreted, or whether someone else is being offered a lower price for the exact same product or service. There is no meaningful way to shop around when the pricing system itself is invisible.

For that reason, I do not believe disclosure is enough. A notice telling someone they may be paying more because of information collected about them does not make the practice fair. It simply puts the burden on the consumer after the harm has already occurred.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to prohibit surveillance pricing based on personal data, vulnerability, or a consumer’s perceived willingness to pay. Americans should be able to purchase ordinary goods and services without wondering whether their private lives are being used to determine how much they can be squeezed for.

Thank you for taking this issue seriously and for protecting consumers from practices they often have no realistic way to see, understand, or avoid.

comment:
I am retired and living on a fixed income. I don't want data about me used to charge me higher prices. I am glad to see the Federal Trade Commission recognize the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but recognition is not enough—the practice itself must be stopped.

The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

comment:
I’m a middle-class woman living in Bloomington, IN. Although I may be able to “afford” higher grocery prices, I shouldn’t be forced to do so. Doing so would put an unfair burden on my budget, forcing me to make sacrifices in other areas of my life. Working-class people like myself should not be forced into difficult choices just because companies think they can squeeze us for a little more.

And disclosure is not enough! Working-class people often don’t have the luxury of time or travel to shop around and price compare when they know their usual grocer uses “personalized pricing”, which really ought to be called surveillance pricing. The most vulnerable consumers will end up paying the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

Even if you think those with more should pay more, why should corporations be the ones who benefit? If you want the wealthy to pay more, tax the rich, and use the money for something useful to our society!

I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks the consumer to opt out of being exploited in real time—which, again, they likely do not have the luxury of time and travel to be able to do. Moreover, the Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it.

Thank you
