comment:
I am glad the Federal Trade Commission recognizes the harms of surveillance pricing, but that isn't enough. Surveillance pricing itself must be stopped. This practice exists to get people to pay the most companies think they can on items, unfairly affecting parents, poor people, disabled people, and those out of town for emergencies. The Federal Trade Commission knows that the better surveillance pricing technology becomes, the less likely consumers are to benefit; the most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices based off of their most intimate personal information. Driving them deeper into debt while the companies unfairly squeeze them out of all the money they have left.

I urge the Federal Trade Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling consumers they are paying more because of a data broker's estimate does not undo the harm. It simply asks those of us who are sick, scared, or stranded to opt out of being exploited when they never agreed to it in the first place. The Federal Trade Commission itself acknowledges that 2/3 of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and consumers can't avoid higher prices they can't see.

I urge the FTC to use its authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely requiring companies to disclose it. Thank you!

comment:
So-called “surveillance pricing" is harmful to consumers, it is invasive!
Sellers use this to charge higher prices of consumers at the time when those same consumers may be squeezed by circumstances such as an urgent need for something because of an emergency or when the consumer may not have other options for buying necessary goods.
The FTC’s own research confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that the most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.
I argue that the FTC must prohibit surveillance pricing outright. Disclosure doesn’t solve much of anything when consumers are in the kind of circumstances mentioned above. More bluntly: Disclosure just is not a substitute for fair pricing.
Telling consumers they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm — it asks sick, scared or stranded people to find some way to avoid being exploited in real time.
As the FTC knows, two-thirds of Americans understand very little, if anything, about what companies do with their personal data, and consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices if they don’t know they are being overcharged.
Ban surveillance pricing. Disclosure just doesn’t cut it!
Thanks.

comment:
Recognition of the dangers of "surveillance pricing" isn't enough. It has to be stopped and stopped NOW.
I live in a lower income area and have seen first hand how this issue is so exploitative. For not only myself but for my neighbors. Prices need to be the same for everyone, not to have life circumstances and how desperate you are to be a factor.

Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. I cannot see any reason for this besides companies exploiting people for life necessities. Water should not be more money because it's a hot day. Milk shouldn't be more money because a mother has to buy milk for her young children.

The data used by these companies were also bought from data brokers that take this info from consumers without permission. It is a long cycle of exploitation with the consumer losing in all of it.
I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

The FTC must BAN this practice.

comment:
am glad to see the Federal Trade Commission recognize the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but recognition is not enough—the practice itself must be stopped.

In a fair and free market, the price of goods should not depend on an algorithm's estimate of how much a particular buyer should pay. Supply and demand should set the price of goods, and that price should be the same for all. Charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime is morally wrong and incompatible with free market principles. I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

comment:
I am submitting this comment because I am deeply concerned about the growing use of personal data to determine how much an individual consumer will be charged for a product or service.

I appreciate that the Federal Trade Commission recognizes the potential dangers of personalized or "surveillance" pricing and is considering stronger disclosure requirements. However, I do not believe disclosure alone adequately protects consumers.

When I walk into a store or shop online, I expect the price I see to reflect the cost of the product, market conditions, or a legitimate sale—not a company's secret calculation of how much it believes I personally can be persuaded or forced to pay.

Companies today can potentially draw from enormous amounts of information about consumers, including shopping and browsing histories, location information, demographics, purchasing habits, and other personal data. Allowing that information to determine individualized prices creates opportunities for exploitation that consumers may never even realize are occurring.

A disclosure telling me that my price was personalized does not make an unfair price fair.

This becomes especially troubling when algorithms determine that someone is unlikely to shop elsewhere or is in circumstances that make a purchase particularly urgent. A consumer dealing with an emergency, illness, travel disruption, family crisis, disability, or limited transportation should not potentially be charged more simply because data suggests that person has fewer alternatives.

People are already struggling with the cost of groceries, housing, utilities, healthcare, transportation, and other necessities. We should not create a marketplace where two people looking at the same product at the same moment can unknowingly receive different prices because an algorithm believes one of them is willing—or desperate enough—to pay more.

There is also a fundamental privacy issue involved. Consumers should not have to surrender detailed information about their lives simply by participating in the modern economy, only to have that information turned around and used to extract the maximum possible price.

The FTC itself has acknowledged that personalized pricing can involve businesses analyzing personal data to estimate how much an individual consumer is willing to spend. That should raise serious consumer-protection concerns.

I therefore urge the FTC to use the full extent of its existing authority to prevent unfair and deceptive personalized-pricing practices, establish the strongest possible consumer protections, and make clear that disclosure alone does not automatically make an otherwise unfair practice acceptable.

Where the FTC believes current law does not provide sufficient authority to prohibit harmful forms of surveillance pricing, I urge the Commission to identify those gaps so Congress can act clearly.

Consumers deserve transparency, but we deserve something more fundamental: fairness.

Technology should make commerce more convenient and competitive. It should not give corporations increasingly sophisticated tools to determine exactly how much money they can extract from each person.

Please protect consumers from a future where our personal information becomes another tool used to make everyday life more expensive.

Thank you for considering my comments.

I strongly oppose Personalized Pricing. This is just another tool to allow large corporations to charge more to certain locations and individuals in order to increase their profits on the backs of consumers. I am already struggling with the affordability of essentials. I am a senior who is going through my retirement savings faster than I should be. I do not live in a wealthy community, but still I could not afford to live where I do if I hadn't bought my home years ago. I shouldn't have to pay more than in the inner city for necessities. This most likely affects the more affluent, but why should they pay more for the same item sold? You could argue that this would help even the playing field, but it doesn't. If you want to even the playing field, the rich should pay their fair share in taxes; that could help the less fortunate. Instead, this will only help big business.

Please do not let this proposed policy proceed.

comment:
I strongly oppose "personalized pricing" First of all it requires facial recognition of every customer that enters a store and there is nothing to protect that person if the store's data base is hacked. We cannot replace our faces and biometric data should not be collected. Whenit is it must be discarded immediately. There are no requirements that stores do this.

Second, stores will maintain records of the exact time that customers enter them. Surely, these will be exploited to determine the customer's urgency in making a purchase based on whether they are coming in at their regular shopping time. Prices will be raised accordingly. Furthermore, the Supreme Court just ruled in Chatrie that location tracking is a Fourth Amendment search. By allowing stores to record every person that shops, you will be enabling location tracking.

Personalized shopping takes advantage of consumers in another way because over time it enables a store to assess the maximum price that a specific customer is willing to pay for any given item and then never offer them a lower price.

The data on what you purchase might even be sold by retail stores to health insurance companies which might raise your rates based on the latest belief about what is healthy to eat.

If you are very wealthy, you probably don't care about personalized pricing. The wealthiest Americans don't even do their own shopping. They either order their food delivered or have a domestic worker shop for it. This is not the situation for the majority of Americans who live on a budget and are struggling right now to balance high prices at the store and the huge costs of health insurance and housing.

Please prohibit personalized pricing because it is an invasive form of surveillance that will hurt the majority of Americans.

comment:
I appreciate that the Federal Trade Commission has taken a first step and recognizes the harms that "surveillance pricing" will bring to consumers. Well and good. But why should it even be allowed? What benefits might accrue to consumers when they are most vulnerable or most in need by being charged higher prices because their situation makes it more likely that they will accept them?

The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm. The remedy of having the option to opt out when you are most in need borders on the absurd.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing to bring fairness to the market, rather than merely requiring that companies disclose it without providing any remedy that would allow the consumer under duress to pay what other less needy customers are paying. Thank you.

As the New Executive Director of an agency, I came to note that the women working for our agency were being charged at a higher insurance rate than I or the men employed. I phoned to ask why and was told that it was because the women were assessed ad costing more because of possible pregnancy. I am a woman, but due to my name the insurance company perceived that I was male and charged less. When I contested the insurance company premise, they adjusted the charge for my insurance to the higher rate, though I had documentation proving that I could not get pregnant. This is ridicules on so many levels.

I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

comment:
It's not personalized pricing -- call it by its name. It's surveillance pricing. It's price gouging. It's extraordinary corporate profits made by morbidly rich corporations off the backs of its the customers. We're not digits, we're not widgets; we are real people with less and less income every day. Disclosure is not enough. Stop surveillance pricing all together!

The Federal Trade Commission recognizes the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but recognition is not enough—again I say, the practice itself must be stopped.

The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous and invasive surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information. This is just wrong.

The Commission has done its due diligence and now must act to protect the public and prohibit surveillance pricing outright. I can't say it enough -disclosure is not enough. It is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The practice of corporations selling our data is sick.

The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

The FTC must use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. If it cannot eliminate data brokers and this insidious practice, banning surveillance pricing is the least it can do.

Stand up for we the people,
Karen Samski.

comment:
The practice of setting individualized prices for the same good or service based on a consumer's personal data, rather than a single price available to all buyers, is fundamentally wrong. This is distinct from conventional dynamic pricing, which reacts to market conditions like supply and demand, or time of day. Surveillance pricing does not react to the market, it reacts to individuals, using personal data to calculate an extraction value. Disclosure of the practice does nothing to protect consumers but rather creates the appearance of transparency, targets the vulnerable, and eliminates the fair market value of the good and/or service from the economic equation.

Shifting to a surveillance pricing model turns businesses into extraction machines rather than entities that try to provide the best value relative to the good and/or service. There are documented examples of this already occurring like Instacart, delta airlines, and supermarkets like Shop-Rite and Price-Rite.

Politically, criticism is coming from all sides as well. Several states including Connecticut, New Jersey, and Maryland have already passed laws prohibiting this practice.

I'm a 38 year old husband and father in Connecticut and am thankful for the action my legislators have taken against surveillance pricing, but in a time where inflation has doubled or tripled prices in the last several years it's easy to see how damaging this would be anyone. I'm urging the FTC to wholly ban surveillance pricing outright because disclosure of a bad practice is not a substitute for fair pricing. Thanks.

comment: Companies already have an enormous informational advantage over consumers. Sites like Expedia claim to offer the best pricing on travel bookings but it's very hard to know whether that is true, and that's when the underlying argument is "demand management". The idea is that as a flight fills up, supply and demand dictates that ticket prices should rise. There is, at least, a fig leaf of respectability to that argument. The idea that any company can aggregate data from all over the web and use that information to decide that I can afford to pay more for a good or service than they think my neighbor will pay is just price gouging. Unless we move to bargaining about everything, which would be horribly inefficient, all trust in commerce will be lost. I would guess that the boost in profits would be short-lived and the end result will be a retrenchment of consumer spending to essential goods and services only. The societally correct way to deal with inequality is to return to a more progressive system of taxation with public allocation of the resulting funds, not facilitating price gouging by large, powerful corporations. Please oppose any and all attempts to permit "personalized pricing" or any other use of technology that further disadvantages consumers.

comment:
I am glad to see the Federal Trade Commission acknowledge the harms of "surveillance pricing" on consumers, but this isn't enough; you need to stop this practice entirely.

Your report is filled with instances of the dangers of surveillance pricing, including charging more based on data that the consumer is homebound, has children, is traveling, has a medical condition, been a victim of crime, and more. Research by the Commission confirmed the more these practices grow, consumers will be irreparably hurt while those companies gain immensely - it's just wrong. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices based on their personal information.

You must outlaw and prohibit surveillance pricing completely. Disclosure is no substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they must pay more because a data broker estimated their willingness to pay doesn't undo the harm nor hold those overcharging them accountable. It simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. You all, the Commission, even acknowledged that 2/3 of Americans don't understand what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot avoid higher prices they cannot see.

I urge the FTC to use your full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Please do this quickly, this practice is creeping up on all of us regular people/consumer. Thank you.

comment:
Please absolutely prohibit "personalized" aka surveillance pricing entirely. No consumer wants this, and we already have seen many instances where this practice has just made necessary purchases more expensive. I myself am a person in my sixties on a limited income, and I'm dismayed that corporations are even trying to institute this tactic. The whole purpose of the government is to work to improve the lives of the people, not to line the pockets of vulture corporations who are surveilling us, selling our data, and developing personalized profiles to sell to retailers so they can set rates according to what they think individual people are willing to pay. If you have more than one person using your family Amazon or Walmart account and one person splurges and makes an expensive purchase, presumable this will artificially inflate what surveillance pricing thinks your whole family might be able to pay. Worse yet, they will then only present you with the highest prices, effectively removing your ability to choose. This also means that other corporations who have bought your data for this purpose will do the same thing, thereby removing any ability to choose. We have already seen digital price tags popping up at Walmart. As someone eon a limited income, I am frightened about what corporations may do to prices for everyday necessities like food and toiletries, and I am angry at the invasion of my privacy. What about all the data these companies have already gathered about us by saying they would keep this data but not use it in such a way that anybody would be personally identifiable? Somehow that promise seems to have fallen to the wayside. Please don't allow surveillance pricing to be legal.
This is a disgusting, immoral practice, and the Federal Trade commission needs not just to recognize the potential for abuse in surveillance pricing but also just shut it down as soon as possible.

comment:
I am delighted to witness the Federal Trade Commission acknowledging the detrimental effects of “surveillance pricing” on consumers. However, mere recognition is insufficient; the practice itself must be curtailed.

The Commission’s report provides numerous examples illustrating the perilous nature of surveillance pricing. It highlights instances where companies charge higher prices based on data indicating a consumer’s homebound status, having young children, traveling for a funeral, experiencing a medical emergency, or having recently been a victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission underscores that as these practices become more sophisticated, the likelihood of consumers benefiting diminishes, and gains for some are accompanied by losses for others. comment: I’ve worked with consumer protection laws since I was an intern in law school. Dynamic pricing that permits businesses to ‘read’ a customer’s need and willingness to pay more than fair market value (which is NOT an ‘individualized’ price) runs contrary to free market capitalism and effectively equips businesses to exploit a part of the pricing spectrum that includes price gouging. AI is already at the point where it can very readily process information that provides a one sided information advantage to commercial sellers with no counterpart benefit whatsoever to consumers: there is no dynamic information flow about excess inventory, poor product reception, or unusually large returns of defective products which alerts consumers where pricing should be lower — dynamic pricing is exclusively a price-raising tool. If you are not yet alert to the risks driven by commercial AI adoption, this dynamic pricing area is replete with opportunities for unintended and unforeseen bad consequences for consumers. Regulators of every stripe should be extremely cautious about enabling commercial applications of AI in ways that can circumvent fair market pricing based on a theoretical willing buyer and willing seller and instead equip one side to re-price on individualized data analysis. I worked for the Dept of Justice for a half dozen years and in private practice for 20 representing primarily business interests; the job of govt incudes a major component of protecting consumers vs business interests; business will take care of itself and hire able advocates and lobbyists.

comment:
It's encouraging that the FTC is finally acknowledging how harmful “surveillance pricing” is for consumers, but it's not enough to really protect people. This practice needs to END.

The FTC's own report makes the danger obvious. When companies can use personal data to charge higher prices to people who are homebound, caring for young children, traveling for a funeral, dealing with a medical crisis, or recovering from a crime, it's unfair and solely down to take advantage of their situations. The research used by the FTC shows that as these tactics grow more sophisticated, consumers benefit less—and any advantage for one group comes at the direct expense of another. Those who are already vulnerable end up paying the most, exactly because their private circumstances are being mined and monetized. This is so cynical, manipulative and troubling. We should be able to trust the companies we deal with, especially in times like these where every dollar is stretched to the limit.

So, I’m urging the Commission to ban surveillance pricing outright. Transparency is not enough to achieve fairness. Telling someone they’re being charged more because a data broker has labeled them “willing to pay” doesn’t undo the harm; it simply forces people who are sick, grieving, or in distress to navigate predatory pricing in the moment. The FTC itself notes that most Americans have little understanding of how their data is used, and consumers cannot avoid price discrimination they cannot see.

Simply put, if the FTC has demonstrated how harmful surveillance pricing is, so why is it allowing to continue? If the government knew that a specific kind of food had an overwhelming chance of causing illness in a consumer, would they simply slap on a label warning the consumer or would they remove the product from the shelves? New Jersey's government recently decided it was right to prohibit retailers from using shoppers’ personal data to charge different prices for identical products and for good reason.

I strongly encourage the FTC to use its full authority to prohibit surveillance pricing rather than merely require companies to disclose it.

Thank you for your consideration.

Summary
The Commission's proposed disclosure-based framework does not merely regulate surveillance pricing — it legitimizes it. By establishing a compliance pathway (disclosure) rather than a prohibition, the FTC signals that surveillance pricing is a permissible business practice so long as procedural boxes are checked. This memo objects on two central grounds, with three supporting concerns.
Objection 1: The FTC Lacks Authority to Confer Permission Through Guidance
The FTC Act empowers the Commission to prohibit "unfair or deceptive acts or practices" — it does not empower the FTC to authorize practices that the underlying statute treats as presumptively unfair. Yet by proceeding through an informal Enforcement Policy Statement rather than formal rulemaking, the Commission avoids the notice-and-comment rigor and judicial scrutiny that would normally attach to a policy change of this magnitude, while still producing the practical effect of a rule: firms that comply with disclosure requirements gain a defensible safe harbor, and surveillance pricing becomes normalized business practice.
This is regulation by press release. An agency cannot use sub-regulatory guidance to accomplish what it lacks authority — or has not sought authority — to do through the procedures Congress and the APA require for binding rules. The disclosure framework does not merely fail to stop surveillance pricing; it affirmatively legitimizes it by giving firms a compliance checklist to follow instead of a practice to avoid. Under Loper Bright, agencies receive no deference on the scope of their own statutory authority — and the Commission should not be permitted to expand the boundaries of permissible pricing conduct through a mechanism designed to avoid that very scrutiny.
Objection 2: Surveillance Pricing Will Raise Prices Broadly, Not Just for the Wealthy
Proponents defend surveillance pricing using classical price-discrimination theory: charging high-willingness-to-pay consumers more allows firms to lower prices for low-willingness-to-pay consumers, expanding output and total welfare. That model was built on a world of static, infrequent, human-set prices and limited firm information about any individual buyer. It does not describe the current environment, in which:
Pricing is now dynamic and individualized at scale. AI-driven systems can adjust prices in real time based on granular behavioral, locational, and inferred financial data — a capability the historical economic models never contemplated and cannot reliably extend to.
The "low-end subsidy" is not guaranteed. Firms are not obligated to pass surveillance-derived margin gains to lower-income consumers as lower prices; nothing in the proposed policy requires it, and competitive pressure to do so is weak in concentrated markets.
Personalized pricing removes the disciplining function of a single posted price. A public price is a competitive signal that other firms and consumers can react to. When every consumer sees a different, privately computed price, that signal disappears — softening price competition market-wide and creating upward pressure on the effective price floor, not just the ceiling.
The practical result is more likely to be a general upward drift in prices, with the data-poor, less price-sensitive, and less tech-literate — not simply "the rich" — bearing disproportionate cost.
Supporting Concerns
Algorithmic collusion. Shared third-party pricing vendors give nominally competing firms a mechanism for tacit coordination without any explicit agreement — the "hub-and-spoke" theory DOJ has already pursued (e.g., the RealPage settlement). A disclosure-only framework does nothing to address this risk and may make such arrangements easier to defend as "compliant."
Perverse data-harvesting incentive. Personalized pricing directly monetizes the collection of consumer data, creating a financial incentive for firms to maximize surveillance — in direct tension with the FTC's own privacy enforcement mission.
Disparate impact. Pricing inputs such as zip code, device type, and browsing history function as proxies for protected characteristics. Absent affirmative safeguards, surveillance pricing risks reproducing discriminatory outcomes without requiring — or permitting easy detection of — discriminatory intent.
Conclusion
The Commission should withdraw the proposed policy statement and pursue any change to its treatment of surveillance pricing through formal rulemaking, with a presumption against — not accommodation of — data-driven individualized pricing absent a clear showing that consumer welfare is protected in practice, not merely in theory.

comment:
I’m strongly against corporations mining my personal and financial data to decide what I can pay for their services. That is what they want to do with “personalized pricing.” This is not a plan to help people afford things, Rather, it is a plan to let corporations decide what I can and cannot afford for me, making extra money from those they deem can “afford” more. Furthermore, how can consumers budget when prices are individualized and variable? “Personalized pricing” is a privacy violation and a greedy scheme that will hurt consumers and the American public.

Using our personal data to set variable prices is not the job of companies in a free market, and consumers won’t put up with it.

Instead of greenlighting this buyer-manopulation scheme, the FTC should be working to protect consumers from corporate manipulation and unauthorized use of our personal data. The FTC should be working with Congress and consumers to protect our data, which belongs to us, not to corporations.

This scheme, and the FTC’s proposal to let it happen if consumers are told ahead of time is yet another corporate giveaway from this adminIstration that has shown its true colors—that corruption, giving our tax dollars to billionaires, and making policies that benefit corporations and wealthy over the majority if Americans is their only focus. Do not greenlight this scheme.

The FTC must reject “personalized pricing” and work, instead, to protect the American people.

comment:
The FTC deserves credit for naming the harm of personalized pricing, but recognition without prohibition leaves the harm in place.

The Commission's own August 19, 2026 proposed policy statement lays out the practice in stark terms: charging more because someone can't leave home, is traveling for a funeral, needs emergency medical transport, was recently a crime victim, or has young children. This isn't hypothetical — it's the FTC's own list.

Research the Commission cites confirms the danger scales with sophistication: the more precisely companies can personalize prices, the less consumers benefit overall, and gains for some come paired with losses for others.

Disclosure is not a remedy. Telling someone mid-crisis that they're being charged more based on a data broker's guess about their desperation does not undo the harm — it just narrates the exploitation in real time.

Two-thirds of Americans (Pew Research, 2023) say they understand little or nothing about what companies do with their personal data. A disclosure regime built on "your data was used to raise this price" asks people to police a system they cannot see and cannot meaningfully opt out of.

The FTC should use its full authority to prohibit personalized pricing built on data about consumer vulnerability — not merely require companies to admit they're doing it.

We are pushing for healthcare institutions to publish their prices but we will allow momentary changes for food items? This is NOT allowing the controls one expects in a marketplace to function. We no longer can shop for the highest quality item at a reasonable price.

Thank you for considering my opinion.
Geralynn Kahn

It seems the epitome of irony for the Federal Trade Commission to both acknowledge the existence of surveillance pricing skewing what we each pay for goods and services, and to let that discriminatory practice remain. In what America would that ever have been okay? Bilking individual consumers in any fashion is wrong; sneaking into our private lives to further augment the thefts is despicable. The saddest part for me is having no choice or control over how much more I may unknowingly pay for something in order to feed the already-best fed billionaies and corporations! Gluttony and greed are destroying us, our earnings, our health, our quality of life.

It feels to me that by acknowledging this greed but not moving to end it, the Federal Trade Commission is perhaps even in on the spoils. I am not a politician nor an economist, but I do know right from wrong, and my heart aches for us all.

Please listen to the people who share their very humbling and personal comments to convince our government to do the right thing and end this atrocious, discriminating practice.

Thank you.

comment:
:

I am glad to see the Federal Trade Commission recognize the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but recognition is not enough—the practice itself must be stopped.

The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.
To be blunt, "surveillance pricing" (what corporations are trying to euphemistically call, "personalized pricing") has no differences from the price-gouging that some unscrupulous individuals have attempted after many natural disasters!! I am reminded of one case from the Pandemic, several years ago (which you may also remember), where some individuals attempted to buy out the entire supply of alcohol-based hand cleaner in their region. They intended to charge many times the usual price for this material, and expected to profit greatly, due to people's need to clean & disinfect their hands during a global emergency. Their plan was exposed, deemed criminal, and they paid a stiff price for their actions. Why should similar behavior be legitimized simply because a large corporation has decided that _they_ are somehow above basic decency & the law??

I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.
I regularly photograph items that I intend to buy where they sit on store-shelves (making sure to include the price-tag on the shelf); too many times a store has tried to charge me more for an item that was, "accidentally misplaced" by the wrong price-tag. Since I keep track of the total price of the items I bring to the checkout, it's easy to know if a price has changed. If I have the time, I take the clerk to the shelf, (show them the photo, too), and prove that the price I saw on the shelf doesn't match what they are now trying to charge (otherwise I just leave the item at the checkout, refusing to pay the altered higher price). comment:
I oppose the concept and practice of Personalized Pricing. I do not want my shopping habits "surveilled" (any more than I want Flock cameras invading my privacy), and I certainly do not want them "surveilled" so that I can be charged more to do my shopping. There is no reason any company or merchant is entitled to my individual preferences. They can figure out larger scale trends and price accordingly, but they have no right to gather data specific to me -- except with my consent and compensation. I always attempt to determine when I'm being 'surveilled' on line with cookies and make a point of turning off targeting/advertising cookies. I do not object to companies gathering mass data that is useful for their business needs but they have absolutely no right to my individual preferences.

The role of the FTC is to promote fair competition and safeguard consumer interests in the marketplace. Why is this even being considered? What people mean by "drain the swamp" is getting rid of practices such as the one being proposed on behalf of the 'big guys' - companies and corporations, and siding with and helping the 'people' - us little guys, the consumers who keep the economy rolling but are having a heck of a hard time right now with the way things are priced. Work for us -- do not allow surveillance that would enable personalized pricing.

comment:
I am glad to see the Federal Trade Commission recognize the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but recognition is not enough—the practice itself must be stopped.

The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it.
It has become too hard to afford everyday living for most people-allowing companies to use this technology to gouge us more will only hurt American families and enrich billion-dollar companies in the short term, harming us all and the economy in the long run. It is getting so hard to continue to afford basic necessities, with prices for everything rising, the American people cannot afford to be squeezed even further-at some point it will break us all and where will the corporations and big-business be able to turn to for profits then? Please do not allow them to have another opportunity rake in even more profit at the expense of the American people-American families need more help and opportunities, not giant corporations again!
Thank you

comment:
As someone who relies on SSI and SNAP to survive (and who often relies on grocery delivery due to mobility issues), "surveillance pricing" worries me greatly. I am glad to see the Federal Trade Commission recognize the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but recognition is not enough.

The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous "surveillance pricing" is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, had a medical emergency, is traveling, has been the victim of a crime, etc. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable of us end up paying the highest prices, based on our most intimate personal information. This is blatantly unfair!

I urge the Commission to prohibit "surveillance pricing" outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban "surveillance pricing" rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you for your time.

comment:
I am writing as an American consumer to express my strong concern about personalized pricing based on consumer data.

I understand that prices naturally change because of supply, demand, location, sales, competition, and changes in a company's costs. That is different from using information collected about an individual consumer to determine how much that particular person may be willing or able to pay.

Consumers should not have to wonder whether the person standing next to them is being offered a different price simply because an algorithm knows more about their shopping history, browsing behavior, location, purchasing habits, or other personal information.

I am especially concerned about what this could mean for ordinary working and middle-class families. The more accurately a company can determine how badly someone needs a product or how unlikely they are to shop elsewhere, the greater the opportunity becomes to extract the maximum amount that particular consumer will tolerate. That creates an enormous imbalance of information and bargaining power between businesses and consumers.

I also believe there is an important difference between offering discounts that consumers knowingly qualify for and secretly calculating individualized prices using data consumers may not even realize has been collected about them.

At a minimum, consumers should have a clear right to know when personal information is being used to determine the price or offer they receive. Consumers should also be able to purchase ordinary goods without surrendering extensive behavioral data simply to receive fair pricing.

Personally, I would prefer stronger protections that prevent retailers from using personal behavioral data to charge different consumers different base prices for the same ordinary product at the same place and time.

Technology can make a business more efficient without being used to determine the maximum amount of money that can be extracted from each individual customer.

A fair marketplace requires consumers to be able to understand the transaction they are entering. Personalized pricing based on hidden consumer profiling threatens that trust.

I urge the Federal Trade Commission to adopt strong protections for consumers and to continue examining how personal data, algorithms, artificial intelligence, and behavioral tracking are being used in pricing decisions before these practices become normalized.

I’m glad the Federal Trade Commission recognizes the harms of “surveillance pricing,” but it must be stopped, not just noted.

The Commission’s report shows how dangerous it is: charging higher prices based on data about a consumer’s homebound status, young children, travel for a funeral, medical emergencies, or recent crime. Research confirms that these practices become more sophisticated, reducing consumer benefits and causing losses to others. Vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices based on their personal information.

I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright. Disclosure alone isn’t enough. Telling consumers they’re being charged more because of a data broker’s estimate doesn’t undo the harm. It only asks them to opt out of real-time exploitation. The Commission acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little about companies’ data practices, and consumers can’t avoid higher prices they can’t see.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing, not just require disclosure.

I am glad to see the Federal Trade Commission finally recognize the threat that “surveillance pricing” poses to American consumers. But another government report is not enough. This abusive practice needs to be stopped.

For years, Americans have watched Big Tech, data brokers, and massive corporations collect more and more information about our private lives. Now that information can be weaponized against us to determine how much companies think they can get away with charging.

The FTC’s own report gives disturbing examples. A company could charge an American more because its data shows that person is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, is dealing with a medical emergency, or was recently the victim of a crime.

That is not capitalism. That is not a free market. That is a rigged system.

In a real free market, Americans see the price, compare their options, and decide whether to buy. They should not be secretly profiled by algorithms and charged a different price because some data broker has decided they are desperate enough, wealthy enough, sick enough, or vulnerable enough to pay more.

Our personal data belongs to us. It should not be weaponized against us.

The FTC should put American consumers ahead of Big Tech, data brokers, and corporate special interests and ban surveillance pricing outright.

No loopholes. No fine-print disclosures. No secret algorithms deciding how much an American can be squeezed for.

Give Americans a fair price and keep our private lives out of it.

comment:
I write as a concerned senior citizen to urge the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) not to condone "personalized/surveillance pricing" by merely requiring businesses to disclose using it, but instead to end the practice entirely.
Documents issued by the FTC itself (e.g., https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/p246202_surveillancepricing6bstudy_researchsummaries_redacted.pdf; https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/p034101-ftc-enforcement-policy-statement-re-personalized-pricing-proposed-for-public-comment.pdf) provide many examples showing how pernicious surveillance pricing is: for example,  charging higher prices on the basis of data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the FTC confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. It is the most vulnerable consumers who pay the highest prices, harmed by the exploitation of their most intimate personal information.
The dangers of personalized pricing were discussed in a hearing held by the Senate Judiciary Committee’s Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism on August 4 entitled “Your Data, Their Profit: The Consumer Cost of AI Surveillance Pricing.” The outcome of the hearing was bipartisan recognition of the pernicious effects of the practice and the need for federal standards and laws; until such legislation is implemented, t was recommended that the FTC employ its existing authority to protect
I urge the FTC to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because its intention to “enforce aggressively” requirements for disclosure is simply not a substitute for fair pricing. The proposal in question effectively leaves Americans with no defense against being exploited. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it merely asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

I strongly urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it.
Thank you for your attention.

comment:
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Federal Trade Commission’s Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing.

The Federal Trade Commission has taken positive step in recognizing the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers. Recognition is not enough and the practice itself must be prohibited.

The Commission's report shows that the most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information. The report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime.

I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm, it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time.

The Federal Trade Commission recognizes the harms that "surveillance pricing" imposes on to consumers, but recognition is the first step—this new business scheme must be rolled back

The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. Money is tight for me because of my low income. People like me who live paycheck to paycheck pay the highest prices, based on my personal information that this business scheme can exploit upon.

I implore the Commission to stop surveillance pricing because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

I seek the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. Money is tight for me because of my low income. People like me who live paycheck to paycheck pay the highest prices, based on my personal information that this business scheme can exploit upon.

I implore the Commission to stop surveillance pricing because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

I seek the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

So called "personal pricing" is a bias system made by to boost corporate profits and nothing more. Price gouging for the modern age.

AI models are already notorious for miscalculations and there is no reliable way to train it to accurately project what a person can or should pay for an item without infringing upon their privacy and/or rights. The software that these models would have to be built upon would be subjective speculation based on a person's appearance (aka how much do they look like they can pay compared to whatever average they are attributing to certain looks) or past spending/earning data either factually (based on facial recognition and personal data collection), or speculative as well depending on how the AI model is trained. BOTH of these options are unacceptable. Why should anyone get to decide who should pay what for the same item based on the way that person looks or how much they make (or theoretically would spend)? Who is held accountable for mistakes when they are inevitably exposed? Would there be a refund or refutal process? What safeguards are there against racism, sexism, ageism, and so on? And more importantly how is this helping anyone except for company bottom lines?

The price of an item should be based on ITS worth and value, NEVER the person buying it. The only acceptable way personal pricing could go would be to allow those who can't afford the deemed fair market price for an item could pay less, but NOT the other way around; and even then it shouldn't be decided by a machine trained by prejudice profiling or dubious data collection.

comment:
I am writing as a Florida consumer to support the Commission's proposed enforcement policy statement and to urge the Commission to go further.

Personalized pricing breaks a basic promise of the marketplace: that the price on the shelf or the screen is the price, full stop. When a retailer charges me more because its data suggests I have children at home, am unlikely to comparison shop, or am standing in its parking lot, it is not responding to supply and demand. It is exploiting what it knows about me. That is not a market price. It is a penalty for being surveilled.

The Commission is right that these practices are deceptive when undisclosed. Consumers cannot avoid a higher price they do not know exists. But I ask the Commission to reconsider footnote 20, where it declines to say whether personalized pricing is unfair even when fully disclosed. Disclosure is not a cure here. Most people cannot audit the data brokers, purchase histories, and behavioral models behind a price, and the tools the statement mentions — VPNs, private browsing, abandoning the transaction — are not realistic defenses for a parent buying milk or a person getting a ride to the emergency room. A clear disclosure that says "you are paying more because we think you can afford it" informs the consumer without protecting her.

The economic research the Commission cites confirms the concern: personalized pricing reliably raises profits while shifting costs onto the consumers least able to avoid them, and it gets worse for consumers as the practice grows more sophisticated. The Commission should not wait for those harms to become entrenched before acting.

I ask the Commission to:

1. Treat undisclosed personalized pricing for everyday goods and services as presumptively unfair under Section 5, not merely deceptive.
2. State that basing prices on sensitive data — health, family composition, financial distress, location inside a store, or victim status — is unfair regardless of disclosure.
3. Require that any permitted personalization be accompanied by a plain-language explanation and an easy way to see and opt out of the non-personalized price.

Consumers should not need to hide from a store in order to be charged fairly by it. Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

I submit this comment as a New York City resident, consumer, and attorney. I support the FTC’s proposed enforcement policy statement regarding personalized pricing, but urge the Commission to strengthen it before adoption.

New York State’s law illustrates the limits of generic notice. It requires: “THIS PRICE WAS SET BY AN ALGORITHM USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA.” That tells a consumer personalization occurred, but not which data were used, what inference was drawn, where the information came from, or whether it raised or lowered the price. A broad reference to “personal data,” “device information,” or “location” is not meaningful disclosure.

During several months in which an injury limited my mobility, I relied more heavily on app-based transportation for medical appointments. I sometimes observed higher quoted fares for trips to medical facilities than for social trips of comparable distance at similar times. I cannot determine whether the destination, my travel history, market conditions, or something else affected those quotations. That inability to know is the problem: the platform possesses the information and controls the pricing system, while the consumer sees only the result.

I have also seen friends perform side-by-side comparisons and receive different quotations for similar transactions, including when an account with a card-linked ride credit appeared to receive a higher quotation that reduced the credit’s value. These informal comparisons do not establish causation. They show why consumers need transaction-specific information. If a stored balance, membership, payment instrument, or credit affects the reference or final price, that fact should be disclosed.

Personalized pricing may give some consumers lower prices, but that does not make it an affordability program. A profit-maximizing system may lower a price for someone predicted to reject a transaction while raising it for someone predicted to buy regardless. “Price sensitive” is not synonymous with “low income,” and “willingness to pay” is not synonymous with “ability to pay.” A person with limited income may pay more because an emergency, disability, caregiving obligation, or lack of alternatives makes a purchase unavoidable.

FTC staff has identified tools capable of using device information, language settings, geolocation, purchase and browsing histories, cart activity, loyalty, promotional responses, and inferred price sensitivity. These tools were marketed as increasing revenue, margins, and profits. Personalized pricing can therefore increase profit without improving the product or service.

These inputs can also act as proxies for sensitive or protected characteristics. A medical destination, mobility pattern, ZIP code, language setting, or household purchasing pattern may reveal information the system never labels as disability, race, national origin, religion, or familial status. The FTC need not rely on group-level disparate impact. Disclosure and preservation of the actual inputs would reveal how an individual was treated.

I recommend that the final statement:

1. Require an adjacent, transaction-specific notice stating that the price was personalized, whether personalization raised or lowered it, and by how much relative to a defined non-personalized benchmark.
2. Require disclosure of the material data and inferences actually used, their sources, and their direction of influence, rather than a generic list of data the company might use.
3. Require companies to retain and provide the contemporaneous non-personalized benchmark.
4. Provide a meaningful non-personalized pricing option where feasible.
5. Recognize that disclosure may not cure pricing based on medical emergencies, disability, inability to leave home, funerals, safety threats, or other circumstances limiting meaningful choice.
6. Require companies claiming affordability benefits to substantiate who receives lower prices, who pays more, and the distribution of both effects.
7. Cover fees, discounts, promotional eligibility, reference prices, rankings, availability, subscriptions, and other terms affecting effective cost.
8. Require separate consent, with access to and correction of material data and inferences.
9. Require retailers, platforms, data brokers, and pricing intermediaries to preserve records identifying the inputs, benchmark, adjustment, and responsible parties.

I submit this comment as a New York City resident, consumer, and attorney. I support the FTC’s proposed enforcement policy statement regarding personalized pricing, but urge the Commission to strengthen it before adoption.

New York State’s law illustrates the limits of generic notice. It requires: “THIS PRICE WAS SET BY AN ALGORITHM USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA.” That tells a consumer personalization occurred, but not which data were used, what inference was drawn, where the information came from, or whether it raised or lowered the price. A broad reference to “personal data,” “device information,” or “location” is not meaningful disclosure.

During several months in which an injury limited my mobility, I relied more heavily on app-based transportation for medical appointments. I sometimes observed higher quoted fares for trips to medical facilities than for social trips of comparable distance at similar times. I cannot determine whether the destination, my travel history, market conditions, or something else affected those quotations. That inability to know is the problem: the platform possesses the information and controls the pricing system, while the consumer sees only the result.

I have also seen friends perform side-by-side comparisons and receive different quotations for similar transactions, including when an account with a card-linked ride credit appeared to receive a higher quotation that reduced the credit’s value. These informal comparisons do not establish causation. They show why consumers need transaction-specific information. If a stored balance, membership, payment instrument, or credit affects the reference or final price, that fact should be disclosed.

Personalized pricing may give some consumers lower prices, but that does not make it an affordability program. A profit-maximizing system may lower a price for someone predicted to reject a transaction while raising it for someone predicted to buy regardless. “Price sensitive” is not synonymous with “low income,” and “willingness to pay” is not synonymous with “ability to pay.” A person with limited income may pay more because an emergency, disability, caregiving obligation, or lack of alternatives makes a purchase unavoidable.

FTC staff has identified tools capable of using device information, language settings, geolocation, purchase and browsing histories, cart activity, loyalty, promotional responses, and inferred price sensitivity. These tools were marketed as increasing revenue, margins, and profits. Personalized pricing can therefore increase profit without improving the product or service.

These inputs can also act as proxies for sensitive or protected characteristics. A medical destination, mobility pattern, ZIP code, language setting, or household purchasing pattern may reveal information the system never labels as disability, race, national origin, religion, or familial status. The FTC need not rely on group-level disparate impact. Disclosure and preservation of the actual inputs would reveal how an individual was treated.

I recommend that the final statement:

1. Require an adjacent, transaction-specific notice stating that the price was personalized, whether personalization raised or lowered it, and by how much relative to a defined non-personalized benchmark.
2. Require disclosure of the material data and inferences actually used, their sources, and their direction of influence, rather than a generic list of data the company might use.
3. Require companies to retain and provide the contemporaneous non-personalized benchmark.
4. Provide a meaningful non-personalized pricing option where feasible.
5. Recognize that disclosure may not cure pricing based on medical emergencies, disability, inability to leave home, funerals, safety threats, or other circumstances limiting meaningful choice.
6. Require companies claiming affordability benefits to substantiate who receives lower prices, who pays more, and the distribution of both effects.
7. Cover fees, discounts, promotional eligibility, reference prices, rankings, availability, subscriptions, and other terms affecting effective cost.
8. Require separate consent, with access to and correction of material data and inferences.
9. Require retailers, platforms, data brokers, and pricing intermediaries to preserve records identifying the inputs, benchmark, adjustment, and responsible parties.

If a store owner said, “I am charging you more because your bag suggests wealth,” or “because you appear exhausted and unlikely to leave,” the reason would plainly be material. An algorithm does not make that reason less material. It only makes it invisible.

comment:
As a suburban shopper for a family of four, I am glad to see the Federal Trade Commission recognize the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but recognition is not enough—the practice itself must be stopped.

The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

Does it account for the money I send her for the things she can't afford herself? Can surveillance pricing guarantee the poor won't become more poor, the middle class more financially vulnerable, and the rich just more rich as if they weren't rich enough? comment:
Attn: FTC:

Although I am glad to see that the Federal Trade Commission recognizes the harm that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, recognition is simply not enough – the practice itself must be stopped.

I live in California where I would expect the obscene practice of surveillance pricing will start, if it has not already! I believe the practice is unethical and wrong, and I would avoid any store that was implementing it. If I wanted to "negotiate" the price on everything I purchased or be tracked in any way, especially for purposes of adjusting an item’s price, I would shop only at "souks.” As it is, inflation is making life more difficult for people to purchase even basic needs. Unfortunately, I have read that even grocery stores might implement this practice – increasing a food item’s price because someone seems to want it is unconscionable. People may circle back to something as they consider if they can afford it and increasing the price makes such concerns even worse! Frankly, it is bad enough that groceries are a stretch for many people, allowing any form of surveillance pricing is simply unconscionable.

The Commission's own report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm – it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot practically avoid higher prices they cannot see.

Personally, I believe it is time for the federal government to come up with strong privacy provisions so people can go about their lives without becoming data points to be exploited by big corporations at every turn. But until such privacy provisions are passed, the very least that should happen is for consumers to be protected from the truly onerous and disgusting practice of surveillance pricing!

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

comment:
I am concerned about the growing use of what is being called “personalized pricing” or “surveillance pricing.” While the terminology may make it sound like a benefit to consumers, I believe it creates a significant risk of allowing corporations to charge different prices to different people based on the personal data they collect about them.

If a retailer such as Walmart can use information about a customer to determine that the customer is likely able to afford more, that retailer could potentially charge that person a higher price for the same product. This is essentially using big data to make goods and services even more expensive for consumers who are identified as being able to pay more.

I am also concerned that simply requiring companies to disclose that they are using this type of pricing would not adequately protect consumers. Disclosure does not make an unfair pricing practice fair. Consumers generally do not have the ability to understand what information is being collected about them, how that information is being analyzed, or how it is being used to determine the price they are offered.

Even if one believes that wealthier consumers should pay more, I do not believe corporations should be the ones making that determination and keeping the additional money as profit. If society believes that people with greater financial resources should contribute more, that should be accomplished through a fair and transparent tax system, with the resulting revenue used for purposes that benefit the public.

I urge the FTC to consider the broader implications of surveillance-based pricing and not treat disclosure alone as sufficient protection for consumers. Americans should not have to wonder whether the price they are being shown is based on what an algorithm has determined they can afford rather than the actual cost or value of the product.

comment:
We are glad to see the Federal Trade Commission recognize the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but recognition is not enough—the practice itself must be stopped.

The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

We urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

We urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

comment:
I strongly support the FTC taking action to protect consumers from undisclosed personalized pricing.
Consumers should be able to reasonably expect that when they see a price for a product, that price is not secretly being increased or decreased based on their individual data, income, purchasing history, browsing behavior, location, or perceived willingness to pay.
There is an important difference between openly advertised discounts—such as loyalty programs, coupons, or membership prices—and a system that secretly calculates what an individual consumer can or will pay and then adjusts the price accordingly. The latter undermines transparency and makes meaningful price comparison nearly impossible.
Personalized pricing also raises serious concerns about fairness and privacy. A consumer who has purchased an item frequently, has fewer competing options, or has previously demonstrated a willingness to pay more should not unknowingly be penalized with a higher price for the same product simply because a company has collected and analyzed information about them.
At a minimum, companies engaging in personalized pricing should be required to clearly and prominently disclose that the price is personalized, what categories of personal information are being used, and how that information affects the price. Consumers should also have a meaningful way to opt out.
I urge the FTC to use its authority under Section 5 of the FTC Act to protect consumers from deceptive or unfair personalized pricing practices. A marketplace cannot be truly fair when consumers do not know whether the price they see is the same price being offered to everyone else.
Consumers deserve transparent prices, meaningful choice, and the ability to make purchasing decisions without being subjected to undisclosed individualized pricing algorithms.

Consumers should be customers—not targets whose personal data is used against them to determine how much they can be charged.

Consumers should be able to reasonably expect that when they see a price for a product, that price is not secretly being increased or decreased based on their individual data, income, purchasing history, browsing behavior, location, or perceived willingness to pay.

Consumers should be customers—not targets whose personal data is used against them to determine how much they can be changed.
