comment:
I am completely opposed to allowing companies to use personalized or surveillance pricing to charge consumers different prices for the exact same product or service based on personal information.

I understand that prices can legitimately change because of supply and demand. But there is a fundamental difference between saying, “This product costs more because demand is unusually high,” and saying, “This product costs more for YOU because our algorithm believes you are willing or able to pay more.” The first reflects the market. The second exploits the individual.

We have already seen how problematic dynamic pricing can become with live-event tickets, where consumers can be shown rapidly changing prices and end up paying dramatically more for the same seats. The FTC has recognized that dynamic pricing itself is currently permitted for live-event tickets, provided the pricing is not misleading. I myself paid $200 per ticket for a Bob Dylan concert and when I asked the person sitting next to me how much they paid, they had paid $150 per ticket. So I have first-hand experience. Why is FTC allowing this?

Today it may be concert or soccer tickets. Tomorrow, it could be groceries. Imagine two people standing next to each other in a grocery store, picking up the exact same bag of pretzels, yet one is charged $3.49 and the other $5.49 because the retailer's algorithm has determined that one shopper is more likely to pay the higher price. That should concern every American.

Consumers should not have to wonder whether deleting cookies, changing browsers, using a VPN, or shopping from a different location will save them money. We should not create a marketplace where the person who knows the least about how they are being tracked is the person who pays the most.

This could also disproportionately hurt people who can least afford it. A company could potentially identify consumers who are under financial pressure, have limited alternatives, live in areas with fewer competing retailers, or have demonstrated a strong need for a particular product, and then use that information to determine how much they should be charged. That turns personal information into a tool for extracting the maximum possible amount of money from each customer.

That is not a marketplace I want to see in America.

The traditional expectation that the same product has a transparent price is an important protection for consumers. If companies are allowed to quietly replace that system with algorithms that calculate the maximum price each individual might tolerate, consumers lose the ability to comparison-shop on equal footing. The FTC itself has warned that widespread surveillance pricing could fundamentally disrupt the longstanding “same-price-for-everyone” model and create opportunities for deceptive practices and other consumer harms.

Government should protect consumers from abusive practices, not give companies a green light to perfect them.

I strongly urge the FTC to reject any policy that would permit companies to secretly use our personal information to determine how much each of us should pay. Consumers deserve transparent, predictable, and fair pricing. We should know the price of a product because of the product and the market conditions, not because an algorithm has been watching us and decided we can be charged more.

**Please put consumers before corporate profits and establish strong protections against personalized pricing. Once this practice becomes widespread, it may be extremely difficult to put the genie back in the bottle.**

comment:
I strongly support immediate FTC action to protect consumers from undisclosed personalized pricing.
In my small town, stores are remodeling and offering fewer choices in a limited geographic area. When options shrink, hidden price discrimination becomes even more harmful.
Consumers should be able to see a price for a product and reasonably expect that it is not being secretly raised or lowered based on individual data—income, purchase history, browsing behavior, location, or perceived willingness to pay.
There is an important difference between openly advertised discounts—loyalty programs, coupons, or membership prices—and a system that secretly calculates what a particular consumer can or will pay and then adjusts the price. The latter undermines transparency and makes meaningful price comparison nearly impossible.
Personalized pricing also raises serious fairness and privacy concerns. A customer who buys an item often, has fewer competing stores, or has previously shown a willingness to pay more should not be charged extra for the same product simply because a company collected and analyzed information about them.
Circumstances also change. Job loss, a death in the family, and higher prices for gas and groceries have reduced what many households—including mine and people I know well—could afford over the past twelve months. An algorithm built on older data can penalize people who can no longer pay what they once could.
At a minimum, companies that use personalized pricing should be required to disclose, clearly and prominently, that the price is personalized, what categories of personal information are used, and how that information affects the price. Consumers should have an easy way to opt out before they shop, and should receive proof at a kiosk or checkout that they have opted out or enrolled.
I urge the FTC to use its authority under Section 5 of the FTC Act to protect consumers from deceptive or unfair personalized pricing. A marketplace is not fair when shoppers cannot tell whether the price they see is the same price offered to everyone else, or whether it can change between the cart and checkout.
Consumers deserve transparent prices, meaningful choices, and the ability to make purchasing decisions without undisclosed individualized pricing algorithms.
Thank you in advance for your work.

comment:
I strongly oppose the use of personal data to determine the price an individual consumer is charged for a product or service. A consumer’s browsing history, location, purchasing habits, income or other personal information should not be used to estimate what that particular person may be willing or able to pay.

Dynamic pricing based on legitimate market conditions is different from personalized pricing based on surveillance of an individual consumer. Two people purchasing the same product under the same circumstances should not unknowingly be offered different prices because an algorithm has determined that one of them can be charged more.

I do not believe disclosure alone makes this practice acceptable, and I believe it should be prohibited. However, if personalized pricing is permitted, disclosure should be mandatory, immediate and conspicuous. Consumers should be clearly told, in prominent language at the point where the price is displayed, that their personal data was used to determine the price offered to them. This information should not be buried in terms and conditions, privacy policies, fine print or other disclosures that consumers are unlikely to see.

Laurie,

The Federal Trade Commission is considering a new rule that could open the floodgates to new ways for stores to raise prices on you: Surveillance pricing.

They’re calling it “personalized pricing,” but let’s be clear: What stores like Walmart are considering is a way to raise prices on people who the data says can afford it. And that money will go straight to their bottom line. It’s a way to use big data to make things even more expensive than they already are.

The rule that the FTC is currently considering would give corporations a green light to price gouge so long as they disclose that they’re doing it. That’s not good enough. Even if you think the wealthy should pay more, why should corporations be the ones who benefit? If you want the wealthy to pay more, tax the rich, and use the money for something useful to our society!

If you or any of your family members have had experiences with surveillance, surveillance pricing, or struggling with affordability.

Sample comment:

I am glad to see the Federal Trade Commission recognize the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but recognition is not enough—the practice itself must be stopped.

The Commission's report is filled with examples showing how dangerous surveillance pricing is: charging higher prices based on data showing a consumer is homebound, has young children, is traveling for a funeral, has a medical emergency, or has recently been the victim of a crime. Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit, and that gains to some come paired with losses to others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

comment: Not only as a consumer, but also as a small business owner, I am STRONGLY opposed to personalized pricing, as I think it is a violation of our privacy and an unfair way of doing business. The price of an item should never be interchangeable based on a persons income or browsing history, ESPECIALLY when they aren’t even aware of it. I feel extremely uncomfortable walking into many of these big brand stores now, wondering if everything down to my eye movement is being recorded and used against me to ‘build a better business model’. It’s actually insane. This is a great way for the government and big corporations to lose whatever small sliver of trust they still have from us, the people, and for what?? More profits? Most people don’t even know they are essentially handing over sensitive personal information just by parking their car or walking into a store, which is actually terrifying. There is no moral or justifiable reason for personalized pricing, especially at the cost of collecting personalized data and biometrics that 1/10 people are unaware of. I can’t see any scenario in which this ends well for the American people. We need to STOP putting profits over people, especially when those profits aren’t even given back to the working people in the form of healthcare or affordable wages (which is well documented with these big businesses like Walmart, etc). We have gotten so far away from a business model for ALL, and it’s beyond disheartening. Personalized pricing is just the beginning of a surveillance state, and we need to stop it now before it gets out of hand. This should be illegal!!

comment: Hello and thank you for your time. The idea of personalized pricing or "dynamic pricing" as it were, baffles me as it makes shopping seem like buying shares in the stock market. Especially when you consider that the companies implementing this model, are gathering infinite amounts of data on everyone that purchases even simple items in the store. I've completely stopped going to places like Walmart and Target for even implementing this kind of garbage. I would rather not even engage with this type of business practice, and many other people feel the same way, just look at what happened to Wendy's when they implemented a similar pricing model. It's extremely unfair, even more so when you consider that many people in the US don't have the free time to research the "best time" to visit any establishment for the "best price". Just make the same item one dang price and leave it at that! Groceries in general are not stocks! They should not be adjusting prices based on arbitrary numbers such as income, time spent in store, spending habits, etc. I also believe it's anti-humanitarian, as many of these data points that companies collect to administer these pricing models are highly invasive, and many people can't control either their environment,  or even abilities, such as people that are disabled or have controlled income. How would companies like Walmart and Target implement pricing for those folks? What about students in college, men and women in the United States Armed Forces and their families living on base, single mothers working 3 jobs to try and pay for the bills? Many Americans are living paycheck to paycheck, balancing their budget to the dollar, and day by day groceries seem to be getting more expensive. These pricing models will change the price for better or for worse and no one knows in which direction it will go. Consider also that Walmart and other massive chain grocery stores get subsidized through food stamps, in the end the government will be footing a majority of the bill for what people are eating. I implore the FTC to make a decision in regards to personalized pricing that benefits the general public, rather than the mega-corporations that are solely making these decisions to turn a profit by doing the bare minimum. Thank you for your time again.

comment:
I applaud the Federal Trade Commission’s acknowledgement of the harms that "surveillance pricing" poses to consumers, but the FTC must go further to protect Americans from corporate price manipulation and end the practice of so-called “personalized pricing.”
Significant evidence in the Commission's own report illustrates the dangers of surveillance pricing: it shows how corporations use data to increase prices to vulnerable Americans, such as those who are homebound, have young children, are traveling to attend a funeral, are facing medical emergencies, or recently have been the victims of a crime. Again, the Commission’s own research confirms that, as these surveillance practices become more sophisticated, benefits to customers decrease, and that gains to some people will coincide with losses to others. Worst of all, the Commission’s report shows that the data corporations collect on people’s most intimate information will result in the most vulnerable American customers actually paying the highest prices. The most vulnerable among us must be the most protected.
I urge the Commission to prohibit surveillance pricing outright, because disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. Simply telling American customers that they are being charged a higher price because a data broker estimated their willingness to do so does not undo the harm—it simply demands that sick, scared, or stranded people opt out of being exploited in real time or accept that exploitation out of desperation. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see. For these reasons—and more—the FTC should stop corporations from using surveillance (“personalized”) pricing.

comment:
Federal Trade Commission’s Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing
Docket ID: FTC-2026-1057

I am submitting this comment as an individual consumer. I strongly support the FTC taking enforcement action against companies that secretly use personal information to determine how much a particular consumer will be charged.

Consumers reasonably expect that people shopping for the same product or service at the same time will see the same base price. A company should not secretly raise a person’s price after analyzing income, location, browsing history, purchase history, device information, credit information, health information, family status, perceived urgency, or an estimate of how much that person is willing or able to pay.

Personalized pricing is especially concerning for essential goods and services, including groceries, housing, transportation, utilities, medicine, healthcare, insurance, credit, education, and children’s necessities. It could cause people who are already financially vulnerable—or who urgently need a product—to pay more instead of receiving fair treatment.

The risks are even greater when companies rely on data that are inaccurate, outdated, obtained without meaningful consent, or connected to identity theft. A consumer should not be charged a different price because another person used the consumer’s identity, account, device, address, or personal information. Companies using personal data to influence prices must be responsible for verifying accuracy and providing a quick, accessible process for consumers to inspect, dispute, and correct that information.

I ask the FTC to make clear that:

1. A company must clearly and prominently disclose personalized pricing before collecting or using personal information for that purpose and before the consumer begins a transaction.

2. A vague privacy policy or statement hidden in lengthy terms and conditions is not meaningful disclosure or consent.

3. Consumers must be told which categories of information affected the price and whether the information came from the company, a data broker, an advertising platform, an algorithm, or another third party.

4. Consumers must be offered the ordinary, non-personalized price and a genuine option to refuse personalized pricing without losing access to the product or service.

5. Companies should not use sensitive information—such as precise location, health information, disability status, financial hardship, credit information, race, religion, family status, or information about children—to increase prices.

6. Companies must maintain records showing how prices were determined, test their systems for inaccurate and discriminatory outcomes, and preserve information needed for FTC investigations.

7. Companies should be responsible when their vendors, data brokers, algorithms, or artificial-intelligence systems cause deceptive or unfair pricing.

8. Consumers must have a straightforward method to report unauthorized data use, identity theft, price discrimination, and inaccurate information, with access to human review and a written response.

9. The advertised price should be genuine. Businesses should not advertise a lower price to attract consumers and then secretly increase it based on personal data.

10. Violations should result in meaningful enforcement, deletion of improperly obtained data, correction of affected records, and refunds or other appropriate relief for harmed consumers.

The FTC should also distinguish legitimate, clearly disclosed discounts—such as coupons or voluntary loyalty rewards—from secret systems designed to determine the highest price an individual can be pressured to pay. A discount that requires surrendering extensive personal information may not be truly voluntary.

Price discrimination powered by hidden surveillance undermines trust and makes comparison shopping nearly impossible. Consumers deserve to know the actual price, what information is being used, and whether someone else is being offered a different price for the same product or service.

I urge the FTC to adopt and strongly enforce the proposed policy statement, while adding clear requirements for advance disclosure, meaningful consent, data accuracy, correction rights, non-personalized purchasing options, protection of sensitive information, recordkeeping, and accountability for third-party data and automated systems.

Thank you for considering my comment.

To Whom It May Concern,
I am writing to formally report a highly deceptive and anti-consumer pricing practice currently being utilized by Sony Interactive Entertainment on the digital PlayStation Store.
While I am a consumer in this market, I am writing because I have become aware of evidence showing that Sony is actively manipulating the prices of digital video games based on whether a user is logged into their account or browsing as a guest. Multiple public consumer reports and comparisons show that when a user is logged out of their account, the PlayStation Store displays steep discounts on specific games. However, when an established user logs into their PlayStation Network (PSN) account, the exact same game shows a significantly higher price or a smaller discount.
This is a form of personalized surveillance pricing. Sony appears to be using consumer account history, library data, and brand loyalty against their own customers. Because they know an active user is already locked into their closed ecosystem, their algorithm determines it can charge them more than a new or unlogged user.
Because Sony maintains a total digital monopoly on the PlayStation 5 platform—preventing players from buying digital game codes from competitive third-party retailers—consumers have no alternative. They are forced to accept whatever algorithmic price Sony's software decides to generate behind a login screen.
Hiding different price tags behind a user login is a deceptive "dark pattern" and an unfair business practice. Consumers have a right to transparent, consistent pricing, rather than being targeted and penalized based on data collection.
I urge your office to investigate Sony’s digital storefront pricing algorithms to protect consumers from these non-transparent, data-driven pricing schemes.
Thank you for your time and for looking into this matter.

I urge the Commission to go a step further than simply recognizing that surveillance pricing poses harm to consumers and prohibit surveillance pricing outright. Telling a consumer they are being charged more because of a data broker's estimate of their willingness to pay does not undo the harm—it simply asks sick, scared, or stranded people to opt out of being exploited in real time. The Commission itself acknowledges that two-thirds of Americans understand little to nothing about what companies do with their personal data, and that consumers cannot reasonably avoid higher prices they cannot see.

I, like most Americans, have paid more for a product in a moment of desperation, and I don't believe it's ethical or fair to put the onus for avoiding a higher price on consumers in vulnerable positions instead of on companies - especially when those companies are well aware that many of the prices they're raising are on goods that should be considered necessities and they're using our intimate personal data to market to us.

I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it. Thank you.

The Commission's own research confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit. Gains for a few come with losses for many, many others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

Disclosure alone is no substitute for fair pricing for consumers. I urge the FTC to use its full authority to completely ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it! Thank you.

Progressive Secretary, Inc.

Dear Mary l.,

Please submit this comment (anonymously or publicly; your choice) by September 25, 2026 (11:59 PM EDT)

Our action supports a More Perfect Union campaign opposing the Federal Trade Commission’s proposed rule on surveillance pricing. “Surveillance pricing” is when companies change prices based on what the data concludes you’re willing to pay.

Here’s how it works. Data collection companies track your real-time actions, such as your location, device type (like an iPhone or Android), browsing history, and items left in a shopping cart.

Artificial intelligence and algorithms analyze this data to guess your maximum “willingness-to-pay”—the highest price you will accept before walking away. Two people shopping at the same minute may see different prices for the same hotel room, flight, ride-share, or grocery item.

Your comment will be submitted to the FTC.

comment:
I strongly oppose the use of personal consumer data to secretly determine individualized prices.

There is an important difference between dynamic pricing and personalized pricing. I understand that prices can legitimately change because of supply, demand, inventory, time, or market conditions. What I object to is changing the price because an algorithm has determined that a particular individual may be willing, desperate, hurried, loyal, financially able, or otherwise more likely to pay more.

A posted price should describe the price of the product—not the seller's assessment of the person looking at it.

I do not believe disclosure alone adequately protects consumers. A notice telling me that my price has been personalized does not give me equal bargaining power, nor does it undo the extensive collection and analysis of personal information that produced the price.

At minimum, consumers should have a clear right to opt out of personalized pricing and receive a non-personalized price. Businesses should also be required to disclose when personalization occurred, what categories of information were used, and what the non-personalized price would have been.

I also urge the FTC to distinguish clearly between ordinary market-based dynamic pricing and individualized pricing based on personal data. The latter creates opportunities to exploit vulnerability, urgency, disability, age, location, income, browsing behavior, purchasing history, or other characteristics that may have little legitimate relationship to the actual cost or market value of a product.

Consumers should not have to disguise themselves from retailers through private browsing, VPNs, deleted cookies, or other technical measures simply to have confidence that they are being offered a fair price.

If the FTC concludes that its existing statutory authority is insufficient to adequately protect consumers from these practices, I encourage the Commission to clearly identify those limitations so Congress can consider additional consumer-protection legislation.

Using an individual’s browsing history, purchasing behavior, location, financial information, or other personal data to determine how much they will be charged is unacceptable. A company should not be permitted to quietly calculate the highest price a particular person may be willing or able to pay.

At a minimum, pricing practices should be transparent, independently monitored, and based on the product or service being sold, not on a private assessment of the customer’s finances or vulnerability. Consumers deserve equal access to fair pricing and meaningful control over their personal information.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the widespread implementation of "personalized pricing" or "surveillance pricing" practices. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) must take decisive regulatory action to prohibit these anti-consumer, opaque, and inherently discriminatory behaviors.

Personalized pricing—the practice of utilizing surveillance data, algorithmic profiling, and predictive AI to charge different consumers different prices for the exact same product or service—subverts the principles of a fair and competitive marketplace. I urge the FTC to intervene for the following critical reasons:

1. Destruction of Market Transparency and Consumer Trust
A foundational element of a fair market is transparent, uniform pricing. When corporations hide the true value of a good behind individual surveillance walls, consumers lose the ability to compare prices, seek better alternatives, or accurately assess market value. This information asymmetry fundamentally destroys consumer trust and distorts healthy competition.

2. Algorithmic Exploitation of Vulnerability
Surveillance pricing algorithms do not merely analyze general consumer preferences; they actively track behavioral vulnerabilities, urgency, and financial distress. If an individual is purchasing a last-minute flight for a medical emergency, buying essential medications, or shopping during peak stress periods, personalized pricing models allow corporations to exploit that desperation by artificially spiking the price.

3. Reinforcement of Systemic Discrimination
The data profiles used to dictate personalized prices often inherit and amplify existing socioeconomic, racial, and geographic inequalities. Because historical and systemic biases are baked into consumer data, algorithmic pricing models threaten to lock low-income or marginalized communities into higher pricing tiers for essential goods and services, exacerbating wealth disparities under the guise of "dynamic optimization."

4. Extreme Asymmetry of Power
The average consumer lacks the technical tools, data visibility, and time to understand or counteract predictive corporate AI. Corporations hold an unfair monopoly on information, knowing the consumer's exact budget, browsing history, and behavioral triggers. This creates an unlevel playing field where the concept of choice is completely neutralized.

Conclusion
Price discrimination driven by invasive consumer profiling is a predatory practice that turns everyday commerce into an algorithmic trap. The FTC must fulfill its mandate to protect consumers from unfair and deceptive trade practices by establishing strict rules that ban surveillance-driven personalized pricing and mandate strict price transparency.

Thank you for your time, consideration, and ongoing efforts to protect the public from corporate surveillance overreach.

comment: The FTC should crack down on deceptive advertising resulting in personalized pricing. I am seeing this happening in Albertsons where a price advertised on shelves is not the actual price a consumer pays either. Only with reading glasses or a special digital APP will customers recognize and take advantage of the sale price advertised on the shelves, however unless the customer is reading very closely they are being deceived. Deceptive advertising in all of its forms must be prohibited. Albertsons is very good at this price deception and those hoping to grab and go to the register will later find out that the advertised big bold price on the shelves is only a selective price to those with their APP. The price tags are very tiny and meant to deceive the customers at large into thinking this is a store wide sale price for all. Selective pricing whether based on a consumers personal data or an APP discount is deceptive and considered robbery. One person paying a higher price for the exact same product advertised on the store shelf or online pricing based on personal data compared to another customer is robbery. These are two different scenarios but Albertsons is committing this very act in a different form. Big bold pricing made to look like a store wide sale only to realize the price is not for you is wrong. I also do not want to be overcharged for the same item as another customer due to my personal data sequences.

comment: We have no rights as consumers. For a country that is built on consumerism, the lack of protections and regulation in place is deplorable. I have seen the way data brokers operate and how large corporate companies make decisions. It very clearly ties into the law being that everything one does that works for corporate has to be for the benefit of corporate, regardless. Sure, be a whistle blower. Protections for you though? LOL. "That's just how the business world works." It is a gross excuse. There are mass levels of people that are in severe poverty. We have nothing to support the masses. We are so focused on things that don't matter in the political world that it drives us to war and causes more havoc than needed. Government was created for the people, by the people. The people sure seems to look different these days. The people are the corporations. Those in high levels of government and those that have not had a net worth of under $500,000 will never understand the reality of the state of everyday-man. People have been exploited by those in the higher offices of government that are absolutely benefiting from the lack of regulation in these markets. AI is going to cause this to become near impossible for some people to do anything. Order anything. Buy anything. It has already been proven by videos from Perfect Union. They ran an experiment with multiple people at the same exact location ordering the exact same item from the exact same store at the same exact time. They ranged a wide percentage on charges for the same items. It's been happening and nothing is being done. I literally upended my life to walk out of an agreement with a corporation because I disagreed with practices that were happening. I was told that they make decisions best for their business, and they understood if I had to make decisions for my business. The thing is, without me paying them corporate franchise fees, monthly dues, annual dues, and portions of my income, they would be absolutely nothing. However, since they are a public company, their business is apparently shareholders, not the person giving them money and keeping their brand relevant. To be told what I was told was very sobering. But I could not be part of the real estate world and know the brand is selling my customers' data without them being warned in giant bold letters. They are supposed to trust me. I am a professional and am bound to be truthful to my customers' by LAW. How can I work with a customer and tell them to use the company website knowing I am not being truthful? Truth can be a gray area, I get that. To me: omission = lie. I have spoken with a marketing company in Canada. They were telling me the differences in our laws vs theirs. We basically have nothing. Privacy laws are a joke. It is wild to me that the US has become what I always thought China was with their constant surveillance. Ours is just quieter to the common man. I live in Alabama and regular wage earners have no clue this is even an issue because the talking points are bought and paid for. Free press is a joke now. If companies want to report news, they should be able to do so. However, if you classify as "entertainment" rather than news, you should NOT be able to cosplay as a news outlet. The word news should not be able to appear and be used in any capacity if you are not truly the press. The real issue no one that is common man knows is that the stock market and banking world dictates everything in their lives. Pandering to the issues that are meaningless in the grand scheme of things compared to actual issues. The amount of misinformation allowed is disgusting. Again, no regulation. Free markets should absolutely be free, but when it becomes unethical to the human race, there should be regulation. Alas....

I strongly oppose allowing personalized pricing based on consumers’ personal data. People should not have to wonder whether a company is quietly charging them more because an algorithm thinks they can afford it.

This practice is fundamentally unfair, undermines transparency, and can distort competition. When businesses use detailed personal information to extract the highest price from individual consumers, it raises serious concerns under the Sherman Act and broader antitrust principles.

Consumers deserve a fair, understandable price—not a secret price calculated from their personal data. The FTC should take a strong stand against discriminatory and anti-competitive pricing practices and protect ordinary people from algorithmic price gouging.

comment:
I support the FTC's scrutiny of personalized pricing, but I am concerned that the proposed policy places too much weight on disclosure without establishing whether consumers actually have a reasonable means of avoiding the resulting injury.

Section 5(n) of the FTC Act requires consideration of whether consumer injury is “reasonably avoidable by consumers themselves.” I believe the final policy should address that question much more directly.

If a company tells me that my price was personalized using my data, what exactly am I able to do about it?

The proposal does not appear to guarantee that I can reject personalization and receive a non-personalized price. Shopping elsewhere may not solve the problem either. Multiple retailers may share corporate ownership, use the same or overlapping data brokers or pricing intermediaries, or otherwise have access to substantially the same profile. Avoiding one retailer therefore does not necessarily allow the consumer to escape the information producing the personalized price.

There is also a fundamental problem with the profile itself. I may have no practical ability to see it, challenge it, or know whether its inferences actually describe me. A household account illustrates the problem. My spouse may make purchases through an account associated with me. The underlying transaction history can be completely accurate while the conclusion that it represents my preferences, behavior, or willingness to pay is completely wrong.

More fundamentally, personalized pricing alters the informational balance of a transaction. A seller traditionally knows its costs, margins, and minimum acceptable price while the consumer knows his or her own maximum willingness to pay. Neither side knows the other's reservation price. Surveillance-based personalized pricing potentially allows the seller to retain its own private negotiating information while using data collected about the consumer to estimate the consumer's maximum price.

The consumer has no equivalent visibility into the seller's negotiating position.

I also question whether the Commission can presume that consumers voluntarily expose themselves to this system simply by participating in modern commerce. Avoiding the generation of digital behavioral and transactional data can require substantial withdrawal from ordinary online and increasingly data-dependent commerce. The fact that avoidance is technically possible does not necessarily mean that the resulting injury is “reasonably avoidable” within the meaning of Section 5(n).

For these reasons, I ask the Commission to address several questions explicitly in the final policy:

What meaningful mechanism allows a consumer to reject personalized pricing and obtain a non-personalized price?
How is injury “reasonably avoidable” when the consumer's underlying profile can follow the consumer across nominally competing sellers?
What ability does a consumer have to inspect, challenge, correct, or reject not merely inaccurate raw data, but inaccurate attribution and inferences drawn from accurate data?
How will the Commission evaluate situations in which avoiding personalized pricing requires significant search costs, privacy measures, technological knowledge, or withdrawal from ordinary digital commerce?
Does disclosure alone make an otherwise unavoidable injury reasonably avoidable?

I am not asking the Commission to prohibit conduct beyond its statutory authority. I am asking it to address an apparent gap within the proposed policy's own Section 5 framework.

Disclosure gives a consumer information. It does not necessarily give the consumer agency.

If the consumer cannot reject the personalized price, cannot obtain a neutral price, cannot reasonably escape the profile by changing sellers, and cannot meaningfully challenge the profile being used, I do not understand how disclosure alone makes the resulting injury reasonably avoidable.

I urge the Commission to address that distinction explicitly before finalizing this policy.

comment:
I am submitting this comment as a consumer who strongly opposes the use of personalized pricing for ordinary goods and services. Companies already collect way too much information about us, often without us fully understanding what is being collected or how it will ultimately be used. Using that information to determine how much an individual person might be willing or forced to pay feels like a serious violation of privacy and trust. My personal data should not become a tool that allows a company to extract the highest possible price from me.

This practice is especially concerning when companies use information about a person’s health, income, family, location, shopping behavior, urgency, or access to alternatives. Charging someone more because the company believes that person is vulnerable, in a difficult situation, or unlikely to shop elsewhere is not simply smart marketing. It is EXPLOITATION.

I support the FTC’s proposal because undisclosed personalized pricing is clearly deceptive. At an absolute minimum, companies should be required to make this practice obvious to consumers before they make a purchasing decision. A disclosure should plainly state that the price has been personalized, what information was used, why it affected the price, and whether the consumer is paying more than the company’s standard price. This information should be displayed directly beside the price, not buried in a privacy policy or lengthy terms and conditions.

However, disclosure alone does not make personalized pricing fair. Consumers may have no realistic way to prevent their data from being collected, correct inaccurate information, or find another company that does not use the same practice. A person facing an urgent need cannot simply comparison shop their way out of being exploited.

This proposal is an important step in the right direction, but consumers need stronger protection. I urge the FTC to use its full existing authority against personalized pricing practices that exploit personal data, vulnerability, or urgency, even when some form of disclosure is provided. I also ask the FTC to support stronger federal protections that would prohibit companies from using personal data to calculate the maximum price an individual consumer can be charged.

Consumers should not have to wonder whether the person next to them is paying less because an algorithm decided they could be charged more. Prices for ordinary goods and services should be based on the product and legitimate market conditions, not on a hidden assessment of each person’s circumstances and willingness to pay.

This practice is unfair and unethical. A mother buying diapers should not have to pay more simply because a company knows she has a baby and believes she has no choice but to purchase them. A family should not pay more for groceries because an algorithm decides they are less likely to shop around.

There is a major difference between prices changing because of normal market conditions and prices changing because a company has collected enough personal information to determine how much a specific person may be willing, or forced, to pay.

Consumers should not be penalized because of their family circumstances, location, purchasing history, income, browsing behavior, or other personal data. This is especially concerning for essential goods such as food, diapers, medicine, and household necessities.

Disclosure alone is not enough. Telling consumers that they are being charged a personalized price does not make the practice fair or ethical.

Companies should not be allowed to use personal data to determine how much more they can extract from an individual consumer.

I urge the FTC to adopt the strongest protections possible against surveillance pricing and to encourage Congress to pass clear nationwide protections if additional authority is needed.

A person’s private information should not be used to decide how much they can be charged for the same product. Please protect consumers from this practice.

It appears that the Federal Trade Commission recognizes the harm that “surveillance pricing” poses to consumers. "Dynamic" is a lie - it's ripping off people, and eliminating transparent pricing. Are prices being dropped for individuals and households with lower incomes/assets? I'd be game for that... but who decides who is "worthy"???

Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit. Gains for some come with losses for others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

Disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. How public will the price point be?? $1 for a can of beans for one family, $4 for another???

I urge the FTC to aggressively use its considerable powers to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it.

PUBLIC COMMENT REGARDING THE FTC’S PROPOSED ENFORCEMENT POLICY STATEMENT ON PERSONALIZED PRICING
Docket No. FTC-2026-1057
FTC File No. P034101
Submitted September 15, 2026

The D.C. Consumer Rights Coalition appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Federal Trade Commission’s proposed enforcement policy statement regarding personalized pricing. Our comment is limited to an important feature of District law: the District’s Consumer Protection Procedures Act (“CPPA”) already regulates much of the conduct addressed by the proposed FTC statement. In addition, the CPPA directs District courts, when construing its prohibition of unfair or deceptive trade practices, to give “due consideration and weight” to the interpretations of the Federal Trade Commission and the federal courts concerning “unfair or deceptive act[s] or practice[s]” under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. D.C. Code § 28-3901(d).
Subject to possible revision of the deferential CPPA provision, the proposed FTC statement may significantly influence the interpretation of District of Columbia law. That influence will become still clearer if the Enhancing Consumer Protection Procedures Amendment Act of 2026 takes effect as currently projected: the Act expressly adds FTC “interpretative guidance” to the authorities that District of Columbia courts must consider. We urge the Commission to clarify that its proposed policy is not intended to displace, diminish, or otherwise modify protections or remedies available under D.C. law or similar laws in other States.
Other states have enacted statutes that, like the DC statute, address conduct also addressed in the proposed FTC statement. An Appendix includes a concise list. In addition, several States and the District of Columbia have considered new statutes with regard to prohibiting businesses from using surveillance-based data to set prices.
See attached file(s) for complete statement

Docket No. 207181377) Public Comment on Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing / Section 5 Policy Application)

SUBJECT: PUBLIC COMMENT REGARDING UNDISCLOSED PERSONALIZED PRICING, UNFAIR MONETARY EXTRACTION, AND DECEPTIVE SETTLEMENT PRACTICES (DOCKET NO. FTC-2026-1057)

Dear Commissioners and Policy Staff,

I am writing to submit a public comment in strong support of the FTC’s Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing. I urge the Commission to apply its Section 5 unfairness and deception theories to mobile telecommunications carriers and third-party insurance administrators that engage in non-transparent price manipulation, dynamic liability extraction, and forced unilateral settlement tactics.

1. DECEPTIVE PRICING & HARDWARE MISREPRESENTATION:
The core premise of the Commission’s policy statement—that businesses violate Section 5 when they conceal individualized monetary variations and exploit consumer information gaps—directly mirrors systemic practices in the mobile device protection industry.

Consumers purchase device protection plans under the reasonable expectation of standardized, static coverage terms (full replacement with authentic manufacturer hardware). In practice, carriers like Boost Mobile (DISH Network) and administrators like Likewize Device Protection collect recurring monthly premiums under the promise of authentic coverage, yet fulfill claims using non-genuine internal hardware. Diagnostic checks on these units reveal permanent iOS "Unknown Part" flags, voiding official manufacturer warranties and stripping the asset of its commercial value. The consumer pays a standard price for a protection product whose actual fulfillment yield is dynamically downgraded without disclosure.

2. UNFAIR UNILATERAL REMEDIATION & FORCED DISBURSEMENTS:
When consumers identify hardware nonconformities, carriers and third-party administrators utilize undisclosed, individualized financial adjustments to force dispute closures:
- Unconsented Account Credits: Unilaterally applying non-refundable account credits ($168.00) without consumer consent to administratively alter the transaction value and claim satisfaction.
- Unsolicited Digital Payment Traps: Issuing unsolicited E disbursement virtual cards ($579.99) designed to trigger legal "accord and satisfaction" waivers upon redemption, effectively manipulating the final cash price and liability of the claim without clear, prior disclosure.

3. SECTION 5 POLICY ENFORCEMENT RECOMMENDATION: The Commission’s enforcement posture correctly identifies that concealed financial manipulation constitutes a substantial injury that consumers cannot reasonably avoid. I urge the FTC to explicitly encompass device replacement claims and insurer-administered E-Disbursements within its final Enforcement Policy Statement. Specifically, the FTC should enforce strict penalties against entities that:
a) Collect uniform protection fees while providing non-conforming, altered hardware;
b) Deploy unsolicited virtual cards or account adjustments to force binding dispute waivers without clear and conspicuous advance consent.

The FTC must enforce full transparency, mandate accurate hardware disclosures, and penalize deceptive claims-handling practices across the mobile and consumer insurance sectors.

Respectfully submitted,

Tyrone Marvin Baker Jr.
Baltimore, MD

Docket No. 207181377) Public Comment on Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing / Section 5 Policy Application)

SUBJECT: PUBLIC COMMENT REGARDING UNDISCLOSED PERSONALIZED PRICING, UNFAIR MONETARY EXTRACTION, AND DECEPTIVE SETTLEMENT PRACTICES (DOCKET NO. FTC-2026-1057)

Dear Commissioners and Policy Staff,

I am writing to submit a public comment in strong support of the FTC’s Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing. I urge the Commission to apply its Section 5 unfairness and deception theories to mobile telecommunications carriers and third-party insurance administrators that engage in non-transparent price manipulation, dynamic liability extraction, and forced unilateral settlement tactics.

1. DECEPTIVE PRICING & HARDWARE MISREPRESENTATION:
The core premise of the Commission’s policy statement—that businesses violate Section 5 when they conceal individualized monetary variations and exploit consumer information gaps—directly mirrors systemic practices in the mobile device protection industry.

Consumers purchase device protection plans under the reasonable expectation of standardized, static coverage terms (full replacement with authentic manufacturer hardware). In practice, carriers like Boost Mobile (DISH Network) and administrators like Likewize Device Protection collect recurring monthly premiums under the promise of authentic coverage, yet fulfill claims using non-genuine internal hardware. Diagnostic checks on these units reveal permanent iOS "Unknown Part" flags, voiding official manufacturer warranties and stripping the asset of its commercial value. The consumer pays a standard price for a protection product whose actual fulfillment yield is dynamically downgraded without disclosure.

2. UNFAIR UNILATERAL REMEDIATION & FORCED DISBURSEMENTS:
When consumers identify hardware nonconformities, carriers and third-party administrators utilize undisclosed, individualized financial adjustments to force dispute closures:
- Unconsented Account Credits: Unilaterally applying non-refundable account credits ($168.00) without consumer consent to administratively alter the transaction value and claim satisfaction.
- Unsolicited Digital Payment Traps: Issuing unsolicited E disbursement virtual cards ($579.99) designed to trigger legal "accord and satisfaction" waivers upon redemption, effectively manipulating the final cash price and liability of the claim without clear, prior disclosure.

3. SECTION 5 POLICY ENFORCEMENT RECOMMENDATION: The Commission’s enforcement posture correctly identifies that concealed financial manipulation constitutes a substantial injury that consumers cannot reasonably avoid. I urge the FTC to explicitly encompass device replacement claims and insurer-administered E-Disbursements within its final Enforcement Policy Statement. Specifically, the FTC should enforce strict penalties against entities that:
a) Collect uniform protection fees while providing non-conforming, altered hardware;
b) Deploy unsolicited virtual cards or account adjustments to force binding dispute waivers without clear and conspicuous advance consent.

The FTC must enforce full transparency, mandate accurate hardware disclosures, and penalize deceptive claims-handling practices across the mobile and consumer insurance sectors.

Respectfully submitted,

Tyrone Marvin Baker Jr.
Baltimore, MD

comment:
I see that the Federal Trade Commission recognizes the harm that “surveillance pricing” poses to consumers. However, recognition is not enough; the practice itself must stop. A fair price must be based on the item's cost to the merchant plus a reasonable profit, and should not change based on who is buying that item and what the merchant thinks the shopper can afford.

Research cited by the Commission confirms that the more sophisticated these practices become, the less likely consumers are to benefit. Gains for some come with losses for others. The most vulnerable consumers pay the highest prices, based on their most intimate personal information.

Disclosure is not a substitute for fair pricing. I urge the FTC to use its full authority to ban surveillance pricing rather than merely require that companies disclose it.

comment:
I am extremely pleased that the FTC intends to take aggressive action against the practice of personalized pricing without clear and conspicuous notice. I would like to make some suggestions to help you accomplish this goal.

1. Page 6 of your enforcement policy statement says "To be effective, personalized pricing disclosures should be clear and conspicuous and include all revelant information, such as the fact that the price is personalized, the basis of that personalization, and the type of data used." I suggest the enforcement policy statement provide more specific guidance about the notice companies are expected to provide if a price is personalized, along with a picture of a notice that the FTC will consider acceptable. For example, the policy could say there should be a box below each personalized price that says "This is a personalized price based on data collected about you." The box should have a link to the data being used to make the personalized price for that specific consumer with an underlined link labeled "Data used for pricing". The policy should specify that the font size, font color and background color of text in this box must be the same as the font size, font color and background color used to display the price. The policy should say the disclosure can not be in a popup. The policy should say that a comment buried in a company's Terms & Conditions or on a different page from the product page will not be considered a clear and conspicuous notice of personalized pricing. By providing a picture of what the FTC will consider an acceptable disclosure, the FTC will prevent companies from using devious user interface designs that disclose personalized pricing in a way that will be ignored, as they currently do with data collection notices.

2. The enforcement policy statement should say that the FTC will consider the use of personalized pricing to be evidence that a firm has too much market power and the FTC will consider this evidence in exercising FTC authority to block such firms from making acquisitions or break up such firms to enhance market competition.

3. The enforcement policy statement should say the FTC intends to impose SEVERE financial penalties on companies that are found to have engaged in personalized pricing that violates Section 5 of the FTC Act or other laws. This will put companies on notice that breaking the law in this way will no longer be tolerated and will be severely punished.

4. The enforcement policy statement should say the FTC may use the public's help to identify firms that engage in personalized pricing without clear and conspicuous notice. The first 100 members of the public who provide proof that a particular firm is engaging in personalized pricing without clear and conspicuous notice will be given a reward equal to a fraction of the financial penality paid by the firm engaging in this illegal activity. When the public is financially incentivized to catch these law breakers, companies will know that they are being carefully watched so they will be less likely to engage in illegal activity. The public should be instructed to take two screenshots a few minutes apart on each computer showing a different price. This allows distinguishing between a rapidly changing price and a personalized price.

5. Amazon has publically disclosed that they have "experimented" with personalized pricing. I have seen computers with different cookies get different prices on Amazon for the same product at the same time. Members of the public could take time-stamped screenshots to provide evidence to the FTC that Amazon is engaging in personalized pricing without clear and conspicuous notice.

6. I disagree with the commenter who said companies should be allowed to provide discounts or coupons to some customers but not other customers. This practice to no different than charging different prices to different customers. If a discount or coupon is available to some customers, it should be available to all customers with clearly described information about how to get the discount or coupon on the product page for the item. The ease of getting a discount or coupon must be the same for all customers.

7. The FTC should work with Congress to create a new law that has mandatory 20 year prison sentences for each of the top 10 most highly paid executives of online retailers found to engage in personalized pricing, even if clear and conspicuous notice is given. This new law should specify that these criminals must serve their full 20 year prison sentence behind bars. Upon release, these executives would be required to reimburse the government for the full cost of their incarceration. A large fine that can be appealed for years is not an effective deterrent for executives who consider fines to be a cost of doing business. The threat of 20 years in prison would be an effective deterrent against using personalized pricing.

comment:
I am writing as both a consumer and a small-business attorney who regularly advises businesses regarding online transactions, disclosures, privacy, and consumer-facing practices. I strongly support the FTC's efforts to address what I believe is more accurately called surveillance pricing.

I use that term intentionally. “Personalized pricing” sounds benign, even beneficial. But when a business collects, purchases, infers, or analyzes information about an individual and uses it to determine how much that particular person may be willing to pay, the personalization is not for the consumer's benefit. It is surveillance being used to inform the (maximum projected) price presented to that consumer.

There is an important distinction between ordinary dynamic pricing and surveillance pricing. Consumers understand that airfare, hotels, and other products may change in price because of inventory, demand, seasonality, or timing. Those are characteristics of the market or transaction. Surveillance pricing introduces an entirely different variable: characteristics unique to the buyer.

Two consumers seeking the same product from the same seller at substantially the same time may potentially receive different prices because an algorithm predicts that one has greater ability, urgency, or willingness to pay. That creates extraordinary information asymmetry: the seller may know a tremendous amount about the consumer, while the consumer may know neither what information the seller possesses nor that it is affecting her price.

Telling a consumer “this price has been personalized” does not tell her what the non-personalized price is, whether personalization increased her price, by how much, or whether she has any realistic way to purchase without individualized pricing.

If surveillance pricing is used, disclosure should appear at or immediately adjacent to the price—not buried in Terms of Service, privacy policies, cookie notices, or other secondary interfaces. Where feasible, consumers should also be shown the corresponding non-personalized price and whether personalization increased the price offered to them.

Consent to data collection should likewise not be treated as consent to surveillance pricing. A consumer who accepts cookies, joins a loyalty program, creates an account, or provides information necessary to complete a transaction has not necessarily made an informed choice allowing that data to be used to calculate what the seller believes she personally will tolerate paying.

I am also concerned by the suggestion that consumers can protect themselves through VPNs, private browsing, clearing cookies, changing devices, or similar measures. That places the burden backwards. Consumers should not need technological sophistication—or need to disguise themselves from a seller—to discover the market price of a product. Such a system also disproportionately disadvantages consumers who do not even know they are being profiled.

A traveler responding to a family emergency, or a consumer purchasing groceries, housing, transportation, or health-related necessities, may have little practical ability to walk away. Data revealing that lack of choice should not become economic leverage against that consumer.

A price should describe the price of the product—not the seller's secret assessment of the person standing in front of it. (**And THIS is just ONE more obvious example of why markets require regulation).

I strongly support the Federal Trade Commission's proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing and encourage the Commission to take the strongest enforcement position available under existing law.
As an individual consumer, I am deeply troubled by the use of personal data and analytics to determine what a particular consumer may be willing to pay and then personalize that consumer's price accordingly.
Consumers understand that prices fluctuate because of supply and demand, competition, inventory, geography, and other legitimate market conditions. That is fundamentally different from a company secretly using information about a particular person to determine how much that individual might be willing to pay.
A market price reflects conditions in a market. A personalized price based on an individual's data may instead reflect a company's estimate of how much value it can extract from that particular person.
If two consumers seek to purchase the same product from the same business at the same time under substantially identical market conditions, they reasonably expect to encounter the same price. comment:
I am angry about this, and I am tired of feeling financially squeezed from every direction.

Whether I’m buying a hotel room, booking a plane ticket, shopping for clothing, , or buying groceries or home goods from a large retailer’s website, I increasingly feel like I have no idea whether I’m getting a fair price. I leave one website and wonder if I should have waited, used a different browser, searched somewhere else, or somehow known that someone else might be seeing a lower price.

And now I am learning that my personal information may be part of the reason I am being charged more.

That is incredibly disturbing.

I thought websites, shopping tools, and personalized recommendations were supposed to help consumers find deals and save money. I did not expect my browsing history, purchasing history, location, or other personal information to be used to figure out how much more a company thinks it can get from me.

I am tired of sitting on a plane looking around and wondering what everyone else paid and why I paid so much. Consumers should not have to play detective just to figure out whether they are being treated fairly.

We need clear, meaningful disclosure. Consumers should be able to easily see which companies use personalized pricing, what information they use, and whether the price they are being shown has been influenced by their personal data. A disclosure buried somewhere in a privacy policy isn’t good enough.

Just because technology makes something possible doesn’t mean companies should be allowed to use it against consumers.

Where the heck is the protection for the American consumer?

I urge the FTC to take strong action against unfair and deceptive personalized pricing practices and to give consumers the transparency and protection we need to know that the price we are being offered is a fair price.

Thank you for standing up for consumers.

comment:
Hello,
I am concerned about the increased prevalence of algorithm based pricing. Seeing these methods being used online is unsettling; knowing that companies could have a discreet account of who I am through data they either bought or retained through potentially immoral means is unacceptable to me as a citizen who believes that privacy is an innate right in this country. I have also seen stories about algorithm based pricing being used in physical stores like Kroger. Since the late 1800s this country has believed in fair pricing for all. Why should we allow this to change? Permitting stores to charge variable prices based off information the consumer doesn’t know they have, gives an insurmountable edge to these companies. I believe this country believes in free market values and so do I, but this situation in my opinion breaks the social contract the public has with the stores they shop at. These methods artificially determine the price elasticity of a good based off each individual person. What I mean by this that a new mother could be more desperate for a batch of baby wipes vs your average consumer, is it morally acceptable to charge more to the mother of a new born vs anyone else just because she is in more need of the product? This person probably wouldn’t even know the store has that kind of information. Not only would this persons privacy be invaded, but they would be getting bilked just for having a child. Algorithmic pricing could also be seen as a regressive form of taxation depending on the methodology used by the algorithm. It is not always taking into account your income, it could take into account your gender, age, sexual orientation or like I stated above if you are a new mother. Charging more for good in cases where people may not have advanced means but are just more desperate for a good is not a path I find acceptable in this country. The public is not meant to be used as a microeconomics experiment. Please do something about this.
Thank you,
A concerned citizen

comment: I understand a firm's need to make a profit, and to charge different prices for convenience, more/less features, comfort and prestige. However, personalized pricing is an unfair trade with the consumer.  We shouldn't pay more/less for the exact same product or service merely because a firm has purchased data or has accumulated data on our purchases which an algorithm, AI model, or analyst predicts would maximize the profit for a particular sale.  Many may use airline and hotel revenue management systems as an example where this is done; however, that's not true.  You pay more/less for the same seat or room based on the supply and demand of the room/seat for that day and time. You are typically rewarded for buying further in advance and penalized if you book last minute (unless there is too much supply in which you save).  With personalized pricing, firms would set their price based on your personal purchase behavior, annual income, wealth, or whatever other data they can get on you REGARDLESS OF ITS ACCURACY.  This practice should therefore be illegal.  Stand up for the consumer and abolish this practice.

comment:
“One price and goods returnable”
–slogan of Wanamaker’s department stores

“I know half the money I spend on advertising is wasted but can never find out which half.”
–attributed to John Wanamaker in 1919

John Wanamaker, founder of one of America’s first department stores, was a pioneer of advertising and pricing. His self-titled department stores were the first to use price tags and among the first to use a “one price for all” model instead of haggling with individual customers to discover the personalized price they were willing to pay. But as the quote above suggests, he recognized that advertising, while worthwhile, was an inexact science. An ad in a newspaper would be in every reader’s paper, but only a fraction of those readers might be likely customers for Wanamaker’s stores. And before online advertising, this wasted ad spend problem was common to newspaper and magazine ads, mailed circulars, tv and radio ads, and billboards. Some segment of those who saw the ads would have little or no interest in the product, and so that portion of the ad spend was wasted.
I use the story and quotes of Wanamaker to convey both the shifting dynamics around and the embedded normativity of the single price. The shift away from newspapers and brick-and-mortar stores to websites and online shopping has changed Wanamaker’s wasted ad spend problem. The Internet connects large numbers of people to websites and online shopping. But unlike a newspaper, it works in both directions. Not only can the shopper see the ad, but the online advertiser can determine who focuses on their ads, for example by observing who “clicks through” for information or sales offers. The ability to collect massive amounts of data and the power of computers to process that data means that an advertiser is not limited by its human workers. As a result, gathering information about customers and targeting advertisers can scale up. The result: unlike John Wanamaker, the online advertiser can find out which of its advertising spending is wasted and recalibrate accordingly.
This is where personalized pricing can emerge. Customer information can be used to raise or lower the prices charged to individual consumers and can also be used to tailor offers to individual consumers, whether by individually targeted offers, coupons, rebates or the like. As the FTC is considering action on a UDAP basis, and not grounded in its antitrust authority, I will confine my concern to non-competition law bases. Fundamentally, I’d like to express the concern that a large-scale departure from single-price selling is likely to have significant negative externalities for American society. Law and the legal system developed in tandem with the traditional market mechanism and the idea that there is a “reference” price. In a variety of areas, such as contract law, commercial law, and competition law, there is an implicit assumption of a baseline reference transaction that would have taken place but for, say, respectively, a breach, a default, or punishable conduct. Both liability and judgments are shaped by this deeply embedded baseline. This idea of a single market price dovetails with an American commitment to equality. While it may have made for good business, John Wanamaker’s stated rationale for his adoption of price tags and single-price sales was grounded in his own personal ethical and religious commitment to equality.

I urge the FTC to consider the potential for personalized pricing to have wider ramifications for law and American normative ethical commitments in crafting its approach to personalized pricing.

Salil K. Mehra
James E. Beasley Professor of Law
Temple University, Beasley School of Law
Philadelphia, PA

I write in strong support of the FTC's Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing. This policy is a meaningful step toward protecting consumers, and I urge the Commission to go further by pursuing the following additional actions within its existing authority.

Recommended Actions

- Require affirmative opt-in consent before personal data is used for pricing, not just after-the-fact disclosure. Disclosure alone allows businesses to bury notices; consent puts the consumer in control.
- Use the FTC's unfairness authority to categorically prohibit personalized pricing in high-stakes contexts where consumers cannot reasonably avoid harm, including medical transport, funeral services, emergency lodging, and food delivery in areas with limited alternatives.
- Require any business using personalized pricing to offer a standard, non-personalized price upon request. Consumers should not have to rely on VPNs or private browsing as workarounds.
- Extend FCRA-style adverse action notices to all personalized pricing. If a consumer is charged above the baseline price based on personal data, they should be entitled to know what data was used and have the right to dispute inaccuracies.
- Explicitly prohibit the use of data that functions as a proxy for race, religion, disability, or national origin in pricing models, using existing Section 5 authority and coordination with DOJ and HUD.
- Require large platforms to file annual reports under Section 6(b) disclosing what data categories feed pricing models, the resulting price variance, and demographic breakdowns of who pays more.
- Pursue a trade regulation rule under Magnuson-Moss that establishes per-violation civil penalties for undisclosed personalized pricing, giving enforcement real deterrent power beyond case-by-case action.

Disclosure is a floor, not a ceiling. American consumers deserve pricing protections that match the sophistication of the data systems being used against them. I urge the Commission to use every tool available to it to make that a reality.

I oppose allowing companies to use personalized pricing. Evidence is mounting that private ride companies like Uber are already employing it. This must be stopped. Airlines should not be permitted to use it. The retail market and online stores should not be allowed to use it.
Private companies are already profiting mightily by collecting and using our personal data, absent any meaningful privacy guardrails from the federal government. Citizens are getting fed up! Don't let this erode further please. And if the Department of Transportation needs to regulate personalized pricing for the transportation sector, then let's get them involved too.

There was this service in the video game industry about a decade ago called Scientific Revenue, with the infamous tagline, "turning players into payers" through predictive pricing. Doesn't that sound scummy? Airline tickets and hotels have seen this kind of exploitation as well, and now it's metastasizing into grocery stores.

The FTC must take action and ban surveillance pricing. This kind of extreme commoditization is perverse and will only exacerbate the cost of living crisis across this country.

Public Comment Submission
Docket ID: FTC-2026-1057

Re: Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing

Submitter: J.B. Turner / Concerned Consumer

I. The Best-Case Scenario for Personalized Pricing:
To fairly evaluate the Commission's policy proposal, we must recognize valid economic arguments supporting personalized and dynamic pricing. Advocates correctly point out that static, "one-size-fits-all" prices aren’t ideal for every market or consumer group. In theory, personalized pricing offers these advantages:

- Expanding Market Access for Price-Sensitive Consumers: Dynamic segmentation allows firms to offer targeted discounts to buyers who might otherwise be excluded due to cost. Lower initial prices enable low-income households to access goods and services like air travel and software that uniform, higher prices would restrict.

- Supporting Free and Affordable Services: Revenue from consumers willing to pay more can subsidize free or low-cost tiers accessible to the broader public. Digital platforms, open-access tools, and streaming services often use this income transfer to maintain universal access.

- Better Resource Management and Waste Reduction: Real-time adjustments promote demand shifts away from peak times (such as off-peak travel or electricity usage), helping to balance supply and prevent waste of perishable inventory like empty hotel rooms or leftover flight seats.

When transparency is upheld and savings are shared with consumers, personalized pricing can boost incivility and efficiency.

II. Market Reality: Limitations of the Model for Consumers
Despite appealing theory, real-world "surveillance pricing" practices reveal a different story. The benefits to consumers are often overshadowed by substantial harms:

- Extracting Consumer Surplus: In practice, algorithms aim not to reduce costs but to maximize willingness to pay. Instead of aiding those in need, they identify urgency or lack of alternatives, such as location or device type, to increase profits.

- The "Loyalty Penalty" Paradox: Studies show that algorithms frequently charge loyal, repeat customers higher rates, knowing they’re likely to stay, while offering cheaper prices to less loyal, deal-seeking buyers.

- Asymmetry and Deception: Unlike transparent traditional markets, algorithmic pricing depends on asymmetrical information. Merchants know details like purchase history, location, and willingness to pay, while consumers remain unaware of others’ prices for the same product.

III. Policy Recommendations for the FTC: To address the unfair exploitation of personalized pricing, I support the FTC’s stance that undisclosed, individualized prices are deceptive and unfair under Section 5 of the FTC Act.

To protect consumers without banning legitimate discounts, I recommend the FTC require:

- Clear, real-time disclosures at point-of-sale (e.g., a visible label stating: "This price is tailored to your profile or activity") rather than hidden terms.

- Explicit explanations of data factors influencing the price, such as location, browsing urgency, previous orders, or device type.

- Banning personalized price increases for urgent needs like emergency transport or essential goods during disruptions.

- Transparency and opt-in rules for data used in loyalty programs, ensuring consumers agree rather than allowing secret price hikes based on collected data.

IV. Conclusion: While personalized pricing could improve market efficiency, current practices often serve as asymmetric surveillance, eroding consumer surplus. An FTC policy demanding full price transparency will restore trust and ensure that competition, rather than covert exploitation, guides the digital economy.

Respectfully submitted.

J.B. Turner
Consumer / Citizen
Utah, USA
