I strongly support greater consumer protections against personalized pricing based on personal data.

Technology should make markets more competitive and transparent for consumers. The internet once gave consumers an extraordinary ability to compare prices and choose among competing sellers. I am concerned that increasingly sophisticated data collection and pricing technology is reversing that advantage by allowing businesses to know far more about individual consumers than consumers know about the market in which they are participating.

There is an important difference between dynamic pricing and personalized pricing. I understand that prices change because of legitimate market conditions such as supply, demand, inventory, or production costs. Personalized pricing is fundamentally different.

If two consumers attempt to purchase the same product from the same company at the same time, one should not secretly be charged more because an algorithm has determined that person is willing, able, or desperate enough to pay more.

A company may know a consumer’s location, browsing history, purchases, shopping habits, device information, or household characteristics. Meanwhile, the consumer may have no idea what other customers are paying, whether their price was personalized, what information determined it, or how to obtain the ordinary price.

That creates an unacceptable information imbalance.

I appreciate efforts to require disclosure when personalized pricing is used, but disclosure alone is insufficient. Telling consumers that their personal information is being used to determine how much they may be willing to pay does not make the practice fair.

Consumers should have meaningful control over whether their information can be used this way.

At minimum, protections should include affirmative consent before personal data is used to determine an individualized price; clear disclosure of what information influenced the price; an easy way to decline personalized pricing without losing access to the product or service; access to the ordinary non-personalized price; and strong restrictions on using sensitive information or circumstances indicating vulnerability.

Consumers should not need private browsing, VPNs, multiple devices, or other technological workarounds simply to determine whether they are receiving a fair price.

I am particularly concerned about personalized pricing for necessities or situations where consumers have limited ability to walk away. Information suggesting that someone urgently needs transportation, food, medicine, housing, security, or another essential service should never become an opportunity to extract a higher price.

This also raises a larger privacy concern. Connected technology is increasingly necessary for employment, education, banking, healthcare, transportation, communication, shopping, and ordinary participation in modern society. “Opting out” of technology is therefore becoming less realistic. Consumers should not have to surrender meaningful privacy simply to participate in the modern economy.

Healthy markets should require businesses to compete for consumers through better prices, products, service, and innovation. Technology should strengthen that competition—not become a tool for determining the maximum amount each individual can be induced to pay.

I urge the FTC to aggressively enforce existing consumer-protection laws against unfair or deceptive personalized-pricing practices and encourage Congress to provide additional statutory authority where existing law is insufficient.

Innovation should improve people’s lives. Markets should empower consumers with choices. A fair marketplace should require businesses to compete to earn the consumer’s money—not use surveillance to determine how much of that consumer’s money they can extract.

According to the policy statement, "Congress has not given the Commission the authority to prohibit personalized pricing in all circumstances," so I am arguing from the assumption that the FTC has its hands roughly tied within the boundary of Section 5. If the FTC does not have authority to outright ban personalized pricing, it should absolutely enforce transparency from corporations that use data collection to raise prices for individual consumers that pay for goods or services. Furthermore, compliance should require an easy, clear way of opting out of such pricing practices.

The FTC seems confident it would be able to enforce penalties against noncompliance on the basis of Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act, specifically where consumers cannot "reasonably avoid" the practice or where corporations may "mislead" consumers about the fact that personalized pricing has occurred. My concern is that companies may be given flexibility to design their own solutions to being compliant with an "opt out" and mandatory disclosure of personalized pricing where it occurs. To best protect consumers from exploitative pricing practices, the language that discloses that personalized pricing has occurred for a user should 1) be standardized across all ecommerce platforms, and 2) should be disclosed on screen as close to the price and/or "Add to Cart" and "Confirm Purchase" buttons as possible. Consumers should know when personalized pricing has occurred before they commit to the price, and they should not have to read each company's individual fine print to determine whether such pricing has occurred. If the disclosure language is standardized (i.e. the words "Personalized Price" right next to the cost of the item) across every online retailer website in the FTC's jurisdiction, it is more likely that consumers will be able to correctly interpret the pricing practice, which is in both the companies' best interest to be in compliance and in the consumer's best interest to avoid misleading practices. Furthermore, the process to opt out of personalized pricing should be standardized and as easy for the consumer as possible. Elina van Kempen and her fellow authors at UC Irvine analyzed noncompliance among the 543 registered data brokers in California. The process for requesting personalized data from these brokers is convoluted, non-standardized, and often resulted in no response. Though different agencies, if a business' compliance to the FTC opt out process for personalized pricing is as loose as the CPPA process for requesting data from these data brokers, consumers will not protected to the degree they should be. Like the language regarding disclosure, the language and process for opting out of personalized pricing should be clear, simple, and as close to the personalized price as possible. To visualize this, imagine the text "Personalized Price" above a given dollar amount and a check box between the price listed and "Add to Cart" button that states "Opt Out of Personalized Pricing."

Anything less than clear language and simple opt out procedures is predatory to the consumer. A business that wishes to personalize prices might scoff at such requirements, arguing that this places an unfair burden on a practice that would otherwise give them a competitive advantage. But, as before AI, the onus should be on the business to identify a fair, market-value price that all consumers pay. A company may also argue that lower-income individuals could benefit from a lower personalized price if higher-income individuals pay more for the same item. We simply should not put our trust in companies having consumers' best interests in such practices. There is already a precedent for such practices that builds actual trust between businesses and consumers, which is (usually independent) businesses having a low baseline price for a good or service while also providing the option to pay more if an individual has the means and desire to support the business beyond the listed price. The idea that a company would make these calculations for us, under the hood, for our benefit, seems like a lie to exploit consumers, and such an argument should be distrusted.

Short of the outright banning of personalized pricing, companies should be forced to place standardized language disclosing that such pricing is occurring, to implement a single-click opt out process that applies to current and future transactions through the same platform, and to place these elements within a standardized distance from the price and relevant purchase buttons. Such measures will maximize a consumer's interpretation and reasonable avoidance of such practices, which ensures compliance to Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act. Businesses that fail to comply with such measures should be charged a fine that is calculated to be more than the profit of the personalized pricing transactions, so that businesses cannot profit from failing to comply with FTC mandates.

Although the FTC is addressing the concept that personalized pricing likely violates Section 5 of the FTC Act, this notice ignores the fact that algorithmic personalized pricing also likely violates Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act. Because nearly all of algorithmic pricing is done by resellers, these platforms are providing collusive opportunities for the original producer to precisely target the final purchaser. I.e., if someone were in the market for purchasing peanut butter, a platform like Amazon could sell the collusive best advertisement (price) to the peanut butter sellers to match the exact seller to the exact purchaser at the highest possible price. Essentially, this system is providing a hub and spoke conspiracy to eliminate competition between the spokes.

But also, Section 5 too.

To the Federal Trade Commission:

I support strong protections against undisclosed personalized or surveillance-based pricing.

I have no objection to businesses setting prices, responding to supply and demand, or offering sales and discounts. My concern is fundamentally different: using personal data and algorithmic profiling to estimate how much a particular individual is willing to pay, while presenting that individualized price as though it were simply “the price.”

Companies can increasingly infer purchasing power, urgency, price sensitivity, loyalty, likelihood of comparison-shopping, and maximum willingness to pay from browsing, purchase, location, device, financial, and behavioral data. The consumer may have no idea this is happening or what another customer would have been charged.

That creates an unacceptable information imbalance. Personal data should not become a hidden negotiating weapon against the person who generated it.

Disclosure alone is not enough. Consumers should be clearly told when a price has been personalized, what categories of information materially affected it, and be given a simple opt-out with access to the ordinary non-personalized price.

The same principle should extend beyond retail pricing. Algorithms capable of estimating the maximum a consumer will pay can potentially estimate the minimum wage or compensation a worker will accept, or influence insurance, lending, housing, and other important economic terms.

Consumers should not need anonymous browsers, VPNs, multiple devices, cleared cookies, or technical expertise simply to discover what something actually costs.

If a business wants to sell me something, tell me the price. I will decide whether it provides sufficient value. My personal data should not secretly determine how much you think you can get me to pay.

ADA Implications
I am submitting this comment as a consumer who is currently homebound because of significant medical problems, and I ask the FTC to consider how personalized pricing, personalized promotions, and differences between in-store and online shopping may disproportionately affect people with disabilities, older adults, and other homebound consumers.

I have a brain tumor and POTS (postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome), which causes fainting and near-fainting episodes. My physician has instructed me not to drive at this time. Grocery pickup and delivery are therefore not conveniences for me. They are currently how I access groceries.

I have been an avid coupon and sale shopper for many years. I know how to compare unit prices, shop sales, use manufacturer and store coupons, and plan meals around promotions. In the past, I could sometimes save close to $100 on a large grocery trip.

My concern is not simply that groceries cost more. I am concerned about a marketplace increasingly built around individualized offers, shopping histories, digital coupons, online product availability, and algorithms that may determine what products, prices or promotions consumers see.

When I could shop normally, if a roast was too expensive, I could compare every package in the meat case, choose a cheaper cut, look for markdowns, change my meal plan, or shop somewhere else. I cannot currently do that.

On a recent Kroger pickup order, for example, I deliberately selected a larger store farther from my home because I expected greater selection. Yet the pickup system offered me very limited meat choices, including chuck roast at $9.99/lb and stew meat at approximately $10/lb. I also encounter products designated “in-store only” or “delivery only.”

Even if an online item has the same price as that identical item inside the store, I question whether that represents meaningful price equality when a homebound consumer cannot access less-expensive alternatives, markdowns, or other choices available to an in-store shopper.

There are additional costs. I pay a monthly grocery membership fee. Delivery also means tipping, and because I live farther from the store, I feel obligated to tip appropriately for the additional distance. A 10% tip on a $300 grocery order is another $30.

I have also received dated perishable products through grocery fulfillment on multiple occasions, including products already beyond their printed date. An in-store shopper can inspect dates before purchasing. A person who cannot drive may also have difficulty returning an unacceptable item.

I am especially concerned about personalized pricing or promotions based on shopping history, location, predicted willingness to pay, likelihood of comparison shopping, or similar consumer data. A system that concludes a consumer is unlikely to comparison-shop becomes particularly concerning when the reason is that the consumer physically cannot do so.

A person with a brain tumor who has been medically prohibited from driving cannot respond to an unfavorable price by simply getting in the car and going to another grocery store.

I urge the FTC to specifically consider people with disabilities, older adults, homebound consumers, and others who depend upon digital commerce for essential goods. Consumers deserve transparency when prices, discounts, promotions, product rankings, or offers are personalized using their data. I also encourage examination of whether online grocery customers have meaningful access to the same economical choices available to people shopping inside the store.

Technology should make essential goods more accessible to people with disabilities, not leave them paying more because they have fewer choices.

For me, grocery pickup is not about saving myself a trip to the store. Right now, I cannot safely make that trip. That difference matters.

To the Federal Trade Commission:

I am writing on the Commission's proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing (August 19, 2026). I support the FTC's decision to scrutinize this practice, and I urge the Commission to adopt a more assertive posture than the disclosure-only framework currently proposed.

**Personalized pricing is not a pricing strategy — it is a tax on trust.**

The traditional price tag tells every consumer, regardless of income or negotiating leverage, what a good costs. Personalized pricing replaces that shared reference point with a private calculation of "the most an individual is willing to pay," built from browsing history, location, device type, and other behavioral signals consumers never agreed to have used this way. Consumers cannot comparison-shop or even recognize when they're paying more than someone else for the same product. That isn't a market functioning efficiently — it's information asymmetry weaponized at scale.

**Disclosure alone does not fix an unequal bargain.**

The proposed statement would require disclosing that a price is personalized, its basis, and the data used. That's a step forward, but disclosure without limits does little to protect consumers. A "just tell people you're doing it" standard puts the burden of self-protection on individuals — expecting them to read fine print or use a VPN just to get a fair price. That burden falls hardest on people with less time, technical literacy, or fewer alternatives, while businesses retain every incentive to keep extracting maximum value as long as a disclosure is buried somewhere in a privacy policy.

**Personalized pricing functions as a hidden, uneven inflation.**

Personalized pricing produces invisible, individualized price increases that never show up in official price indices, because no two consumers necessarily pay the same amount for the same good. A household under financial strain — the exact household whose data may signal urgency or inelastic demand — can be quietly charged more than a wealthier household buying the identical item. This compounds real inflation by stripping away consumers' ability to seek the lowest price, one of the only tools people have when costs are already rising.

**Personalized pricing undermines the competitive foundation of capitalism itself.**

A functioning market rests on one mechanism: competition disciplines prices. When consumers can compare offers and walk away, sellers must compete on price and quality — that pressure is the only real leverage an individual has against a business with far more resources and information. Personalized pricing breaks this at the root. If every consumer sees a different, privately calculated price, there is no shared price signal left to compete against — comparison shopping becomes meaningless. That is not competition; it is each business quietly capturing maximum value from each individual, immune from ordinary market discipline. A policy limited to disclosure risks entrenching this by treating it as acceptable so long as it's labeled, rather than recognizing it as an erosion of the price competition capitalism depends on to protect consumers. Restoring transparent price competition isn't an anti-market position — it's the precondition for markets to function as intended.

**Recommendations:**
1. Use Section 5 unfairness authority to prohibit personalized pricing based on sensitive inferred data (financial vulnerability, health status, demographic proxies) — not merely require disclosure.
2. Mandate a visible, standard reference price alongside any personalized price.
3. Investigate cumulative harm to lower-income and vulnerable populations over time, not just individual transactions.
4. Treat algorithmic pricing collusion, where firms use shared third-party pricing algorithms, as a distinct enforcement priority, since it can approximate price-fixing without an explicit agreement.

Thank you for considering these comments. I urge the Commission to treat personalized pricing not as a disclosure problem to be solved with better fine print, but as a fairness problem requiring real limits on how personal data can be used to set prices.

Best,
Dhruti Patel

comment:
I oppose the proposed statement as drafted.
The Commission acknowledges that Congress has not authorized a ban on personalized pricing. A policy statement should not create a new three-part disclosure duty and then declare that noncompliance is “likely” an unfair or deceptive practice that the agency will enforce aggressively. That is rulemaking without rulemaking: it chills lawful conduct, imposes primary obligations, and skips the findings and cost-benefit analysis a trade rule would require.
The liability trigger is too vague. “Where consumers reasonably expect that prices will not vary based on their personal data” does not tell a business when ordinary variation—by time, inventory, channel, membership, coupon, location, or device—becomes “personalized pricing.” A standard that uncertain produces selective enforcement, not clearer markets.
The disclosure regime is overbroad. It does not cleanly separate targeted discounts, loyalty prices, and personalized offers from concealed markups. Treating those practices as one category will put dense notices on programs that lower prices for many shoppers, or cause firms to drop the offers rather than try to describe “willingness to pay” and “types of data” at checkout. A short notice risks being called misleading; a complete notice is unreadable and may expose proprietary methods. That is not a workable compliance path.
The economics do not support a presumption of harm. The welfare effects of price discrimination are ambiguous. Personalized pricing often expands sales to price-sensitive customers. In competitive markets, quietly charging someone above the going price loses the sale. If the practical result of this statement is fewer targeted discounts and one higher uniform price, the shoppers the policy claims to protect will be worse off.
Extreme examples—funeral travel, medical emergencies, crime victimization—do not justify a market-wide disclosure code for routine algorithmic merchandising. If those practices occur and are concealed, existing Section 5 already reaches material deception and unfair injury. The Commission does not need a new presumption that any undisclosed use of personal data in pricing is likely unlawful.
The Commission should withdraw or sharply narrow the statement. At minimum, any final version should:
state that it creates no independent legal duty;
exclude loyalty programs, coupons, membership prices, and other reductions from a disclosed list or public price;
drop the presumption that non-disclosure is “likely” a Section 5 violation;
require case-specific proof of a material misrepresentation or omission; and
avoid compelling firms to label ordinary pricing as an estimate of a consumer’s willingness to pay.
Respectfully submitted,
Concerned Consumer
Massapequa, NY

Dear Regulators:
I understand that “Personalized Pricing” actually allows EXTRACTING SYSTEMATICALLY, FROM THE POOR and the MOST VULNERABLE AMONG US, in a way as PURPOSELY designed by our modern-day, corporate profiteers, who now collect enough details about nearly everyone’s likes, dislikes, medical and physical needs and fondnesses which effectively financially grind down exactly whom?
Well, to rif on the important children’s picture book called
Alexander and the Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Day, by Judith Viorst from 1972, please think it through and OPPOSE this terrible, horrible, no good, very bad pricing policy rule. Aren’t you too, very sure that systematizing the most necessary, generally the cheapest, and the bottom of our economy, mass-produced goods sold thru our big box stores to have routinely HIGHER PRICES, SPEARHEADED DIRECTLY TOWARDS YOUNG, AMERICAN CHILDREN AND THEIR EXHAUSTED PARENTS, IS TRULY A POLICY THAT WILL MAKE EVEN MORE FREQUENT, ROUTINE, AND WORSE, BAD DAYS to be the primary shopping experiences of our currently youngest , and likely future adult citizens? Disclosures absolutely do not protect anyone looking for food or toys from being subjected to rapacious pricing if we, with this proposed rule herein, systematize charging more just because someone—really anyone (please note that struggling adults are also not exempt) , is having A Terrible, Horrible, No Good Very Bad Day??? What do you call it, if a usually distant oil corporation raises one’s price by 200 bucks for a semi’s relatively small-ish, 100 gallon tank of diesel gas because we have had a capricious influence on prices—this time, an unwise-leadership, that bombed a country producing an important 5pct of world oil. And further, the opponent country seems to be easily capable of blocking 20-25 pct of that same oil derivative? How’s that working for those making a living driving diesel trucks and farmers now, during harvest season? How’s that working for people like me, who have to pay the 50pct price (~$4 to ~$6/gallon) increase due to these currently EXTRACTIVE Fuel PRICES? What we need to be looking for in our economy, is an at least predictable, and hopefully fair (not rapacious) profit-based price in our big box, corporate stores. There is ZERO benefit to allowing systemization of algorithmically higher, to any specific human shopper, when prices can be wielded against the child whose family has just had a crime recorded against them! Or a family that is low on gas in their car, or who is shopping for food on the way to mom’s work rather than on Saturday like they usually do. Nor should 10pct more for a tricycle, be charged to the parent who sought medical care for their child’s cancer and needs something to distract their child’s thoughts from an existence marked by a likely, early demise. It is a need for children and their over-worked and under-paid, (by the same oligarchy) , who may be routinely under-resourced (by the frequently minimized days off work, and by overly restricted, access to creative free time ), and dangerously distracted parents of young children ( that the already legalized, psychologically-consuming electronic device addictions prey upon—we see you, Facebook). Instead we should completely FORBID surveillance pricing since our personal data is so widespread in the computer systems of our corporate-dominated marketplaces. So please, hold the line and choose that a 2dollar toy should be 2dollars so our young can learn accurate math through more consistent, relatively cost-related pricing, rather than find their parent’s financial capacity consumed by out-of-sight-and-behind -the-algorithm, predatory pricing.
Which meds you are on in the pharmacy, must not be used to charge more to the cashflow-strapped families, who goes to the store together, than from the wealthy family who hires a worker to shop on their behalf, thereby evading the whole predatory system! I believe young Alexander’s Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Days should not be used against him or any of us, to effectively allow systemizing the actions of corporate Big Box Store, Pick-Pockets!
Please withdraw this policy immediately!!Truly yours, for the Benefit of All Humanity, by a concerned working person, a Parent and a Decent Human Being—Please Join me in opposing this policy with every government, community and company policy maker you can interact with.

Please, Stop! this inhumane policy in its tracks! No ones’s life is improved by a higher percentage of Terrible, Horrible, No Good, Very Bad Days!

comment: Personalized pricing and all forms of dynamic pricing are inherently predatory, designed to systematically extract as much money as possible from consumers by exploiting their specific circumstances. At its worst, this practice takes deliberate advantage of people when they are at their most vulnerable, such as a frantic parent desperately searching for urgent medical care, medicine, or last-minute supplies for a sick child, only to be gouged simply because they need help quickly.By pricing goods and services based on real-time demand, urgency, or individual data rather than fixed costs, dynamic pricing completely disconnects the price paid from the actual value received. There should be one fair, transparent price that everyone pays, regardless of who they are or how dire their situation is. Dynamic pricing in any form is an abusive business model that should be made strictly illegal.

Docket No. FTC-2026-1057 — Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing
I strongly support the Federal Trade Commission’s proposed enforcement policy statement regarding personalized pricing.
As a consumer who regularly researches and comparison-shops significant purchases online, I expect that the price displayed for a product is generally the price available to other customers viewing the same offer at the same time. I understand that legitimate pricing can vary because of broad market conditions, inventory, location, shipping, taxes, time-limited promotions, loyalty programs, or individualized products such as insurance and credit. What concerns me is a different practice: using a consumer’s personal data, inferred willingness to pay, browsing activity, location, device information, or other behavioral signals to quietly charge that individual more than another person for the same item or service.
Consumers cannot make informed choices when they do not know that a displayed price was tailored to extract the highest amount a company believes they will pay. A person who needs an item quickly, is shopping from a mobile device, appears unlikely to compare prices, has a history of purchasing premium products, or is located near a store should not silently be treated as a higher-value target for a higher price. That is especially troubling for necessities and high-stakes purchases, including groceries, transportation, travel, home security, health-related goods and services, and automotive repairs or parts.
The Commission is right to distinguish personalized pricing from ordinary, transparent price variation. Consumers can understand a publicly available sale, a disclosed member discount, or a price change that reflects supply and demand. They cannot reasonably assess or avoid a hidden price increase driven by data they may not know was collected, purchased, inferred, or connected to them.
I support the proposal’s central expectation that, where a consumer would reasonably assume prices are not individualized, businesses should clearly and conspicuously disclose:
That the quoted price is personalized.
Whether personalization can result in a higher price, a lower price, or both.
The principal basis for personalization, such as prior purchases, browsing behavior, approximate location, device or account information, or inferred likelihood of comparison shopping.
The types and sources of data used, including whether third-party data brokers, affiliates, or advertising technology providers contributed to the pricing decision.
A practical method for the consumer to view a non-personalized price, opt out of personalized pricing, or request correction of inaccurate data.
The FTC should also make clear that disclosures cannot be hidden in a privacy policy, terms-of-service document, cookie banner, or vague marketing language such as “a special price for you.” The disclosure should appear next to the price, before the consumer begins checkout or provides payment information, and it should work on a phone screen without requiring extra clicks, scrolling, or legal interpretation.
For example, a useful disclosure could state: “This price was personalized using your account purchase history and approximate location. It may differ from prices shown to other customers. View the standard price or turn off personalized pricing.” This is concise, understandable, and gives consumers a meaningful choice.
Finally, enforcement should give particular attention to personalized price increases based on sensitive or hardship-related information. It should never be acceptable to charge more because a company infers that a consumer is in a medical emergency, facing bereavement, has limited transportation options, has children in the household, has been the victim of a crime, or lacks practical alternatives. These practices can exploit consumers precisely when they are least able to shop around.
The proposed statement is an appropriate use of the FTC’s authority to address deceptive and unfair practices. It preserves legitimate competition and transparent discounts while protecting consumers from covert, data-driven price discrimination. I urge the Commission to finalize the policy and to emphasize prominent, standardized disclosures, affirmative consumer choice, meaningful opt-out rights, and strong enforcement against exploitative uses of sensitive personal data.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

comment: I write to urge the Commission to institute a total ban on personalized surveillance pricing. This practice is not legitimate 'supply and demand' economics; it is a predatory mechanism that destroys the foundational principles of a free market.Healthy capitalism requires price transparency so that competitors can openly compete and underbid one another. By generating secret, individualized prices based on consumer surveillance, corporations eliminate price discovery and create artificial, transaction-specific monopolies.Furthermore, this practice is inherently deceptive under Section 5. A posted price carries a universal market expectation of value; manipulating that price based on hidden personal vulnerabilities is a structural deception that cannot be cured by disclosures. Because consumers cannot realistically audit algorithms or negotiate against surveillance data, they are stripped of their role as rational market actors. To preserve a competitive, transparent, and functional free market, the FTC must prohibit personalized pricing entirely

comment:
I am writing in support of strong protections against personalized pricing and to urge the Federal Trade Commission to prohibit the practice when it relies on consumer-specific data.

Personalized pricing allows companies to charge different consumers different prices for the same product or service based on personal information, behavioral data, demographics, location, browsing history, purchasing history, or algorithmic predictions about an individual's willingness or ability to pay. While businesses may argue that this improves efficiency, the practice creates significant risks of unfairness, discrimination, and consumer harm.

First, personalized pricing undermines the principle that consumers should be able to compare prices fairly in a transparent marketplace. When each consumer is shown a different price, comparison shopping becomes substantially more difficult. Consumers cannot know whether they are receiving a fair offer, and competition becomes less effective.

Second, personalized pricing can lead to discriminatory outcomes. Even when protected characteristics are not explicitly used, algorithms may rely on proxies that produce disparate impacts on consumers based on income, age, race, disability, or other characteristics. Consumers who are less able to shop around or who have fewer alternatives may end up paying more simply because an algorithm predicts they will tolerate higher prices.

Third, consumers generally do not have meaningful knowledge of, or control over, the vast amount of personal data used to determine individualized prices. Most people reasonably expect that the listed price for a product is the price available to all similarly situated customers. Using extensive surveillance and data collection to extract the highest possible price from each individual violates that expectation and erodes trust in the marketplace.

Fourth, the practice creates incentives for companies to collect and analyze ever more personal information. This increases privacy risks while providing little direct benefit to consumers. Businesses should compete by offering better products, services, and prices rather than by using personal data to determine how much can be extracted from each consumer.

For these reasons, I urge the FTC to determine that personalized pricing based on individual consumer data is an unfair and deceptive practice and to prohibit it.

Thank you for considering this comment.

I am submitting this comment to urge the FTC to investigate and ban personalized pricing practices among retailers, as this practice is an egregious misuse of consumer data and not a transparent business practice at all, where consumers ultimately pay the price.

Personalized pricing undermines fair markets by engaging in active discrimination among consumers. Given all of the business consolidation and already few options consumers have, this creates a system of extracting maximum value from consumers who are left with no other purchasing options. Furthermore, the methods used to create this price discrimination is invasive and an abuse of consumer data collection. Consumers are left with no choice but agree to provide their data to retailers in order to make a purchase. Since all retailers require engage in this practice, consumers do not have other options to shop with retailers engaging in more ethical business practices and must forcefully participate in a system that collects their data when they want (NEED) to purchase essentials, only for it to be used against them. This will ultimately erode trust and quality of goods and services provided, as consumers will also eventually have no benchmark to price products at market value anymore.

Disclosure won't cut it - this practice needs to be outright banned. The FTC needs to do their jobs and regulate this among retailers who have only offered lower quality products for the highest price they can get from consumers.

comment:
I support the Commission's Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing and urge it to adopt the statement promptly and strengthen it.

A listed price is a promise. Consumers reasonably assume the price they see is the price others see at the same moment. Setting prices based on a company's estimate of what an individual will tolerate, using browsing history, location, device type, purchase history, or inferred income, breaks that assumption without the consumer's knowledge. It shifts value from consumers to sellers through information asymmetry, not better products or service.

As an IT professional, I can say plainly that consumers have no practical way to detect this. They cannot see the data brokers, tracking pixels, or models involved, and cannot compare their price against what others were offered. Harm that cannot be observed cannot be avoided, which is why enforcement is needed rather than reliance on market discipline.

I ask the Commission to:

Require disclosure at the point of price display, not in a privacy policy or terms of service.
Treat inferences (estimated willingness to pay, likelihood of comparison shopping, financial stress) as personal data subject to the same rules as collected data.
Guard against relabeling: a personalized price presented as a "discount," "member offer," or "loyalty price" should face scrutiny when the baseline itself is inflated by personalization.
Give special attention to essentials such as groceries, medicine, housing, and utilities, where consumers cannot easily walk away.
Scrutinize use of sensitive data (health, location, protected characteristics, and proxies for them) under the unfairness authority, not only deception.

Disclosure is a floor, not a solution. Where the Commission's authority allows, it should treat personalization of essential goods based on inferred vulnerability as unfair regardless of disclosure.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

comment: The FTC should prohibit personalized pricing because it undermines consumer fairness and transparency. Although companies may gain additional revenue by charging different consumers different prices, implementing these systems also creates significant technological and administrative complexity. More importantly, consumers may pay different amounts for the same product without knowing why, making it difficult to compare prices or determine whether an offer is fair. Personalized pricing can also enable companies to use personal data to charge each consumer the maximum amount they are willing to pay, potentially disadvantaging people based on their location, income, or other characteristics. A prohibition would protect consumers from opaque, discriminatory, and unnecessarily complex pricing practices while promoting a clearer and more trustworthy marketplace.

There has been a wave of momentum when it comes to protecting consumers from surveillance pricing. New Jersey just became the third state to pass a surveillance pricing ban into law.

Similar to states, the FTC has the authority to ban surveillance pricing. Currently, however, the FTC’s proposed policy would only require companies to disclose that they are doing personalized pricing and the specific types of data used to change the price you see. While it is encouraging that the agency is taking steps to address unfair pricing practices, it should not be on consumers to read detailed disclosures to try and figure out whether companies are trying to charge them more. Historically, the FTC has recognized that disclosure may not be enough. If there’s an unfair practice – they have the power to ban it!

I should not have to pay more based on who I am – or who a company thinks I am.

comment:
Dear Commissioners and Staff,

I submit this public comment in response to the Federal Trade Commission’s ongoing inquiry into the widespread commercial adoption of surveillance pricing. The practice of leveraging granular personal data—including precise geolocation, device metadata, real-time browsing history, purchasing power inferences, and behavioral profiling—to quote different prices to different consumers for identical goods and services represents a structural threat to consumer welfare and honest market competition.

The FTC must exercise its regulatory authority under Section 5 of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. § 45) to issue an administrative rule declaring undisclosed, personalized surveillance pricing an unfair and deceptive act or practice.

I. Surveillance Pricing Constitutes an Unfair Trade Practice
Under Section 5, an act or practice is unfair if it causes substantial injury to consumers that is not reasonably avoidable by consumers themselves and is not outweighed by countervailing benefits to consumers or competition. Surveillance pricing satisfies all three legal prongs:

Substantial Injury: Surveillance pricing is explicitly engineered to extract maximum consumer surplus—converting individual value assessments into corporate economic rents. By weaponizing private vulnerabilities, stress indicators, or immediate need, algorithms systematically overcharge individuals based on personal characteristics rather than cost of service or baseline demand.

Not Reasonably Avoidable: Commercial data extraction pipelines are ubiquitous, opaque, and near-impossible to opt out of. Even when consumers utilize privacy-enhancing technologies, such as virtual private networks (VPNs) or privacy browsers, pricing algorithms frequently flag these tools as markers of higher technical literacy or higher income, paradoxically triggering elevated price quotes.

Absence of Countervailing Benefit: Unlike traditional yield management, which optimizes static supply against general market demand, personalized surveillance pricing merely shifts wealth from consumers to data-dominant intermediaries without expanding output, improving product quality, or enhancing market efficiency.

II. Surveillance Pricing Relies on Deceptive Market Signals
Surveillance pricing inherently distorts baseline market expectations:

Erosion of the Public Benchmark Price: In a functioning market, a posted price communicates objective information about supply, demand, and seller costs. Substituting a transparent price with a secret, individualized quote exploits consumer trust and prevents meaningful comparison shopping.

Exploitation of High-Stress Vulnerabilities: Algorithmic systems detect real-time behavioral signals indicating urgency—such as late-night transportation needs, urgent travel, or limited mobile battery capacity—and elevate prices when consumer bargaining leverage is at its absolute lowest.

III. Systemic Disparate Impact and Competitive Harm
Surveillance pricing creates broader structural harms across the economy:

Algorithmic Redlining: Personal data metrics such as residential ZIP code, hardware model, credit history, and browsing habits serve as direct proxies for race, socioeconomic standing, and age. Pricing algorithms regenerate historic discriminatory patterns without explicitly identifying protected attributes.

Market Consolidation: Dominant digital platforms with multi-faceted surveillance ecosystems hold an unassailable advantage over small and medium-sized businesses. Deprived of comparable data infrastructure, independent firms cannot compete with platform-level price discrimination.

Horizontal Algorithmic Collusion: The proliferation of third-party pricing software across competing vendors enables tacit, automated price coordination, effectively suppressing price competition across whole market sectors.

IV. Recommendations for Action
To protect consumers and restore transparency to digital commerce, the Commission should take the following actions:

Initiate Section 5 Rulemaking: Promulgate a clear trade regulation rule deeming the use of individual profile data to set personalized prices an unfair method of competition and an unfair trade practice.

Impose Strict Prohibitions on Sensitive Data Inputs: Ban the use of location data, health indicators, credit status, and real-time behavioral signals in dynamic pricing models.

Enforce Intermediary Accountability: Target third-party data brokers, software vendors, and algorithmic intermediaries that collect, package, and supply personalized pricing machinery to retail platforms.

Thank you for your leadership and commitment to maintaining fair, open, and competitive markets.

comment:
The core statutory mandate of the Federal Trade Commission is unambiguous: to protect consumers from unfair, deceptive, or anticompetitive business practices and to maintain fair, transparent market competition.

The emergence and rapid expansion of "surveillance pricing"—the practice of harvesting detailed personal data, location metrics, browsing histories, and behavioral profiles to charge individualized, algorithmically inflated prices—directly subverts this core mission and violates the fundamental protections guaranteed under Section 5 of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. § 45).
​Surveillance Pricing Violates Section 5 Standards.

​Section 5 empowers the Commission to prohibit acts or practices that cause substantial injury to consumers which are not reasonably avoidable and not outweighed by countervailing benefits to consumers or competition.

Surveillance pricing fails every element of this legal standard:

​Substantial, Hidden Financial Harm: By leveraging opaque consumer profiles to extract each individual’s maximum "willingness to pay," corporations systematically strip surplus value from buyers, turning routine market transactions into predatory, asymmetrical extraction.

​Unavoidable Consumer Exploitation: Data tracking is ubiquitous across connected platforms. Because real-time dynamic pricing algorithms operate in secret, consumers cannot reasonably avoid or negotiate against individual price hikes.

​Destruction of Market Transparency: Markets depend on equal access to price signals. When two consumers viewing the exact same item at the exact same moment are offered vastly different prices based on secret algorithmic profiling, fair competition is fundamentally undermined.

​Historical Precedent: Brick-and-Mortar Price Discrimination
​The unfairness of surveillance pricing becomes undeniable when measured against established historical precedents governing physical brick-and-mortar retail:
​Congress and the FTC have long recognized the dangers of arbitrary price discrimination in physical storefronts. Enacted to curb discriminatory practices in physical retail, the Robinson-Patman Act of 1936 (15 U.S.C. § 13) established that charging different prices to different buyers for commodities of like grade and quality without cost justification damages market integrity.

Similarly, the FTC and federal courts established clear precedent against localized predatory pricing, preventing companies from selectively manipulating prices based on geographic location to harm consumers and competitors (e.g., FTC v. Morton Salt Co., 1948).

​In a physical brick-and-mortar store, basic market fairness demands that every consumer walking down an aisle sees the exact same price posted on the shelf. If a physical retailer instructed clerks to inspect a customer's neighborhood, shopping history, or device model at the cash register and secretly mark up the price solely for that individual, it would instantly be recognized as an unconscionable, abusive trade practice.

Digital surveillance pricing merely recreates this exact same abuse behind a screen. Corporations must not be permitted to bypass nearly a century of consumer protection precedents simply by converting physical shelf tags into algorithmic software.

​Conclusion and Requested Action
​Allowing corporate entities to weaponize personal privacy against a consumer’s wallet contradicts the foundational purpose for which the Federal Trade Commission was created. Simple disclosures or opt-out notices are entirely insufficient remedies; informing a consumer that they are being target-priced does not lessen the underlying economic coercion.

​I urge the FTC to fulfill its statutory duty, uphold its commitment to consumer protection, and exercise its full authority under Section 5 to declare data-driven surveillance pricing an unlawful and unfair trade practice.

​Respectfully,

Concerned Consumer and solopreneur.

comment: During this time of economic stress, people should not have to wonder if companies are using their personal data to charge more than the next shopper for the same goods and services. It should not be on consumers to read detailed disclosures to try and figure out whether companies are trying to charge them more. Historically, the FTC has recognized that disclosure may not be enough. If there’s an unfair practice – they have the power to ban it. Consumers want fair prices and not to be profiled. Please ban “personalized” pricing.

Personalized pricing is a top issue confronting the American public. It hurts consumers, takes advantage of people who might be desperate enough to pay much inflated prices, and breaks how markets are intended to work. There has been momentum to address this issue, from states banning personalized pricing to a bipartisan Congressional hearing on the topic.

Under Section 5 of the FTC Act, the FTC has the authority to ban personalized pricing. In addition to banning personalized pricing, we are calling on you to set strong safeguards around personalized discounts. Personal data must not be weaponized by corporations to squeeze even more money out of consumers. This is common sense and does nothing to benefit the public. I urge the Federal Trade Commission to take a firm stance in opposition to personalized pricing and ban its application across the country.

comment: As a citizen and consumer, I adamantly oppose personalized pricing - especially when based on assumed ability or willingness to pay.  I appreciate that the FTC is willing to enforce a policy - but I do not believe that transparency alone (i.e. disclosing that prices have been personalized) is enough to stop abusive practices by companies.  The FTC statement offers several clear examples where personalized pricing would be unfair to consumers - and these types of practices need to be banned (not just disclosed).  Companies will bury the details in the fine print - making it unnecessarily difficult for consumers to figure out they are being ripped off.  The FTC can and should use its power to ban these practices in the first place - and not leave the burden on the consumer to figure it out.  I was appalled to see the results of the Consumer Reports investigation of grocery shopping - where different people shopping online with Instacart for the same items in the same store at the very same time were often given wildly different prices.    No amount of disclosure would offset the injustice of this practice - especially when online grocery shopping is a lifeline for some folks who are housebound.    Please use the FTC's power to strengthen the enforcement policy to prevent abusive personalized pricing before it happens.

comment:
From groceries, clothing, and household necessities to gasoline, the cost of everyday life continues to rise. Consumers should not also have to worry that companies are secretly using our personal data to decide how much each of us should pay for the exact same product or service.
Companies can collect information about where and when we shop, what we search for online, what device we use, and countless other details about our lives. Using that information to determine that one consumer should pay more than another for the same goods and services is simply discrimination with a new face. It is an unacceptable way to squeeze more money out of consumers, especially in the economy we currently have.
I strongly oppose the FTC’s proposal to merely put pressure on companies that use consumers’ personal data to set individualized prices. The FTC has the authority to do more to protect consumers, and it should use that authority.
It is the FTC’s job to protect consumers from surveillance pricing—not to put the burden on consumers to protect themselves. New Jersey is the latest state to enact a ban on surveillance pricing. That should be a clear signal that stronger action is both necessary and possible.
Simply requiring companies to disclose that they use personalized pricing—and to identify the types of data they use to determine prices—is not enough. Consumers should not be expected to read complicated disclosures, understand sophisticated pricing algorithms, and somehow determine whether a company is charging them more because of their personal information.
Transparency is not a substitute for protection.
The FTC has historically recognized that disclosure alone may not be sufficient when a practice is unfair or deceptive. If the practice is unfair, the FTC should not simply require companies to disclose it. The FTC should prohibit it.

Most of the "personalization" of prices equates to "how much can we get away with charging this person." It will always be against the consumers' best interests. This already happens to an extent where certain goods cost more or less depending on the region, and in some cases laws are already in place to prevent exploitation, such as laws limiting the percentage price hikes following a natural disaster.

The other concern is, what type of personal information is being used to control the prices? Is it just spending habits, or does it also include protected group information, such as religious affiliation or gender orientation? Will they charge more to a pregnant woman buying snacks in the middle of the night because they know she will buy the item regardless of the price? Please enforce the laws as strictly as possible to protect consumers from this predatory behavior.

comment: Businesses should charge customers the same price for the same product. This is a basic principle of fairness in business practices that has been upheld for years already: you can't charge different people different prices based on their race, religion, gender, etc. because it would be obviously discriminatory. Now, technology has made  possible even greater capabilities for predatory discrimination between people in pricing, using collected and inferred patterns in our behavior. Not only is it unfair to target people with different prices based on their current ability to pay, their personal preferences for a product or service, or their temporary desperation for that product or service - the data analysis methods used to draw these conclusions are often statistical interferences, not direct evidence, and may not even be true. This makes it even more difficult, if not impossible, for consumers to understand and appeal the data companies are using to discriminate against them. Surveillance pricing is nothing more than the latest predatory and unfair business practice, and ought to be fully banned.

Businesses should offer goods and services at a fair price to everyone - not pick and choose the price based on who wants to buy. Your groceries shouldn't cost more because you're wearing fancy clothes, or because the store's cameras recorded you getting out of a very expensive car. A plumbing service shouldn't quote you a higher price because the computer you used to contact them was recently used to check the price of an airplane ticket. An airline shouldn't charge you more for a flight because you visited their web site using a more expensive computer. A clothing store shouldn't charge you a higher price because your address seems to indicate a more expensive neighborhood.

All of these are examples of surveillance pricing. The FTC should ban surveillance pricing outright, not leave it to consumers to try to determine whether a company is using surveillance pricing and then try to determine whether the company has used that to inflate their prices.

comment:
I am writing as an everyday consumer to express my strong opposition to personalized pricing and to urge the Commission to treat algorithmic, individualized price discrimination as inherently unfair and deceptive.
Navigating the modern economy already feels like running an obstacle course of hidden fees, automated surcharges, and constant upsells. We are nickeled and dimed for basic necessities, travel, groceries, and digital services at every turn. Allowing companies to weaponize our private data—harvesting our browsing habits, device types, zip codes, and perceived desperation—to charge each person a different price cross the line from standard commerce into predatory behavior.
Transparent, uniform pricing is the bedrock of fair market competition. When two people standing in the same aisle or visiting the same website are quoted different prices for the exact same item simply because an algorithm deduced one person had slightly less time or fewer alternatives, the market ceases to be competitive. It becomes an extractive system designed to squeeze every last cent of consumer surplus out of working families who are already stretched thin.
Personalized pricing does not reward customer loyalty; it penalizes necessity and exploits asymmetric information. Consumers have virtually no ability to negotiate with a black-box algorithm, nor do we have the visibility to know when we are being unfairly targeted.
I urge the FTC to take a decisive, uncompromising stance against these practices. Strong enforcement should ban surveillance-based individual pricing, mandate clear price transparency across both digital and physical storefronts, and hold companies accountable when they leverage personal data to extract maximum financial toll from consumers simply trying to make ends meet.
Thank you for your time and for protecting consumers from unchecked algorithmic exploitation.]

comment: Although in early years of commerce, barter was common and admittedly, items may have different value to different individuals, commerce has so diversified and automated that most common items are commodities and we have for years gotten accustomed to fixed pricing. No one should be charged more than their peers for typical daily commodified necessities. I know that for some time now, airlines, hotels and others have used variable pricing. Although I am not really happy with that, to the extent that it is based on general supply vs. demand, it has some rationale. However, to charge someone a higher or lower price for a commodity item such as food, clothing, toys, or whatever based on personal data such as search history, length of time item in shopping cart, previous purchase history or indirect financial information such as zip code, type of credit card, home ownership vs. rental is unreasonable. None of these factors impacts the value of, need for or use of the item being purchased. One possible exception is the offering of a discount if an item sits in a shopping cart for a long time. This could be viewed as an incentive to make the purchase, saves the purchaser money and presumably still benefits the vendor or the offer would not be made.

comment: Hello. I write this to be heard, not to be dumped into a pile of similarly ignored sentiments. I write this to urge the Federal Trade Commission to step in and bar the use of Personalized Pricing, or as I believe is a more fitting term, "Surveillance Pricing". To keep it brief, citizens' right to privacy has been quickly eroding and being chipped away at from all angles due to various incentive structures. One in particular which I am writing about in this comment is corporations' ability to set the price depending on the customer. Why would they do this? To maximize their potential profit based on a pattern of history they've acquired through surveilling their customers, potential and actual and trying to figure out what is the most they'd be willing to pay for any particular good or service. This is a clearly predatory practice, violating the privacy of our citizens while simultaneously squeezing them out of their hard-earned money as much as possible in a time of unheard of inflation. The government constantly speaks of wanting to help the economy, the problem is, from the perspective of the average citizen, it no longer it feels like the good of the economy equates to the good of the people when it seems all that economic focus is based completely and entirely around the corporations which do nothing to give back. I request the Federal Trade Commission to take a firm action against these practices, both by enacting new laws that prohibit these behaviors, but by also enforcing them as well, and actually backing them up with severe penalties. A couple hundred dollar fine against a global corporation does nothing if not enable them further. You must actively work to stop this practice from continuing.

comment:
I have been seeing more stories lately about surveillance pricing, retail surge pricing, and similar potential fluid pricing models in stores. I am appalled that they are even being considered as possibilities. The idea of seeing a product online at a certain price, seeing a different price on the shelves, and then being charged a potentially different price at the register makes no sense. Notwithstanding that inflation is already squeezing everyone, these predatory pricing practices seem tailor-made for price-gouging and customer-hostile policies. Further, these are policies that will ultimately impact retail workers hardest, while the upper management and boards who implement them are shielded from hostile customers angry about an utterly baffling pricing system that appears to arbitrarily charges one person more for an item than another. Having worked in retail, I could easily envision angry customers becoming violent about a policy that someone working at Walmart for minimum wage has no control over (but they will get the hospital bill for any serious injuries).

All of this is before we address the technological component. Many of these programs will likely be powered by AI, which remains one of the least reliable tools in our current arsenal. Regardless of the promises that retailers who want to implement surveillance pricing say, we cannot trust these tools to be impartial or even accurate arbiters of who gets what prices. In my time working with AI, I was unable to get it to follow even basic instructions. I have had experiences where it directly ignores my instructions.

comment:
I support strong protections for consumers against the use of personal data to secretly determine the prices they are charged.

Consumers should be able to expect that when they shop for ordinary goods and services, the price they see is not being increased because a company has collected information about their browsing history, shopping habits, location, device, previous purchases, or other personal data and concluded that they may be willing to pay more.

There is an important difference between legitimate dynamic pricing based on factors such as supply, demand, timing, or market conditions and personalized pricing based on information collected about an individual consumer. When two people shopping for the same product at the same time can be offered different prices because an algorithm has analyzed their personal information, consumers deserve to know that clearly and before making a purchase.

I support the FTC's proposed enforcement policy and encourage the Commission to use the full extent of its existing authority to prevent unfair or deceptive personalized pricing practices. Companies should not be permitted to conceal the fact that personal data is affecting a consumer's price. At a minimum, businesses using personalized pricing should be required to provide clear and conspicuous disclosure that the price is personalized, what types of personal information are being used, and how that information affects the price offered.

I also encourage the FTC to continue examining whether additional consumer protections are needed in this area and to pursue the strongest protections available under its legal authority. Consumers should not have to surrender their privacy simply to receive a fair and transparent price.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comment: The issue of "personalized pricing" seems clear.  Retailers should set a reasonable retail price for what they sell and it should be what each purchaser pays. comment:
I support the Commission's proposed policy statement on personalized pricing, and I'd ask it to go further in a few places.

When I see a price on a shelf or a website, I assume it's the same price my neighbor sees. I decide where to shop and whether to compare prices based on that assumption. If a store is quietly setting my price from data about me, I can't shop smart, because I don't know what I'm comparing. That gets worse as stores move to electronic shelf tags and app prices that can change while I'm standing in the aisle. A price has to hold still long enough for me to compare it.

Here's a specific case I'd like the Commission to address. Smart carts and scan-as-you-shop apps can tell a store what I've picked up. If I put a jar of spaghetti sauce in my cart, the store could raise the price of pasta and ground beef on my app or cart screen, because it knows I'm likely to need them and I'm already in the building. I don't know that any store does this today, but the tools exist. I'd ask the Commission to name it as unfair or deceptive, alongside its example of raising a website price when a shopper is in the store.

The bigger risk is where this could go next. Today a shelf tag, paper or digital, at least shows one price to everyone in the aisle. If stores drop shelf prices and make shoppers use an app, I'd have no way to know what the person next to me pays, and I wouldn't see my own price until I opened the app or reached the register. At that point the price can't be compared at all. I'd ask the Commission to treat removing a common posted price, in favor of app-only or checkout-only pricing, as a sign that personalization is being hidden.

I'm not against every price that varies. Surge pricing on a busy Friday night applies to everyone in the area. Insurance and loans have always been priced on the person. A loyalty discount at a store I shop at regularly is fine with me, because I know about it and it only lowers my price. My concern is a price that goes up because a company has guessed how much I'll tolerate, using data I didn't know it had.

Disclosure is the right starting point, but on its own it won't do much for most people. A line in the terms of service or a small icon near the price will be ignored, especially on a phone. I'd ask the Commission to be specific about what counts as clear and conspicuous:

1. Put the disclosure next to the price, before checkout.
2. Show the price the customer would pay without personalization, so the difference is visible.
3. Let customers see the data used to set their price and correct it, the way credit reports work today.
4. Require opt-in consent before personal data is used to raise a price.

Footnote 20 says the Commission isn't taking a position yet on whether some personalized pricing is unfair even when fully disclosed. I'd ask it to take that position for the examples it already lists: charging more because someone is having a medical emergency, traveling for a funeral, was recently the victim of a crime, or has kids at home. Those people often can't walk away from the purchase, so a disclosure doesn't protect them. Telling someone you're charging more because their situation is desperate doesn't make it fair.

If the Commission's current authority can't reach those cases, I'd ask it to tell Congress so.

Thank you for taking public comment on this.

comment:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to surveillance pricing, the practice of using consumers' personal data to set individualized prices for goods and services.

As a Massachusetts resident who works professionally in cybersecurity, I see firsthand how much personal data is collected, aggregated, and traded without meaningful consumer awareness. Browsing history, location, device type, purchase patterns, and inferred characteristics are now being used not just to target ads, but to determine what each of us is charged. This turns the data economy against the very people it harvests from.

Surveillance pricing is fundamentally unfair. It deliberately charges people more based on what algorithms predict they will tolerate: their urgency, their perceived wealth, their lack of alternatives, or their inability to comparison-shop. Two people buying the same product at the same moment should not pay different prices because one was profiled as less likely to walk away, or because they have a higher/lower income.

It is also invisible. Consumers cannot see the price others were offered, cannot know which data points drove their price, and cannot contest it. A market where prices are secret and individualized is not a competitive market; it undermines the price transparency that competition depends on.

Finally, these systems risk reproducing discrimination. Even when protected characteristics aren't used directly, proxies like ZIP code, device, and shopping behavior can produce outcomes that disproportionately burden vulnerable and lower-income consumers.

I urge the Commission to treat surveillance pricing as an unfair and deceptive practice, to require clear disclosure whenever personal data influences a price, to restrict the use of personal data for individualized pricing, and to use its full enforcement authority against companies and intermediaries that build and sell these tools.

Respectfully,
Eric Breen
Methuen, MA

comment:
From groceries to gasoline, the cost of everyday necessities continues to rise. During a period of significant economic stress, consumers should not have to worry that companies are using their personal data—including where and when they shop, what they search for online, and what type of phone they use—to charge them more than another shopper for the same goods or services.

Surveillance-based—or “personalized”—pricing is an increasingly troubling practice in the United States. Companies may collect and analyze detailed information about consumers to estimate how much they are willing or able to pay, then use that information to set different prices for different people.

Consumers deserve transparency and equal treatment. Companies should clearly disclose when prices are personalized, what information is used to determine them, and whether consumers are being charged more because of their data. They should not be permitted to use sensitive personal information to exploit people’s financial circumstances or make essential goods and services less affordable.

The Federal Trade Commission should investigate surveillance-based pricing, establish strong limits on the collection and use of consumer data for pricing decisions, and prohibit deceptive, discriminatory, or unfair individualized pricing practices. Consumers should be able to compare prices confidently and know that the price they see is not inflated because a company has profiled them.

comment:
I strongly oppose the use of personally identifying information to adjust or influence the prices consumers see, including prices displayed through digital shelf labels. It is indefensible for companies to collect, infer, or purchase sensitive personal data and then use it to determine what an individual consumer pays for an identical product.
Personalized pricing based on private information can unfairly penalize people because of factors such as their location, income level, browsing history, device type, or other characteristics they may not know are being used against them. Consumers should not have to surrender privacy in exchange for fair and consistent pricing.
The FTC should establish clear rules requiring transparency, meaningful consent, and limits on the use of personal data in pricing decisions. Companies should be prohibited from using sensitive or identifying information to raise prices for particular individuals, especially when consumers cannot easily detect, understand, or challenge the practice. Digital price tags should not become a tool for hidden, individualized price discrimination.
Consumers deserve to know the real price of an item and to be treated fairly at the point of sale.
please further fact check that response against Electornic Frontier Foundation and Consumer Reports, or any other consumer watchdog
Your core point is well supported by the EFF and is consistent with the FTC’s proposal, but it should be phrased more precisely: the FTC proposal does not ban all personalized pricing outright; it focuses on undisclosed or unfair/deceptive uses of personal data.
Fact-checked revision
I strongly oppose the use of personally identifying information, or data derived from it, to adjust the prices consumers see—including through digital shelf labels. Consumers should be able to expect that a price displayed for an ordinary retail product is the same price offered to other shoppers at the same place and time, rather than a price based on an assessment of their personal data or perceived willingness to pay.
Using browsing history, location, purchase history, household information, device data, or data obtained from brokers to set individualized prices is an invasion of privacy and undermines price transparency. The Electronic Frontier Foundation describes this practice as “surveillance pricing” and warns that it can burden vulnerable groups, incentivize excessive data collection, and make it difficult for consumers to understand or challenge why they were charged more.
The FTC should require clear, conspicuous, and specific disclosure whenever a price is personalized. The disclosure should state that the price may differ from the price shown to other customers, explain why it was personalized, and identify the categories of data used. The FTC should also require meaningful, informed consent before businesses collect, purchase, or use personal information for individualized pricing.
Disclosure alone may not be enough. The FTC should closely scrutinize, and where appropriate prohibit, the use of sensitive information or opaque inferences to charge different prices for everyday goods—especially when consumers cannot reasonably avoid the practice, verify the data used, correct errors, or compare prices fairly.
Digital shelf labels may have legitimate operational uses, such as updating prices for all shoppers at once. However, they should never become a mechanism for silently charging different customers different prices based on private information. Consumers should not have to give up their privacy in order to receive a fair price.

comment:
The practice of personalized pricingleveraging vast amounts of consumer data to tailor prices to an individual's perceived willingness to pay represents a significant threat to market transparency and consumer autonomy. By replacing a transparent, uniform price with an opaque, algorithmic one, firms can effectively extract more consumer surplus and shift the balance of power further away from the individual.

First, personalized pricing creates a profound information asymmetry. In a traditional market, price serves as a signal of value and competition. When prices are personalized, that signal is destroyed. Consumers can no longer determine if they are receiving a fair market price or if they are being penalized based on their browsing history, device type, or demographic data. This lack of transparency prevents consumers from making informed decisions and undermines the efficiency of the marketplace.

Second, these practices frequently rely on the exploitation of vulnerable populations. Algorithms designed to maximize profit often identify and target consumers who have fewer alternatives, less time to shop around, or limited digital literacy. When pricing is based on "willingness to pay," it often becomes a proxy for "lack of options," effectively taxing those who are already disadvantaged.

Finally, the shift toward personalized pricing encourages an invasive cycle of data collection. To refine their pricing models, companies are incentivized to collect increasingly intimate data on consumer behavior, further eroding privacy.

The FTC must take a firm stance against these practices. We urge the Commission to establish a policy that prioritizes price transparency and prohibits the use of personal data to engage in discriminatory pricing. Competition should be driven by firms offering better products or lower prices to all, not by their ability to more accurately predict the maximum amount a specific individual can be coerced into paying.
