comment:
I strongly urge the Federal Trade Commission to take aggressive action against surveillance pricing and the use of consumers’ personal data to determine the prices they are individually offered.
I find the idea that a company could monitor my behavior, location, browsing history, shopping history, device information, or other personal characteristics and then use that information to determine how much I should pay for the exact same product or service deeply troubling. A consumer should not have to wonder whether the price displayed on a screen is the real market price or whether an algorithm has decided that the specific person looking at it can be charged more.
This is fundamentally different from ordinary supply-and-demand pricing. Prices can legitimately change because of inventory, time, transportation costs, demand, or other factors affecting the product or service itself. But when the price changes because a company has profiled the individual consumer standing on the other side of the transaction, the consumer is no longer simply responding to a market price. The consumer is being evaluated and potentially exploited based on information they may not even know was collected.
The FTC's own investigation has demonstrated that this is not merely a theoretical concern. The Commission reported that companies and pricing intermediaries can use detailed information, including consumers’ locations, demographics, browsing behavior, shopping history, and other behavioral data, to develop individualized prices and promotions. The FTC also found that some intermediaries had hundreds of business clients. This demonstrates the potential scale of the problem.
I am especially concerned about the information asymmetry this creates. Companies can collect enormous amounts of information about consumers and use sophisticated algorithms to determine what price they believe each person will tolerate. Consumers generally do not have comparable information about the company, its pricing algorithm, the data it uses, or the price it offers to other consumers.
Simply requiring disclosure is not an adequate solution.
Consumers should not be expected to read complicated privacy policies or pricing disclosures and then somehow determine whether an algorithm is secretly charging them more than another person. Most people cannot realistically audit an algorithm or determine what data was used to calculate a price. A disclosure after the fact does not undo the economic harm caused by an unfair price.
I therefore urge the FTC to use every lawful authority available to prevent deceptive and unfair surveillance-pricing practices and to pursue additional rulemaking or other measures if existing authority is insufficient.
At a minimum, consumers should have a meaningful right to know:
1.Whether personal data was used to determine or modify the price they were shown.
2.What categories of personal data were used.
3.Whether the price offered to them differs from the price offered to other consumers for the same product or service under substantially similar circumstances.
4.Whether information obtained from third-party data brokers or other sources was used.
5.Whether sensitive or highly revealing characteristics were used directly or indirectly to determine pricing.
6.Whether an automated algorithm or artificial intelligence system was used to determine an individual's price.
More importantly, consumers should not have to accept the premise that disclosure makes every form of personalized pricing acceptable.
There should be clear limits on the use of personal information to determine the maximum price a company believes an individual consumer is willing to pay. The ability to collect increasingly detailed information about people should not automatically create a corresponding right to use that information against them at the point of sale.
This issue is particularly important during a period when Americans are already struggling with the rising cost of necessities such as food, housing, transportation, insurance, and energy. Consumers should be able to comparison shop based on transparent prices rather than wondering whether their digital history has led them to receive a worse deal.
I strongly encourage the FTC to continue investigating surveillance pricing, hold companies accountable when they use personal information unfairly or deceptively, and establish meaningful protections against individualized pricing practices that exploit consumers’ personal data.
The basic principle should be simple: A person's private information should not be used to secretly charge them more.
Consumers deserve transparent, fair, and understandable prices. I urge the Commission to act accordingly.

comment: The very concept that an item may be charged different prices by the same company to different individuals reflects a practice that is grossly unfair. Today's products that are mass-produced yield products with consistent quality & took a consistent cost to produce, at any point in time. But to charge a different price for the same item based on the limits of what a customer will pay is discriminatory, & should be outlawed, with severe financial penalties for those companies who attempt such practices.

comment:
Everyone should pay the same price for the same product under the same conditions. That's the basic deal a market economy runs on. When a company instead prices you individually — based on data it collected about you, often without your knowledge — it breaks that deal. It stops selling a product at a price and starts selling you, specifically, the most expensive version of yourself it can calculate.

This isn't a hypothetical harm. Regulators have found real households paying hundreds to thousands of dollars more a year because a company's algorithm decided they could bear it. One airline reportedly charged a grieving customer more than triple the normal fare for last-minute funeral travel — not because the flight cost more to run, but because the algorithm read desperation as opportunity. A major grocery delivery app quietly tested different prices on different shoppers for the identical cart of groceries, until public pressure forced it to stop. These aren't edge cases; they're what the practice looks like when it's working exactly as designed.

Two principles should be non-negotiable:

First, price must be consistent and fair. A price should reflect the product and the market — supply, demand, cost — not a profile of the individual buyer. Charging people differently based on what a company has learned about their desperation, their inattention, or their inability to shop around isn't "personalization." It's discrimination dressed up in the language of customization. If a discount is available, it should be available on terms anyone can meet — not secretly, and not because an algorithm decided you specifically would pay more without it.

Second, personal data cannot be collected, bought, or sold without real, informed, opt-in consent. Data gathered for one purpose — running a loyalty program, enabling location services, remembering a shopping cart — should not be quietly repurposed to figure out how much more a person can be charged. Consent has to mean something: it has to be specific, it has to be visible, and it has to be something a person actually agreed to, not something buried in a terms-of-service update. If a company wants to use someone's data to set their price, it should have to ask, plainly, and accept "no" as an answer.

The reason these two principles have to travel together is simple: personalized pricing only works because of data collected without meaningful consent. Cut off the second and the first mostly takes care of itself. That's why the growing wave of state laws — bans in Maryland and Connecticut, disclosure mandates in New York and Connecticut, investigations by the FTC, Congress, and California's Attorney General — all converge on the same fix: consumers are owed transparency about how their data is used and a real choice about whether it's used at all.

None of this requires banning discounts, loyalty programs, or normal supply-and-demand pricing. It just requires that pricing be based on the product and the market, not on a covert profile of the person buying it — and that using someone's personal data for anything, including pricing, requires asking them first.

To: Federal Trade Commission

Personalized pricing has been a top issue for Consumer Reports. It hurts consumers, takes advantage of people who might be desperate enough to pay much inflated prices, and breaks how markets are intended to work. There has been momentum to address this issue, from states banning personalized pricing to a bipartisan Congressional hearing on the topic.

Under Section 5 of the FTC Act, the FTC has the authority to ban personalized pricing. In addition to banning personalized pricing, we are calling on you to set strong safeguards around personalized discounts.

comment:
I strongly support meaningful consumer protections against undisclosed personalized or “surveillance” pricing.

I understand that prices legitimately change because of supply and demand, inventory, timing, geography, promotions, and other normal market factors. My concern is something very different: a company using information collected about me—such as my browsing history, purchasing history, location, device information, demographics, previous interactions, or other personal data—to determine how much it believes I personally am willing to pay.

Two consumers looking at the same product or service at the same time should not unknowingly be quoted different prices simply because an algorithm has concluded that one of them can or will pay more.

This creates an enormous information imbalance. Companies can know a great deal about an individual consumer, while the consumer may know virtually nothing about how the price being displayed was determined. That undermines meaningful comparison shopping and makes it impossible to know whether you are seeing a generally available market price or a price specifically engineered for you.

At a minimum, if a business uses personal information to determine or influence the price shown to an individual consumer, that practice should be disclosed clearly and conspicuously before the purchase. Consumers should be told what categories of personal information are being used and should have a meaningful opportunity to opt out and receive a price that is not based on their personal profile.

I also believe there is an important distinction between dynamic pricing and surveillance pricing. Consumers understand that an airline seat, hotel room, concert ticket, or other product can change in price as market conditions change. What consumers should not have to accept is a hidden system in which the price changes because a company has profiled the particular person asking for it.

The ability to collect increasingly detailed information about consumers should not become an invisible mechanism for determining how much more each individual can be persuaded to pay.

I urge the FTC to establish strong transparency requirements and to aggressively enforce existing consumer-protection laws when personalized pricing practices are deceptive or unfair. Consumers deserve to know when their personal information is affecting the price they are being offered.

Pricing should be transparent enough that consumers can make informed choices and comparison shop effectively.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Subject: Request to investigate and prohibit surveillance pricing

I request that your agency investigate and prohibit the use of personal data to set individualized prices for the same goods or services.

On [date], I observed the following conduct by [company]: [describe exactly what happened]. The price for [product or service] was [amount] under [conditions] and [amount] under [different conditions]. I have attached [screenshots, receipts, URLs, and other evidence].

I believe the company may have used [browsing history, location, account status, demographics, purchase history, device information, inferred income, or other data] to determine the price or eligibility for a discount. The company did not clearly disclose [that prices were personalized, the data used, or the reason for the difference].

This practice harms consumers by [charging different consumers different prices for the same item / withholding discounts / forcing consumers to accept tracking / creating discriminatory or unaffordable outcomes]. It also undermines meaningful comparison shopping.

I ask the agency to:

investigate [company and conduct];
require companies to disclose when prices are personalized, the data categories used, and the basis for the price;
prohibit companies from using personal data or inferred characteristics to set individualized prices for the same product or service;
prohibit retaliation or higher prices for consumers who decline tracking;
require deletion of data used unlawfully and provide refunds or other relief where appropriate; and
refer the issue for legislation if the agency lacks authority to impose a complete ban.
Please treat this submission as a request for enforcement and as public input supporting a rule or policy against surveillance pricing.

Sincerely,
Marcia Lahaie

The use of surveillance pricing must be ban. This predatory practice has no moral or legal justification. As this activity is facilitated by access to personal data, data-broker information, or inferred characteristics of the individual, it is imperative that changes be made to prevent access to that information. There are already U.S. states and other countries that have implemented strong protections. These should be available to everyone. In addition, a monitoring system is needed, with independent audits, records of company compliance, and refunds for unlawful overcharges.

comment:
I strongly oppose any personalized pricing. We are already experiencing this in the airlines industry where we are being charged for our airplane seats based on what we have been willing to pay in the past. This is abusive because people's lives and circumstances change and a price should be based on the value of a commodity or service as seen by society as a whole, not manipulated to extract the maximum value out of each consumer.

This should apply even more when it comes to purchasing groceries or pharmacy items. Companies are now attempting to predict not just the maximum that a specific customer will pay but also their degree of urgency in any given shopping trip. So, if you run out to get milk and it is not your typical shopping day, the store infers that you have run out of milk and desperately need that milk for your child's cereal so they mark up the price for you. The same would occur if you go out and purchase a bunch of over the counter remedies for a family member with the flu. This is just profiteering and should not be allowed.

Another serious and perhaps even greater concern with personalized pricing is that companies are using facial recognition to identify you so that the minute you start shopping they know who you are. You cannot eliminate your face print and if someone gets a hold of it, they will be able to access your bank accounts and potentially your government benefits and a lot more. With the AI-associated mass escalation in hacking of databases (see https://qz.com/gateway/anthropic-claude-opus-55-cost-performance-092226 and https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/09/fbi-probes-service-selling-153m-drivers-licenses/) , it is just a matter of time until vulnerabilities allow nefarious actors to secure troves of consumers' facial prints. It is extremely risky for companies to be storing your face print merely for the purpose of personalizing prices so I ask that you completely prohibit this.

From groceries to gas, the cost of necessities is continuing to skyrocket. During this time of economic stress, you should not have to wonder if companies are using your personal data – from where and when you shop to what you search for online and the type of phone you use – to charge you more than the next shopper for the same goods and services.
Surveillance or “personalized” pricing is a growing trend among U.S. corporations using my personal data to squeeze more money out of me. I urge you to ban the use of personal data to set the prices I pay. It's simply not fair or right to allow companies to profit off of my personal data to determine that I should pay more than somebody else based on their mining of my personal data! And you can't expect people to read the find print merely because they are alerted to the possibility of surveillance pricing. How about protecting us consumers instead of the greedy companies!

comment:
Please work to ban surveillance pricing.

In these financially difficult times, we need MORE financial stability, not less. And none of us should not have to wonder if companies are using our personal data – from where and when we shop, to what we search for online, or the type of phones we use – to charge any of us more than the next shopper for the same goods and services. This is fundamentally unfair, and clearly wrong.

Airlines already do this (just try looking for the same tickets on a Mac and a PC to see how much the prices differ) to know how unfair (and infuriating) it is.

As citizen consumers, we don't need or want to be manipulated in this way, so please outlaw "personalized" pricing.

P.S. I will personally vote against any politician and / or public official who is in favor of it.

The FTC is proposing a plan that would put pressure on companies that use our personal data to set the prices I pay. However, the agency has the power to do more to protect consumers. Surveillance or “personalized” pricing is a growing trend among U.S. corporations using our personal data to squeeze more money out of us.

The FTC has the authority to ban surveillance pricing. Currently, however, the FTC’s proposed policy would only require companies to disclose that they are doing personalized pricing and the specific types of data used to change the price we see. While it is encouraging that the agency is taking steps to address unfair pricing practices, it should not be the consumer's obligation to read detailed disclosures to try and figure out whether companies are trying to charge them more. Historically, the FTC has recognized that disclosure may not be enough. If there’s an unfair practice, they have the power to ban it!

comment:
I am submitting this comment as an individual who studies financial services, AI, and consumer protection. For consumers, it is a reasonable assumption that what they see as posted price is the same price that everyone would see. To enable personalized pricing to work, I'd like to offer a few recommendations.

1) Make disclosure verifiable. Firms need to keep records of the data used to set a given price.
2) Define personalization by inputs, not labels. Any price that uses consumer or device specific data as an input, such as battery level, device model, installed apps, or location, should count as personalized, regardless of what the firm calls it.
3) Address pricing on urgency directly. Some of the examples shared here, including funeral traveler and medical emergency, price a consumer's lack of alternatives. Mere disclosure does little to help consumers who are in need right at that moment. And these harms fall hardest on those with the least slack and options.

Consumers have the right to know when a price has been built around them, on what basis, and from what data.

"Personalized" pricing is a threat to capitalism. It is, in no way, fair. Use your authority to protect consumers and our economy.

comment:
A free market economy depends on more than libertarian economic viewpoints to maintain itself in the long term. I believe that proper regulation is necessary to maintain equality and balance within our markets and our financial system. As such, I believe it is the proper role of government to minimize the impacts of “exploitation economics“.

There are far too many examples within our current business models that find ways to generate profit margins through overly burdensome or constantly shifting information provided to the consumer. The success in this model is based upon the fact that most individuals do not have the desire or ability to navigate an overly complex situation just to make a purchase or negotiate a fair price. Nowwe find that the business practice is taking the information that is available about the consumer, and changing the pricing based on that information.

As such, I believe that proper legislation and/or regulation that limits the ability of corporations to harness their technical and computing power to change their pricing based on information gathered about the consumer, that was not deliberately offered by the consumer, should be implemented.

comment:
Any person who enters a store and purchases an item should be guaranteed to get the best available price on that item for that day. No one should be charged more or less than the next person buying the same item. This is the honest weights and measures morality that made for an agreeable exchange system. Shopping for the things I need should not be an adversarial event that I have come to hate.

The first irritating violation cane with discounting the price for people who can afford to buy and use (or store) more than a reasonable amount of any one (or mix or match) of items. I am a single senior who does not consume large quantities of items nor do I live in a space where I can store more than I can use in a reasonable amount of time. Why should I subsidize the person who is in a position to buy and use more?

Most egregious of all are the "customer loyalty" programs designed to figure out the highest price I will pay for an item and then remembering what that is and always charging me more than the shelf price that the non loyal shopper has to pay. Beyond that the "digital discounts" that come out and change every week seem to have a high percentage of failures. Just to keep my aging mind sharp I tote up the price I should paying for every item in the shipping cart. Nearly every time I shop I have to go to customer service to get digital failure relief. This does not make me feel rewarded for being a loyal customer. This is irritating but doable.

I have only the basic level of rewards. People who have the paid for level of rewards do not have any less digital failure rates. I know one woman who takes her receipt home (way out in the slough area) does her audit and brings all the documents back with her the next week to get adjusted for last weeks errors.

I have seen many senior persons in one particular store struggling with some phone app that is supposed to provide discounts and special pricing or rewards but the app is not easy to use and suffers from the same digital failure of most rewards programs.

Just give me the best all over available prices on the items I buy and skip the (I am sure not free, why do they want me to pay to play) programs and random reinforcement generated by all the digital failures. Should not everyone shipping at any moment in time get the best available price the store has to offer?

Offering the same best available price to everyone who ships at the store is truly the fairest way to conduct business. No one person or group of persons should be subsidizing other groups of shoppers and especially not if the goal is to artificially (and unfairly) increase same store profitability at the expense of the shoppers who may not have any choice to go elseward.

Customer loyalty should be earned the old fashion way, good prices and exceptional customer service. Fleecing the shopper with fancy gimmicks does not cut it in these tough economic times.

comment:
Dear FTC,
I am appalled that companies are using personalized pricing. This is unfair and disingenuous, and consumers need protection from these practices. The listed price on something should be the price, full disclosure. It's not a company's job to decide how much I should or can afford to pay for something. How do they even base these decisions? However they do it, it's not fair.

I am an illustrator and independent art suppy stores are getting fewer and father between. The one remaining store that has multiple locations does not use personalized pricing, but they do something that is endlessly frustrating to me because I have no idea what the prices are. If I look up the prices online, they seem reasonable, and then when you go to a store, the prices are way more. There's some kind of math where they factor in the shipping cost, and who knows what else, but I just want to know the prices of items I want or need so I can decide what I can afford.

I just looked up the FTC and it states : "The Federal Trade Commission is an independent agency of the United States government whose principal mission is the enforcement of civil antitrust law and the promotion of consumer protection." The reason why the US government was created was to give us all the opportunities for life, liberty, and happiness, and our tax dollars are collected so the government can provide services to give us those opportunities.

Please do your job and protect us from this unfair consumer scam.
Thank you.

comment:
Federal Trade Commission
Re: Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement on Personalized Pricing
I'm submitting this comment as an independent commercial food broker and business owner. I manage wholesale pricing, retail markups, and supply chain logistics in the retail grocery sector. I know the mechanics of how goods are priced from the manufacturer to the checkout counter.
The FTC’s proposal to mandate disclosure for surveillance pricing fails to solve the core problem. Disclosures shift the regulatory burden directly onto consumers. Shoppers don't have the time, technical data, or market leverage to decipher complex algorithmic pricing models before buying necessities. Relying on fine-print disclosures doesn't protect consumers; it gives corporations a legal shield to continue exploiting private data.
While the retail grocery sector relies on tight margins and visible competition, broad digital commerce currently operates in a black box. Retailers use personalized data—browsing history, device type, geographic location—to dynamically inflate prices for targeted individuals. This practice fundamentally distorts fair market competition. It creates massive information asymmetry where the retailer holds every advantage over the individual buyer.
The FTC must aggressively classify algorithmic personalized pricing as an "unfair and deceptive practice" under Section 5 of the FTC Act. You don't need to wait for a new statutory ban to act. When a digital platform alters a price based on a user's hidden digital profile, rendering them incapable of accessing the baseline market rate, the practice is inherently deceptive.
Stop treating surveillance pricing as a transparency issue. It is a structural market abuse. I urge the Commission to apply Section 5 and penalize the specific algorithmic tactics corporations use to penalize consumers.
Manuel Garcia

comment: Surveillance or “personalized” pricing is unfortunately a growing trend among U.S. corporations that are using personal data of consumers to squeeze more money from consumers.  Fortunately, there has recently been a wave of momentum about protecting consumers from surveillance pricing.  New Jersey just became the third state to pass a surveillance pricing ban into law.  Similar to states, the FTC has the authority to ban surveillance pricing.   Currently, however, the FTC’s proposed policy would only require companies to disclose that they are doing personalized pricing and the specific types of data used to change the price for any consumer.  While it is encouraging that the FTC is taking steps to address unfair pricing practices, it should not be on consumers to read detailed disclosures to try and figure whether companies are trying to charge consumers more.  Historically, the FTC has recognized that disclosure might not be enough. If there is an unfair practice, then the FTC has the power to ban it!  As a result, I request the FTC to please soon ban surveillance pricing.

comment:
Personalized pricing presents a problem extending beyond conventional information asymmetry. The more significant concern is the combination of information asymmetry and leverage asymmetry, which can create a fundamentally unbalanced bargaining relationship.

Ordinary bargaining contains a degree of reciprocal uncertainty. The seller generally does not know the maximum price a particular buyer is willing or able to pay, just as the buyer does not know the minimum price the seller will accept. That uncertainty creates bargaining space and disciplines each party’s ability to extract the entire value of the transaction.

Data-intensive personalized pricing can fundamentally alter that relationship. A seller may possess extensive information concerning a particular consumer’s purchasing history, location, browsing behavior, financial circumstances, available substitutes, switching costs, urgency, prior willingness to pay, and predicted likelihood of abandoning a transaction. Increasingly sophisticated analytical systems may use these data not merely to estimate demand across a market, but to infer the bargaining constraints of an individual human being.

The consumer ordinarily possesses no reciprocal capability. The consumer may not know the seller’s reservation price, the prices being offered simultaneously to other consumers, the information used to generate the consumer’s price, the inferences drawn from that information, or the price that would have been offered had the algorithm possessed different information about the consumer.

The resulting asymmetry is therefore not merely an informational disadvantage. Information asymmetry can produce leverage asymmetry, and leverage asymmetry can produce a wholly unbalanced bargaining relationship.

This distinction is particularly important where personalization identifies circumstances that constrain the consumer’s practical ability to refuse the transaction. An algorithm capable of determining that a consumer faces an emergency, lacks practical substitutes, is subject to severe time pressure, has unusually high switching costs, or otherwise has a diminished ability to walk away can convert those constraints into pricing leverage.

In such circumstances, the price increase does not necessarily reflect an increase in the seller’s cost, scarcity of the good, increased risk, or additional value supplied to the consumer. Instead, the seller may charge more because its informational advantage has revealed that this particular consumer has less bargaining power.

From a human-flourishing perspective, that distinction matters. Markets serve human flourishing in part because voluntary exchange enables individuals to pursue their own purposes, allocate resources according to their own priorities, and choose among competing alternatives. Technology can enhance that function by reducing transaction costs, improving matching, expanding access, and creating new choices.

But technology can also be used for the opposite purpose: identifying the limits of an individual’s practical freedom and monetizing those limits.

The appropriate policy question is therefore not simply whether a price has been personalized. Nor is disclosure necessarily an adequate remedy. The more important question is whether personalization creates value for the transaction or extracts value from an informationally disadvantaged party by identifying and exploiting constraints on that party’s ability to exercise meaningful choice.

A sound enforcement policy should preserve beneficial personalization while recognizing a limiting principle: a firm’s informational superiority should not become a mechanism for systematically converting knowledge of an individual consumer’s diminished bargaining power into economic leverage against that consumer.

The objective is not equality of information or bargaining power in every commercial transaction. Markets have never required such equality. The objective is to prevent technological capabilities from transforming ordinary differences in bargaining position into engineered and systematically exploitable asymmetries.

In that sense, personalized pricing presents an institutional-design problem as much as a consumer-protection problem. The relevant question is whether the rules governing the market preserve sufficient reciprocal uncertainty, meaningful choice, and practical ability to exit for bargaining to remain genuinely voluntary rather than becoming technologically optimized extraction.

I am submitting this comment in response to the Federal Trade Commission's Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing, FTC-2026-1057-0001.

I strongly support the FTC's efforts to address the use of consumers' personal data to determine individualized prices. I urge the Commission to use the fullest extent of its authority to prevent companies from using personal information to determine how much an individual consumer can be charged for the same product or service.

Consumers understand that prices can legitimately change because of supply and demand, location, timing, promotions, or other market conditions. That is fundamentally different from a company collecting or acquiring information about an individual—such as browsing history, purchase history, location, device information, search activity, demographics, or other behavioral data—and using that information to estimate how much that particular person may be willing or able to pay.

I do not believe disclosure alone provides adequate consumer protection.

A notice stating that a price has been personalized still leaves the consumer facing a price potentially derived from information that the consumer never reasonably expected would determine what he or she pays. Consumers should not have to use private browsing, a VPN, multiple devices, logged-out sessions, or other techniques simply to determine whether they are being offered the same price as another customer.

This practice also creates a serious transparency problem. If two consumers receive different prices, they may have no practical way of discovering the difference, determining which personal information produced it, or knowing whether declining tracking or withholding data would have resulted in a lower price. The information imbalance overwhelmingly favors the seller.

I therefore urge the FTC to establish the strongest protections permitted under its existing statutory authority. In particular, the Commission should closely scrutinize—and where legally authorized, prohibit—the use of personal data to increase the price offered to an individual based on an inferred willingness or ability to pay when consumers would reasonably expect the price to be generally available on equal terms.

Any permitted personalized pricing should, at minimum, require meaningful transparency before the consumer is presented with the price. Companies should be required to identify clearly that the price is personalized, what categories of data were used, and whether the consumer can obtain a non-personalized price. These disclosures should be prominent and understandable, not buried in privacy policies, terms of service, or lengthy disclosures.

The FTC should also distinguish personalized discounts that consumers knowingly choose to participate in from systems that covertly determine that a particular consumer can be charged more. A consumer voluntarily using a loyalty program or coupon is materially different from an algorithm silently concluding from personal data that the consumer is unlikely to comparison-shop and can therefore be charged a higher price.

Finally, if the Commission concludes that existing law prevents it from adequately restricting these practices, I encourage the FTC to clearly identify those statutory limitations so that Congress can consider whether additional consumer-protection authority is necessary.

Personal data collected as consumers participate in modern life should not quietly become a mechanism for determining the maximum amount each individual can be persuaded to pay. Consumers deserve a marketplace in which prices are transparent, understandable, and not secretly manipulated according to a company's profile of the person standing behind the screen.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comment:
I strongly support the Federal Trade Commission taking a strong enforcement position against deceptive and unfair uses of personalized or “surveillance” pricing.

Consumers should be able to shop with a basic expectation that the price they see is based on the product, market conditions, and other legitimate factors—not a hidden calculation of how much an algorithm believes that particular person can be persuaded or pressured to pay.

The use of personal information such as browsing history, purchase history, location, demographics, device information, behavioral data, or other consumer-specific information to determine an individualized price creates a significant imbalance between businesses and consumers. Consumers cannot meaningfully compare prices or make informed purchasing decisions when they do not know that the price itself may have been personalized based on surveillance of their behavior.

I encourage the FTC to adopt and vigorously enforce a strong policy in this area.

In particular, the Commission should make clear that simply mentioning personalized pricing somewhere in lengthy terms of service or a privacy policy is not adequate disclosure. If personal information affects the price offered to a consumer, that fact should be disclosed clearly, conspicuously, and at the point where the price is displayed.

Consumers should also be told what categories of information materially influenced the personalized price and, where practicable, be given the ability to purchase the product or service without having their personal data used to personalize the price.

The Commission should pay particular attention to practices that exploit information suggesting urgency, vulnerability, limited alternatives, or a consumer's willingness or ability to pay more. The ability of increasingly sophisticated algorithms and artificial intelligence systems to combine large amounts of consumer data makes strong oversight increasingly important.

There is an important distinction between ordinary dynamic pricing and surveillance pricing. Prices changing because of supply, demand, inventory, time, or broadly applicable promotions are familiar market practices. Secretly charging or offering different prices because a business has developed a profile of an individual consumer raises fundamentally different transparency and consumer-protection concerns.

Enforcement should also address the entire ecosystem. Businesses should not be able to avoid responsibility simply because personalized prices or consumer profiles are generated by a third-party data broker, pricing platform, artificial intelligence system, or other intermediary.

Finally, I encourage the FTC to require meaningful recordkeeping and accountability. Companies using individualized pricing systems should be able to demonstrate what information their systems use, how it affects prices, what consumers are told about the practice, and what safeguards exist to prevent discriminatory, deceptive, or unfair outcomes.

Technology can make markets more efficient, but efficiency should not come at the expense of transparent pricing and informed consumer choice. Consumers should not need to use private browsing, clear cookies, conceal their location, or otherwise disguise themselves simply to determine whether they are being offered a fair price.

I encourage the Commission to adopt a strong final enforcement policy and to use its existing authority aggressively when companies secretly use consumers' personal information to manipulate the prices or offers presented to them.

The use of personal information such as browsing history, purchase history, location, demographics, device information, behavioral data, or other consumer-specific information to determine an individualized price creates a significant imbalance between businesses and consumers. Consumers cannot meaningfully compare prices or make informed purchasing decisions when they do not know that the price itself may have been personalized based on surveillance of their behavior.

I encourage the FTC to adopt and vigorously enforce a strong policy in this area.

In particular, the Commission should make clear that simply mentioning personalized pricing somewhere in lengthy terms of service or a privacy policy is not adequate disclosure. If personal information affects the price offered to a consumer, that fact should be disclosed clearly, conspicuously, and at the point where the price is displayed.

Consumers should also be told what categories of information materially influenced the personalized price and, where practicable, be given the ability to purchase the product or service without having their personal data used to personalize the price.

The Commission should pay particular attention to practices that exploit information suggesting urgency, vulnerability, limited alternatives, or a consumer's willingness or ability to pay more. The ability of increasingly sophisticated algorithms and artificial intelligence systems to combine large amounts of consumer data makes strong oversight increasingly important.

There is an important distinction between ordinary dynamic pricing and surveillance pricing. Prices changing because of supply, demand, inventory, time, or broadly applicable promotions are familiar market practices. Secretly charging or offering different prices because a business has developed a profile of an individual consumer raises fundamentally different transparency and consumer-protection concerns.

Enforcement should also address the entire ecosystem. Businesses should not be able to avoid responsibility simply because personalized prices or consumer profiles are generated by a third-party data broker, pricing platform, artificial intelligence system, or other intermediary.

Finally, I encourage the FTC to require meaningful recordkeeping and accountability. Companies using individualized pricing systems should be able to demonstrate what information their systems use, how it affects prices, what consumers are told about the practice, and what safeguards exist to prevent discriminatory, deceptive, or unfair outcomes.

Technology can make markets more efficient, but efficiency should not come at the expense of transparent pricing and informed consumer choice. Consumers should not need to use private browsing, clear cookies, conceal their location, or otherwise disguise themselves simply to determine whether they are being offered a fair price.

I encourage the Commission to adopt a strong final enforcement policy and to use its existing authority aggressively when companies secretly use consumers' personal information to manipulate the prices or offers presented to them.

comment:
To: Federal Trade Commission

I am adamantly opposed to personalized pricing. This aggressive invasion of privacy hurts consumers takes advantage of people who might be desperate enough to pay much inflated prices and breaks how markets are intended to work. There has been momentum to address this issue, from states banning personalized pricing to a bipartisan Congressional hearing on the topic.

Under Section 5 of the FTC Act, the FTC has the authority to ban personalized pricing. I am asking the FTC to exercise this authority to ban this process as well as to set strong safeguards around personalized discounts. Both of these practices are invasions of the privacy of the people living in the United States of America and block the free market principles of our American economy.

There is another term that could be used to describe personalized pricing. It is called a “shakedown!” To look into an individual’s personal assets and then set pricing based on the amount the seller thinks the buyer is “able” to pay, isn’t that far from finding out someone has ample funds and then “holding an object for sale” hostage to an inflated price! What kind of democracy do we live in if all customers do not have the opportunity to purchase items for sale at the same price? This concept violates Adam Smith’s principle of the invisible hand that is used to justify following the economic principles of capitalism being the most democratic policy in managing free markets in this country. Being allowed to spy on customers and then control their access to pricing based on private information regarding their assets is equivalent in practice to prices set by a monopoly!

Hence, this practice violates not only the rights of privacy provided by our Constitution but also the rights of equal access! It is unfair and undemocratic!

comment:
I am writing to express my opposition to the corporate practice of "commercial surveillance"—specifically, the collection, tracking, and monetization of my personal data to target me with higher, discriminatory pricing. I have personally experienced situations where companies track my browsing history, device type, or location data to increase prices. Instead of a fair, transparent market price, I am charged more simply because an algorithm predicts my maximum willingness or necessity to pay. I specifically noticed higher prices for flights and hotels on my devices than on my husband’s or son’s devices when researching prices for a trip. Using personal profiles to extract maximum profits distorts basic consumer protections. It disproportionately harms individuals who lack the time or digital literacy to bypass tracking systems (such as using VPNs or constantly clearing cookies). This algorithmic optimization treats consumers as data points to be exploited rather than participants in a fair economy.
I strongly urge the Commission to implement strict, binding trade regulation rules that:
1. Prohibit Surveillance Pricing - Forbid companies from using consumer behavioral data, cross-site tracking, or inferred profiles to implement automated dynamic pricing.
2. Enforce Data Minimization - Restrict companies from collecting or retaining any data beyond what is strictly necessary to provide the immediate service requested by the user.
3. Increase Transparency - Require complete algorithmic transparency and an absolute right to opt out of automated decision-making and profile-building.

Thank you for considering my comments as you work to protect consumer privacy and market fairness.

From groceries to gas, the cost of necessities is continuing to skyrocket. During this time of economic stress, you should not have to wonder if companies are using your personal data – from where and when you shop to what you search for online and the type of phone you use – to charge you more than the next shopper for the same goods and services.
The FTC has the authority to ban surveillance pricing. Currently, however, the FTC’s proposed policy would only require companies to disclose that they are doing personalized pricing and the specific types of data used to change the price you see. While it is encouraging that the agency is taking steps to address unfair pricing practices, it should not be on consumers to read detailed disclosures to try and figure out whether companies are trying to charge them more. Historically, the FTC has recognized that disclosure may not be enough. If there’s an unfair practice – they have the power to ban it!

Finally it introduces information asymmetry allowing Amazon, armed with a trove of individual consuner behavior data, to outcompete the local enterprises which Amazon seeks to shutter, which do not have such access.  I encourage the FTC to advocate as is its mandate in the interest of the consumer, not in the interest of data brokers and exploiting firms. Signed, Eric Berlin

comment:
Generally, I think the FTC’s approach is reasonable, and a good start to solving the issue. The primary issue I see with the proposed approach is that it mostly serves the purpose of making people aware of personalized pricing so that they aren’t taken advantage of by businesses. This is a good step. It relies heavily on the FTC Act Section 5, which prohibits unfair or deceptive practices in or affecting commerce, applying this part of the act to businesses creating personalized pricing, trying to ensure that any business who engages in such behavior is transparent about it. While I agree that a line needs to be drawn, I believe the proposed approach draws that line later than it should. An argument could be made that the fact businesses are collecting, storing, and using shopping data against people to begin with is already in violation of the FTC Act in of itself.
There is no question that people being fed personalized prices without being aware of it is a terrible thing that should be avoided, but that isn’t the only issue here. The FTC document does briefly mention the issue inherent to data collection towards the end, but it doesn’t really address it besides mentioning that it might be illegal. Policy wise, it seeks to fix the transparency surrounding data-use for personalized pricing in particular but fails to provide a solution for the more abstract, yet still harmful data collection and profiling that underlies personalized pricing itself. The data-collection, and its usage for the purpose of profiling, already seems to fit into the boundaries set by Section 5 of the FTC Act. Section 5 specifically prohibits unfair or deceptive practices in or affecting commerce. When a person enters some kind of marketplace, whether it be online or offline, they usually purchase something. The current system enables the business to keep a record of that, and all other purchases. They then build profiles of customers using these purchase histories, delving into people’s private lives through a combination of data and inference. A perfect example of this is Target, which began identifying pregnant customers based on purchasing habits and engaged in marketing specifically designed to appeal to those customers. This is very similar to the data-collecting and personalized pricing the FTC seeks to mitigate. It is important to note that people grew very uncomfortable, if not outright angry once they were made aware that Target took their data without their consent and profiled them. Even Target was likely cognizant of how morally questionable its actions were, given that it didn’t openly and immediately reveal what it was doing. This evidently affects commerce by changing the way goods are advertised and distributed. It could also easily fall under the category of “deception,” as Target went out of its way to keep quiet about its actions, using the information it dubiously extracted to inform its marketing strategy, with no one, except itself, knowing about it. I believe this case demonstrates the major hole with the FTC’s approach.
The FTC seems to acknowledge that a company engaging in personalized pricing is committing a wrong by gathering information, building a customer profile, and targeting those customers with tailored prices without being transparent about it. In the aforementioned Target case, Target also committed a wrong by gathering information, building a customer profile, and targeting customers with tailored advertisements, all with zero transparency. The harm in both these cases is overwhelmingly similar. Target engaged in the exact same practices, with the only difference being that Target used information to tailor ads, while the companies at issue here tailor prices specifically. I believe the FTC would agree that both practices are morally questionable at best. Despite this, the FTC’s approach only appears to be focused on personalized pricing by itself, excluding other, comparably harmful consequences of profiling caused by silent data-collection. Instead of drawing a line at that lack of transparency when using information to decide pricing, I propose that the FTC should consider drawing that line at companies conducting untransparent data-collection and using it to profile customers in a more general manner. The use of data to profile customers without their knowledge is a harmful act that deserves to be addressed just as much as the more specific consequences that branch off from it. Doing so would allow the FTC to herd together a significantly larger number of similar cases, better combatting this harm.

comment:
I am concerned about the growing use of consumers’ personal information to determine the prices they are offered.
When I shop for a product or service, I expect the price I see to reflect the product, the market, or other legitimate business factors. I do not expect a company to analyze information about me and determine how much it believes I am personally willing or able to pay.
Consumers should not need to understand complicated algorithms or read pages of fine print to know whether their personal information is affecting the price they are being charged. If personalized pricing is being used, that information should be clearly disclosed before the consumer makes a purchasing decision. Consumers should also be told what types of information were used and why that information affected the price.
I am particularly concerned about the potential impact on people who may already have fewer choices or less financial flexibility. Personal information should not become a tool for determining which consumer can be charged more simply because data suggests that person may be willing, desperate, loyal, or unlikely to shop elsewhere.
I encourage the FTC to establish strong transparency protections so consumers can make informed decisions. Businesses should not be able to describe a personalized price as a special offer or individualized deal without clearly explaining that the consumer’s data played a role in determining that price.
Technology has changed dramatically, but the basic expectation of fairness in the marketplace should remain. Consumers deserve to know when their personal information is being used to influence what they pay.

comment:
Public Comment on Personalized Pricing

I am very concerned about companies using our personal information to determine how much they think we are willing or able to pay for a product or service.

I live in an affluent area, but my personal income does not necessarily reflect the average income of the people who live around me. I don’t believe a company should be able to look at my ZIP code, where I live, my shopping history, browsing history, household information, or other personal data and use that information to decide what price to charge me.

If a company wants to charge $10 for an item, then charge $10. I should not be charged $12 while someone else is charged $10 for the exact same product simply because an algorithm has determined that I may be willing or able to pay more.

Consumers already give companies an enormous amount of information simply by shopping online, using apps, joining loyalty programs, and going about our everyday lives. I don’t believe that information should then be used against us to determine how much more a company might be able to get us to pay.

I understand that prices can legitimately vary because of things like location, shipping costs, supply, or demand. That’s different from secretly using information about an individual consumer to determine how much that particular person will pay.

At the very least, consumers should have the right to know when their personal information is being used to determine the price they are being offered. We should also have the ability to opt out without being penalized for doing so.

Personally, I would like to see stronger protections that prevent companies from secretly using personal information to charge different consumers different prices for the same product or service.

Consumers should be able to look at a product, see the price, and know that’s what the product costs. We shouldn’t have to wonder whether we’re seeing a higher price because of what a company knows or assumes about us.

comment:
To the Federal Trade Commission,

I am commenting to express my support for the FTC's proposed crackdown on personalized, Al-driven surveillance pricing. As a consumer, allowing corporations to weaponize personal data to quietly manipulate prices on shelves or at the checkout is an unacceptable abuse of market power.

The American consumer has already been pushed to the brink by systemic macroeconomic pressures. We’ve endured global supply shortages and sweeping tariffs that drove the baseline cost of groceries through the roof. Even after the tariffs were overturned, we have watched corporate shelf prices fail to come back down. Everyday citizens are the ones paying the price for these massive economic shifts, while corporate entities keep the record margins.

Allowing retailers to layer automated Al pricing algorithms onto this already exhausting cost of living crisis is a direct tax on the public. Traditional coupons and visible loyalty discounts have existed transparently for decades, but surveillance pricing is entirely different. It uses our location tracking, internet browsing history, and inferred financial profiles to silently calculate the absolute maximum price we can tolerate before walking away.

We cannot fix large, systemic issues by allowing corporations to extract maximum profit from the consumers who have the least amount of power to say "NO," and then allow them to claim our non-compliance threatens loyalty programs and couponing. Hyper-personalized, hidden pricing forces families to suffer in silence and destroys the foundation of a free and fair market.

If a corporation cannot maintain fair margins without predatory data surveillance, then they should be forced to raise their visible, uniform sticker prices so the public can see it, react to it, and hold them accountable.

I applaud the Seattle City Council and the states of New Jersey, Maryland, and Connecticut for recently passing bans on grocery surveillance pricing, and I urge the FTC to establish a strict, permanent national framework to protect all Americans from this deceptive practice. Anything other than an outright ban on the practice paves the way for future exploration. Don’t allow that Pandora’s box to be opened. Privacy should not be a luxury good that we must trade away just to afford baseline necessities.

Thank you for your time and for stepping in to protect the public welfare.

Respectfully,
Stephanie Whiddon

comment:
I am deeply concerned about the growing use of personalized pricing because it represents an invasion of consumer privacy and autonomy.

Consumers should not have to wonder whether a company is examining their personal information, shopping behavior, location, browsing history, purchasing history, or other characteristics to determine the maximum price they might be willing to pay. There is a fundamental difference between a price changing because of legitimate market conditions and a company changing an individual's price because it has profiled that individual.

If personalized pricing becomes widespread, I believe it could fundamentally change the way consumers interact with businesses. Instead of making purchases directly, consumers may begin looking for ways to prevent companies from identifying them or associating their personal information with a purchase. One foreseeable response would be the increased use of proxy shoppers, intermediaries, separate accounts, or other purchasing methods designed to prevent a seller from knowing who the actual consumer is.

That outcome should be a warning sign. Consumers should not have to hide their identities or ask someone else to make ordinary purchases on their behalf simply to have confidence that they are being offered a fair price.

The burden should not be placed on consumers to become experts in privacy technology, create multiple identities, use different devices, or find proxy shoppers in order to avoid being economically penalized for information that a company has collected about them.

If a company uses personal information to determine the price offered to an individual, consumers should receive clear and meaningful disclosure before completing the transaction. They should be told that personalization is occurring, what categories of personal information are being used, and the general factors that materially affect the price.

I also encourage the FTC to consider the broader consequences of personalized pricing. Once consumers believe that revealing who they are can cause them to receive a higher price, trust between consumers and businesses can deteriorate. Consumers may reasonably respond by withholding information, avoiding loyalty programs, creating alternative accounts, using intermediaries, or otherwise attempting to prevent companies from building an accurate profile of them.

That is not a healthy direction for the marketplace.

Consumers should be able to shop as themselves without having to assume that transparency about their identity and behavior will be used against them at checkout. Personal information should not quietly become a mechanism for determining how much an individual consumer can be charged.

I urge the Federal Trade Commission to provide strong protections requiring meaningful transparency around personalized pricing and to ensure that consumers are not subjected to undisclosed price discrimination based on personal information.

Thank you for considering my comment.

comment:
I write in strong support of the FTC’s inquiry into surveillance pricing and urge the Commission to implement a complete, proactive ban on individualized dynamic pricing. While the Commission’s recognition of the harms stemming from surveillance pricing is a critical step, mere transparency or disclosure requirements are insufficient to protect the public. The FTC must prohibit this practice outright and impose severe enforcement penalties on corporations that continue to extract unfair margins through personal data tracking.

Individualized surveillance pricing fundamentally undermines the fairness of the consumer marketplace. Under normal market conditions, price reflects value and objective market supply; surveillance pricing severs the connection between the price paid and the value received, turning pricing into an algorithmic attempt to extract the maximum amount of money an individual is deemed capable of paying. This practice is inherently predatory and directly harms ordinary consumers.

Furthermore, individualized pricing provides a dangerous backdoor to unchecked discrimination. Under the veil of proprietary algorithms, machine-learning models can use consumer proxies that replicate or hide illegal bias based on race, religion, sexual orientation, or geographic demographic data. Charging different individuals different rates for identical goods or services is fundamentally unfair and antithetical to competitive market principles.

A system where consumers face unpredictable, personalized markups erodes trust across the economy. Transparency mandates will not resolve the power imbalance; a consumer notified that their price has been adjusted due to surveillance cannot effectively negotiate against automated systems or avoid inflated costs for essential goods and services.

To ensure an equitable and fair marketplace, I urge the Commission to:

* **Enact an explicit ban** on individualized dynamic pricing based on consumer surveillance and personal data.

* **Institute proactive compliance monitoring** across digital marketplaces, platforms, and automated pricing software.

* **Levy severe penalties and fines** against companies deploying algorithmic surveillance tools to price-gouge individual consumers.

Every consumer deserves equal access to transparent, uniform pricing. I urge the FTC to take decisive, enforceable action to eliminate surveillance pricing nationwide.

comment:
While I agree that consumers should be told when their personal information is being used to determine the prices they pay, I am concerned that the Commission’s emphasis on disclosure leaves a much more fundamental problem unresolved. The proposed enforcement policy does not fully address the fact that personalized pricing can, and often will (in my view), be unfair and detrimental to the consumer, even when the consumer has the opportunity for full disclosure of the practice. Quantifying harm by using financial benefit/cost is an easy and measurable metric, while the harm to consumer autonomy at scale is more difficult to measure. And yet, I would argue it is the more critical issue. It is possible, if not likely (with the way the market is evolving), that a person may fully understand what a commercial entity is doing with their data, and nonetheless be powerless to refuse or choose alternatives.

I also have concerns that determining what counts as proper disclosure will be challenging. Disclosing to a potential customer that their data/shopping patterns are being monitored and analyzed to provide them with a unique price may not convey the full picture to the customer, e.g., that their price is increased or decreased relative to the average customer. Corporate marketing and legal teams spend hours behind closed doors trying to develop the ideal way to communicate with customers, where the focus is on profit, and not customer understanding. I could very easily see a company creating a disclosure statement that technically gives notice to a consumer, while construing the process in a manner that unfairly causes the consumer to think they are receiving only a benefit from the process.

Adopting a default position of neutrality on the issue risks allowing further predatory business practices, and forcing consumers to bear the burden of both the costs of these practices and raising the issue through slow enforcement mechanisms. Even a full and accurate disclosure cannot create an alternative that the market does not offer. For example, if all reasonably accessible grocery stores in a low-income community make affordable prices conditioned on participation in personalized pricing programs, consumers may understand the arrangement, object to it, but still be compelled to participate because of necessity if they cannot afford the alternative (or if one is not available). In such a situation, consumer acquiescence to a pricing program is a product of financial necessity, and should not be considered acceptance of the underlying practice.

comment:
In its statement on proposed personalized pricing, the Federal Trade Commission described several "non-exhaustive examples of scenarios without adequate disclosure.” One of the examples involved a “hotel charging a higher price to a consumer on the basis of data personal to that consumer leading the hotel to believe that the consumer is traveling for a funeral or some other can’t-miss personal business. This example reminded me of something I encountered when I was buying tickets to fly to Boston, Massachusetts for fall break. In the course of buying tickets, I checked multiple websites to compare prices over the span of a few days. This process led me to visit the same website more times than I normally would when purchasing an item or goods. Every time I returned to one of the websites, it seemed that the prices had gone up. Based on my recollection, I do not believe that any of the airline websites provided any kind of disclosure notice in terms of utilizing my data for personalized pricing. I was confused by this increase in pricing and wondered if this was personalized pricing or simply an increase in demand. As a consumer, I could argue that the airlines were using my personal data to determine that I intended to travel to Boston during a specific day and time and using my repeated searches to learn insights into my purchasing habits and willingness to buy a ticket. However, from the airline’s perspective, I could argue that the price increases were unrelated to my personal browning activity and instead reflected broader changes in demand for those flights over several days that I searched. Would the Federal Trade Commission consider this a deceptive or unfair personalized pricing practice? Is this experience similar to the example of the hotel that the Federal Trade Commission described? Or is it simply supply and demand?
Another question I would pose to the Federal Trade Commission is how do sales and discounts factor into personalized pricing. Specifically, how can we ensure that an item or good is actually on sale rather than that a company is creating the illusion of a discount based on my personal data and spending habits. For example, as a shopper, I might not be inclined to buy an item that is regularly prices at $20. However, if I see that the same item advertised as normally costing $30 or $40 but currently on sale for $20, I may be more inclined to purchase it because I believe I am getting a good deal. Could a company’s use of personal data to determine not only the price I see but also the discount presented to me fall within the Federal Trade Commission’s concerns about personalized pricing?

comment:
Part of the Commission’s argument is that the higher price paid by consumers is unfair because the benefits to consumers and competition do not outweigh the potential for substantial injury and unavoidable issues arising from its opaqueness. They argue this is because those benefits could be conferred without concealing the fact and nature of personalized pricing. However, I believe that this argument fails to properly address the unique benefits that non-disclosure could offer, particularly when it comes to offering services at temporarily or permanently discounted prices to users in need.
Consider this counterfactual to one of the scenarios presented as raising Section 5 concerns: If, instead of raising the price of food delivery for consumers they believe are less likely or unable to leave their homes, the delivery company chooses to lower it based on that hidden data. The company may decide to do this because they believe that the long-term profits from a reliable user outweigh those that could be gained by squeezing them for as much as possible in the short term. This trade of reduced profits for more guaranteed business shows that personalized pricing can be a win-win, but disclosure can disincentivize companies from making these offers at all. The main benefit of non-disclosure allows personalized pricing with no strings attached.
If a company is forced not only to label when personalized pricing is in effect but also to list the parameters on which it is based, it establishes consumer expectations, which can have significant consequences for the company. For example, in the food delivery scenario, the key question is how the company determines when a consumer is unlikely to leave their home frequently. Are they using GPS data? Is it based on information that correlates with certain disabilities? Is income taken into account? Is it merely the frequency of orders? Regardless, the moment they have to disclose the factors they consider when determining whether a person is eligible for a personalized price reduction will expose them to a variety of liabilities and a far higher degree of scrutiny.
There are likely to be significant disputes from consumers who believe they meet a sufficient number of the eligibility requirements. There are also likely to be consumers who actively attempt to game those factors to get a lower price, such as leaving a phone at home all day to use GPS data, googling specific things, etc. Lastly, it also exposes them to significant criticism and public controversy over how they use their internal data to make business decisions. For all these reasons, it seems likely that the prudent decision for any business would be to avoid personalized pricing altogether. Despite the fact that it could have greatly benefited classes of people who they know would make more frequent use of their services if there was a price reduction, such as people with severe physical disabilities using delivery services.
Even if they choose to implement these sorts of measures, there are still other issues raised by even simple disclosure. For example, to prevent disputes and scrutiny, companies may choose to rely on a single, simple data point they can cite. Imagine the food delivery company still wants to reduce prices for those who are unlikely to leave their homes. Under public scrutiny, they may require medical documentation to verify a person’s mobility issues. This would force a person to disclose more sensitive data to the company, which otherwise could have been inferred from a larger number of data points, a possibility they may avoid due to the scrutiny placed on their calculations. It would also force people to obtain clear documentation, which is a frequent difficulty for many people with disabilities, including myself. Imagine someone who is bedridden with chronic pain. Due to the often underrecognized nature of their disability, they would have a much harder time getting the kind of documentation to prove a fact that otherwise could have been inferred, and thus would be barred from a beneficial price reduction. Lastly, a company having to disclose that it uses personalized pricing creates a persistent specter of unfair price increases, even if it is only using it to lower prices to what consumers can pay. If consumers are given the option to turn it off, most would likely choose to do so despite any potential benefits; if that is not an option, they may simply avoid the business entirely, which could hurt competitive upstarts attempting to use it for growth.
All of this is not to say that the Commission’s concerns over personalized pricing are not legitimate; they are. However, it is at the very least worth considering that there are unique benefits to the non-disclosure of these systems. Those benefits need to be considered and rebutted to make the strongest possible argument against personalized pricing.

comment:
I have to disagree with the policy statement’s immediate conclusion that Congress has not provided the Federal Trade Commission the authority to prohibit personalized pricing in all circumstances. I am also unimpressed with the idea that the proper remedy for deceptive or unfair personalized pricing practices under Section 5 of the FTC Act is to require disclosure of the practice. Based on my own study, this policy statement is a circuitous argument for what is a very clear antitrust conclusion: using personal data collection to set prices for individuals is illegal horizontal price fixing. Monopolists use price-fixing to maximize their returns, and they do so to avoid having to exert the effort to create efficiencies, which a free market would require of them. In Addyston Pipe and Steel Co. v. United State (US 1897), naked price-fixing was effected through territorial divisions that a cartel used to arbitrarily fix prices and defeat competition among members in geographic territories created by competitors.

The modern issue here is that corporations may go beyond creating territorial divisions and instead divide individuals based on data that has been collected. Rather than fix prices based off of what people in one territory may be expected to pay, one of the three evils may now be easily created by singling out citizens based on their income, age, sex, job status, career, or any other status useful to a corporation. A system in which this data may be used can also lend itself to collaboration amongst competing corporations to set prices for one individual through the creation of formal or informal cartels. For example, as offered by the FTC, Target and Wal-Mart may agree to set the price of milk for Rebecca at $5 dollars per gallon based on her having three children, while Michael may have to pay $4 because he has only two children. They will encounter these prices at every Target or Wal-Mart store they purchase from in-person or online. The FTC has acknowledged this possibility but has identified the problem as being one of disclosure under the FTC Act.

Federal courts have never held horizontal price-fixing to be fair simply because it has been disclosed. The operative language in the FTC Act here should be that the individual price-fixing is “unfair,” not that it is creating harm through its not having been “disclosed” to consumers. Although individual price-fixing may not be a traditional form of per se anti-competitive conduct, the holding in Polygram Holding, Inc. v. FTC (D.C. Cir. 2005) makes clear that the FTC wields the power to identify new restraints that resemble old ones and act according as economic conditions change. Undoubtedly, economic conditions are changing with the advent of data farming. The FTC should not shy away from its duties with weak disclosure requirements; it must use its long-held power to prevent naked price-fixing.

Personalized pricing hurts consumers, takes advantage of people who might be desperate enough to pay much inflated prices, and breaks how markets are intended to work. There has been momentum to address this issue, from states banning personalized pricing to a bipartisan Congressional hearing on the topic.

Under Section 5 of the FTC Act, the FTC has the authority to ban personalized pricing. While it is encouraging that the agency is taking steps to address unfair pricing practices, it should not be on consumers to read detailed disclosures to try and figure out whether companies are trying to charge them more. Historically, the FTC has recognized that disclosure may not be enough. If there’s an unfair practice – the FTC has the power to ban it! In addition to banning personalized pricing, we are calling on you to set strong safeguards around personalized discounts.
