comment:
Comment Opposing Surveillance Pricing — Docket No. FTC-2026-1057

Federal Trade Commission
Office of the Secretary

Dear Commissioners:

I am writing to urge the Federal Trade Commission to take strong action against surveillance pricing and other forms of personalized pricing that use consumers’ personal information to determine the prices they are shown.

Consumers should not be charged more because a company has analyzed their browsing history, location, purchase history, demographics, device information, mouse movements, loyalty-program activity, or other behavioral data. A price based on supply, demand, inventory, or a clearly disclosed discount is fundamentally different from a price secretly adjusted according to what an algorithm believes a particular person is willing to pay.

Surveillance pricing harms consumers in several ways:

It makes prices opaque and prevents consumers from knowing whether they are being treated fairly.
It can cause people with fewer resources, less technical knowledge, or limited ability to comparison-shop to pay more.
It creates serious risks of discrimination based on sensitive or inferred characteristics.
It undermines meaningful competition because consumers cannot accurately compare prices.
It encourages companies to collect excessive personal information unrelated to providing the product or service.
It is especially troubling when applied to essential goods and services, including groceries, housing, transportation, health care, utilities, and financial products.
I urge the Commission to make clear that businesses should not use personal data to set or vary an individual consumer’s price unless they provide prominent, understandable, and timely disclosure before purchase. That disclosure should identify:

That the price has been personalized;
The categories of data used;
Whether sensitive or inferred characteristics were considered;
How the data affected the price;
Whether the same product is offered at different prices to other consumers; and
How consumers can opt out and obtain a non-personalized price.
Disclosure alone may not be sufficient in high-risk circumstances. The FTC should also prohibit personalized pricing based on sensitive personal information, protected characteristics, precise location, health information, financial hardship, browsing activity involving sensitive topics, or data obtained without meaningful consent. Companies should not be permitted to evade these protections by using data brokers, inferences, proxies, or third-party pricing platforms.

The Commission should also require companies engaged in algorithmic pricing to maintain records sufficient to demonstrate that their systems are lawful, accurate, nondiscriminatory, and subject to human oversight. Businesses should be prohibited from misrepresenting prices as standard, fixed, or generally available when prices are actually individualized.

The use of personal data to secretly determine what each consumer can be charged is unfair and deceptive. I support vigorous enforcement under the FTC Act and urge the Commission to adopt the strongest possible policy statement, pursue enforcement against undisclosed personalized pricing, and work with Congress and state authorities to establish clear nationwide protections.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Sincerely,
DeWitt S. Goulbourne
Yucaipa, California

comment: I am a private citizen who just happened to be a volunteer for the Consumer Reports team investigating personalized pricing earlier this year.  I am not an employee of CR, nor did I receive any compensation for my participation.   I just saw an email asking for volunteers and, curious, I signed up for it.  My two or three cents on this whole data driven pricing issue is this:  Data should not be used to characterize customers with the intention of charging a customer a higher price based on this data.  All customers walking into a store should expect to pay the price displayed on the item or shelf.  Customers making a purchase online should not be charged higher prices based on any data the seller may have on a customer.  End of story.  Meanwhile, I have seen news articles where at least one major retailer (Safeway, I believe) may have threatened to cancel its customer loyalty program and associated data collection processes over this proposed enforcement policy. comment:
"Surveillance Pricing" is a weapon deployed against consumers. It uses data obtained or inferred (often without affirmative consent, and often highly inaccurate) about consumers' habits, income, family structure, health and medical needs, and countless other data points that no one other than the consumer should have access to. Some stores (such as Kroeger) now require customers to assent to being monitored in stores including how long they are in a particular aisle, which products they touch and which may be place in their basket; allowing them to compile a profile (dossier) of any information they can obtain through any means; even what other apps are present on their personal devices and whatever statistics or utilization information their app can get access to.

Consumer information must be 100% under the consumer's control, and not used for any purpose the consumer does not affirmatively consent to. Discount card programs are intrusive enough, but being forced into agreeing to a merchant's acquisition of all manner of personal information and not only to set pricing at the shelf because they think you meet certain demographic criteria is extreme overreach. Retailers and other collectors of consumer information must be required to fully disclose their use of that information, including who they make the information available to. Consumers must be able to review, revise, or fully remove their information. Those willing to share information must have the ability to restrict every use or access category. Consumer directives must be honored in perpetuity or unless consumer makes specific changes. Consumers shall not be "punished" with higher prices or denied service for declining to share information. All existing "add-on" profile data must be deleted and profiles rebuilt with customer direction. Any undisclosed or unapproved use of information shall have a meaningful financial penalty to the business(es) involved, including meaningful financial restitution to harmed consumer(s).

comment: I support the FTC’s efforts to address personalized pricing, but I believe the Commission and Congress should go further. Personalized pricing should not merely require disclosure; it should be prohibited in markets where consumers have traditionally been offered the same price for the same product or service. More broadly, I believe variable pricing practices that allow businesses to charge consumers different prices for substantially identical goods or services based on demand, location, browsing behavior, personal data, or perceived willingness or urgency to pay deserve much stronger restrictions. Consumers should be able to make purchasing decisions with confidence that the price presented to them is not being manipulated because an algorithm has determined that they are willing, able, or desperate enough to pay more. Businesses should retain the ability to adjust generally advertised prices when legitimate costs or market conditions change, but those changes should apply consistently to similarly situated consumers rather than being tailored to extract the maximum possible amount from each individual. Disclosure is an important first step, but transparency alone does not eliminate the underlying harm. Consumers should not have to use private browsing, VPNs, multiple accounts, or other methods simply to determine whether they are being offered the same price as everyone else.

comment:
In a traditional market, price serves as a signal of value and competition. When prices are personalized, that signal is destroyed. Buyers can no longer determine if they are receiving a market price or if the price they see is based on their browsing history, device type, or demographic data. This prevents consumers from making informed decisions and undermines the efficiency of the marketplace.

Moreover, the shift toward personalized pricing encourages an invasive cycle of data collection. To refine their pricing models, companies are incentivized to collect increasingly detailed and intimate data on consumer behavior, further eroding privacy.

I urge the Commission to establish a policy that prioritizes price transparency and prohibits the use of personal data to engage in discriminatory pricing. Competition should be driven by firms offering better products or lower prices to all.

At the very least, FTC regulations should require companies using personalized pricing to prominently display that they do so, and not be allowed to bury the disclosure in fine-print terms that are seldom read.

comment:
Re: Docket No. FTC-2026-1057, Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing

Submitted by: Matt Vegas, Founder, LSAS Platform

I build runtime governance infrastructure for AI agents — the software layer that decides what an AI agent is allowed to do before it acts, and keeps a tamper-evident record of what it did. I write in support of the Commission's disclosure framework, and to flag a gap that will swallow it: disclosure only works if someone can later prove what was disclosed, to whom, and under whose authority.

Three points from practice:

1. Agentic commerce breaks the disclosure model. The draft statement assumes a human consumer sees the price. Increasingly, an AI shopping agent sees it instead — authorized by the consumer to transact within limits the consumer never wrote down. "Clear and conspicuous disclosure to the consumer" is meaningless if the only party that saw the price was software. The Commission should clarify that when a transaction is agent-mediated, the disclosure obligation attaches to a record the consumer (or their auditor) can inspect after the fact.

2. Require the record, not just the disclosure. A workable rule needs four fields per transaction: what authority the agent was granted, what price and terms were presented, what the agent accepted, and a tamper-evident record binding all three together. Six global banks just published a paper calling for exactly this kind of auditable trail for AI shopping agents. The industry is asking for the standard; the Commission can set it.

3. Post-hoc logs are not enough. A log written after the fact, by the same system that set the price, proves nothing. The authority check has to happen before execution, and the record has to be tamper-evident by construction — otherwise enforcement will be arguing about whose database to believe.

Disclosure without proof is a promise. The Commission should require both.

comment:
While I believe the policy itself is noble in its intentions, I would also like to highlight a related personalized pricing practice that may be overlooked. In my previous job, I traveled frequently for work and regularly needed to book last minute flights. Because these trips were often arranged on short notice (and because I would have to place these flights on my personal card before being reimbursed) finding an affordable and convenient flight was an important part of the booking process.

My first step in finding a flight was usually to a search engine, most often Google, and type something like “flight from DC to . . .” followed by the city I needed to visit. Like many consumers, I assumed that the results presented through these search engines would give me a reasonably complete picture of the flights available and their prices. I also generally expected that the flights appearing as the cheapest option would accurately represent the most affordable available.

However, I have noticed that the flights displayed first are not always the least expensive options available. When I have conducted the same search through a dedicated travel website I can sometimes find cheaper flights that fail to appear as a result from the search engine. This has made me wonder how search engines determine which flights consumers see first and whether consumers have enough information to understand how those results are organized. I am not sure what the term would be for failing to accurately represent the prices of a third party, but I fear how this technology could be applied across other products that people search for.

Similarly to the prioritized pricing schemes being targeted by the FTC these systems seem to take advantage of people who are busy and have less time to cross-reference pricing with other sources. Consumers may not understand which factors are influencing what they see. Someone who conducts a basic search for a flight may reasonably assume that the results appearing at the top are the cheapest, most relevant, or otherwise best options available. If that is not the case, consumers may end up paying more simply because they do not realize that alternatives are available elsewhere.

I believe this issue is worth considering alongside other policies designed to increase the transparency of how things are priced. The way search engines and other intermediaries display pricing can play a significant role in shaping what consumers consider and ultimately purchase. Especially in this day and age where affiliate links are so prevalent. Greater transparency could help consumers better understand the options presented to them and help them make more informed purchasing decisions.

comment:
Under 15 U.S.C. § 45(n), an act is unfair if it causes substantial injury not reasonably avoidable by consumers and not outweighed by countervailing benefits.

A. Substantial Injury
Personal data pricing systematically expropriates 100% of consumer surplus, transforming competitive market exchange into personalized rent extraction. When applied to essential items, urgent travel, or life circumstances (e.g., higher rideshare prices for medical emergencies or funeral travel), it functions as algorithmic price gouging. In trading, it should equally establishes substantial injury. When every consumer sees a unique, ephemeral price generated in real time via proprietary software algorithms, comparison shopping breaks down across the market, creating market friction that suppresses competition. The data exploitation and personalized pricing is within the FTC's core, historic mandate of commercial fraud, extortionate pricing under duress, and consumer data protection, avoiding broad macroeconomic management claims.

B. Inability to Reasonably Avoid Injury
In concentrated digital markets or urgent purchase scenarios, disclosure gives consumers no choice. A consumer who needs an emergency rideshare or essential groceries cannot "shop around" when pricing algorithms instantaneously price-discriminate across platforms. Knowing that you are being exploited does not allow you to avoid the exploitation.
Unlike dynamic pricing based on macro supply and demand (which allocates scarce resources, such as peak-hour tolling), individual price discrimination based on personal surveillance generates no new market supply or consumer efficiency. It is a zero-sum transfer of wealth from consumers to digital intermediaries.

C. Absence of Countervailing Consumer or Competitive Utility
Unlike macro-environmental dynamic pricing (e.g., peak-hour tolling or seasonal lodging adjustments), which allocates scarce physical inventory based on aggregate demand, setting individualized prices based on private behavioral data creates no new market supply, expands no output, and offers no consumer efficiency. It is a zero-sum transfer of wealth from consumers to platform sellers, generating significant deadweight loss across the digital economy.

D. Third-Party Algorithmic Intermediation
Retailers frequently deploy third-party black-box pricing APIs, claiming ignorance of the underlying optimization mechanics. Establishing a direct regulatory prohibition on commercial pricing engines ingesting user-level behavioral data places liability on both the software vendor and the retail platform, preventing regulatory arbitrage.

Under the FTC’s standalone UMC authority (15 U.S.C. § 45), the Commission can prohibit practices that undermine the competitive process:
- Surveillance pricing destroys market-wide price discovery. In a functioning market, posted prices allow consumers to discipline sellers through comparison shopping.
- Banning the ingest of user-level, device-level, or behavioral data into price-setting models provides an objective evidentiary standard for enforcement audits.
- When every consumer sees a unique, ephemeral price generated in real time via proprietary software algorithms, comparison shopping breaks down across the market, creating market friction that suppresses competition.

The Commission is recommended a Trade Regulation Rule under Section 18 featuring the following core operative provisions:
1 Prohibited Act: It shall be an unfair act or practice and an unfair method of competition for any person, partnership, or corporation to set, adjust, or alter the price, fee, or discount offered to an individual consumer based, in whole or in part, on user-level personal data, behavioral history, location telemetry, device characteristics, or derivative willingness-to-pay profiles.
2 Permissible Pricing Systems: Nothing in this Rule shall prohibit dynamic pricing based solely on real-time aggregate market demand, total available inventory, uniform regional supply metrics, or broadly published, non-targeted promotional discounts.
3 Audit and Compliance Standard: Regulated entities deploying automated pricing software must maintain technical documentation demonstrating that price-setting algorithms are structurally isolated from user-level, device-level, and behavioral data pipelines.
